steps.title: 소비 습관
steps.scene_desc: 12월 첫 토요일 오후, 동네 마트 통로. 천장에 연말 세일 현수막(글자 없이 색 띠와 별 모양만)이 걸려 있고, 클로이가 물건이 가득 찬 휴대폰 속 장바구니 화면(글자 없이)을 지우에게 보여 주며 웃음. 지우는 샐러드 채소와 쿠키 상자가 든 장바구니를 들고 고개를 갸웃함. 진열대에 상품(글자·상표 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "The thing is, …" (소비 습관). Goal: 행동 뒤의 이유를 분석하기. Today's scene: 12월 첫 토요일 오후, 동네 마트 통로. 천장에 연말 세일 현수막(글자 없이 색 띠와 별 모양만)이 걸려 있고, 클로이가 물건이 가득 찬 휴대폰 속 장바구니 화면(글자 없이)을 지우에게 보여 주며 웃음. 지우는 샐러드 채소와 쿠키 상자가 든 장바구니를 들고 고개를 갸웃함. 진열대에 상품(글자·상표 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "The thing is, ___.".

steps.when: 겉으로 드러난 말 뒤의 *진짜 이유·문제*를 꺼내요. 말할 때는 쉼표 뒤에서 잠깐 쉬어요.
steps.extra: I love sales. The thing is, I don’t need most of it.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "The thing is, ___." (사실 문제는 ~예요. 중요한 건 ~예요.). When to use it: 겉으로 드러난 말 뒤의 진짜 이유·문제를 꺼내요. 말할 때는 쉼표 뒤에서 잠깐 쉬어요. Note: I love sales. The thing is, I don’t need most of it.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "We’re constantly told that ___.".

steps.when: 광고·사회가 되풀이하는 메시지를 짚어요. *be told* = (남에게서) 듣다.
steps.extra: We’re constantly told that we need the newest phone.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "We’re constantly told that ___." (우리는 늘 ~라는 말을 들어요.). When to use it: 광고·사회가 되풀이하는 메시지를 짚어요. be told = (남에게서) 듣다. Note: We’re constantly told that we need the newest phone.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s less about ___ and more about ___.".

steps.en: It’s less about ___ and more about ___.
steps.when: 겉보기 이유에서 *진짜 초점*으로 옮겨 가요. 두 자리에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: It’s less about the price and more about the feeling.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s less about ___ and more about ___." (~보다는 ~의 문제예요.). When to use it: 겉보기 이유에서 진짜 초점으로 옮겨 가요. 두 자리에는 명사나 -ing. Note: It’s less about the price and more about the feeling.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Year-End Sale · 12월 첫 토요일 오후, 동네 마트에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Year-End Sale · 12월 첫 토요일 오후, 동네 마트에서

lines.en: Ooh, look! “Year-end sale. Buy two, get one free.” Maybe I should take the lot.
lines.ko: 우와, 봐요! ‘연말 세일, 두 개 사면 하나 더.’ 몽땅 사 버릴까 봐요.

lines.en: For one dinner? We only need salad greens and cookies.
lines.ko: 저녁 한 끼에요? 샐러드 채소랑 쿠키만 있으면 돼요.

lines.en: True. And look at my online shopping cart. Forty-two items!
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그리고 제 온라인 장바구니 좀 봐요. 마흔두 개예요!

lines.en: Forty-two? Are you going to buy all of them?
lines.ko: 마흔두 개요? 그걸 다 살 거예요?

lines.en: Probably not. {{The thing is,}} the ads follow me everywhere. {{We’re constantly told that}} one more thing will make life easier.
lines.ko: 아마 아닐 거예요. 문제는 광고가 어디든 따라온다는 거예요. 하나만 더 있으면 삶이 편해진다고 늘 듣잖아요.

lines.en: I know. That’s why I try to wait a week before buying. Usually, I don’t want it anymore.
lines.ko: 알아요. 그래서 저는 사기 전에 일주일 기다려 봐요. 보통은 더 이상 갖고 싶지 않더라고요.

lines.en: A week? I’d forget what I wanted! But last month my closet was full of things I’d never used. Some still had tags on.
lines.ko: 일주일이요? 뭘 원했는지 잊어버릴 거예요! 그런데 지난달 보니 옷장에 안 쓴 물건이 가득했어요. 가격표 붙은 것도요.

lines.en: So why do you think you bought them?
lines.ko: 그럼 그걸 왜 샀다고 생각해요?

lines.en: Honestly? {{It’s less about}} the things {{and more about}} the moment I click “buy.” It’s retail therapy.
lines.ko: 솔직히요? 물건보다는 ‘구매’를 누르는 그 순간의 문제예요. 기분 전환 쇼핑이죠.

lines.en: Buying things feels good for a moment. But clutter weighs you down. I feel calmer with less.
lines.ko: 물건을 사면 잠깐은 기분이 좋죠. 그래도 잡동사니는 사람을 짓눌러요. 저는 물건이 적을 때 더 편해요.

lines.en: Nice “clutter”! That soft “t” sounded so natural. But minimalism has become a trend itself. People show off “minimal” hauls.
lines.ko: clutter 좋았어요! 부드러운 t 소리가 자연스러웠어요. 그런데 미니멀리즘도 유행이 됐어요. ‘미니멀한’ 쇼핑을 자랑하잖아요.

lines.en: True. Maybe we also buy to fit in.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 남들과 어울리려고 사는 것도 있는 것 같아요.

lines.en: Fair enough. OK, I’m emptying this cart. Well, most of it.
lines.ko: 그렇네요. 좋아요, 이 장바구니 비울게요. 음, 거의 다요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Year-End Sale · 12월 첫 토요일 오후, 동네 마트에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Ooh, look! “Year-end sale. Buy two, get one free.” Maybe I should take the lot." (우와, 봐요! ‘연말 세일, 두 개 사면 하나 더.’ 몽땅 사 버릴까 봐요.)
2. Jiwoo: "For one dinner? We only need salad greens and cookies." (저녁 한 끼에요? 샐러드 채소랑 쿠키만 있으면 돼요.)
3. Chloe: "True. And look at my online shopping cart. Forty-two items!" (맞아요. 그리고 제 온라인 장바구니 좀 봐요. 마흔두 개예요!)
4. Jiwoo: "Forty-two? Are you going to buy all of them?" (마흔두 개요? 그걸 다 살 거예요?)
5. Chloe: "Probably not. The thing is, the ads follow me everywhere. We’re constantly told that one more thing will make life easier." (아마 아닐 거예요. 문제는 광고가 어디든 따라온다는 거예요. 하나만 더 있으면 삶이 편해진다고 늘 듣잖아요.)
6. Jiwoo: "I know. That’s why I try to wait a week before buying. Usually, I don’t want it anymore." (알아요. 그래서 저는 사기 전에 일주일 기다려 봐요. 보통은 더 이상 갖고 싶지 않더라고요.)
7. Chloe: "A week? I’d forget what I wanted! But last month my closet was full of things I’d never used. Some still had tags on." (일주일이요? 뭘 원했는지 잊어버릴 거예요! 그런데 지난달 보니 옷장에 안 쓴 물건이 가득했어요. 가격표 붙은 것도요.)
8. Jiwoo: "So why do you think you bought them?" (그럼 그걸 왜 샀다고 생각해요?)
9. Chloe: "Honestly? It’s less about the things and more about the moment I click “buy.” It’s retail therapy." (솔직히요? 물건보다는 ‘구매’를 누르는 그 순간의 문제예요. 기분 전환 쇼핑이죠.)
10. Jiwoo: "Buying things feels good for a moment. But clutter weighs you down. I feel calmer with less." (물건을 사면 잠깐은 기분이 좋죠. 그래도 잡동사니는 사람을 짓눌러요. 저는 물건이 적을 때 더 편해요.)
11. Chloe: "Nice “clutter”! That soft “t” sounded so natural. But minimalism has become a trend itself. People show off “minimal” hauls." (clutter 좋았어요! 부드러운 t 소리가 자연스러웠어요. 그런데 미니멀리즘도 유행이 됐어요. ‘미니멀한’ 쇼핑을 자랑하잖아요.)
12. Jiwoo: "True. Maybe we also buy to fit in." (맞아요. 남들과 어울리려고 사는 것도 있는 것 같아요.)
13. Chloe: "Fair enough. OK, I’m emptying this cart. Well, most of it." (그렇네요. 좋아요, 이 장바구니 비울게요. 음, 거의 다요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

7. Chloe: "A week? I’d forget what I wanted! But last month my closet was full of things I’d never used. Some still had tags on." (일주일이요? 뭘 원했는지 잊어버릴 거예요! 그런데 지난달 보니 옷장에 안 쓴 물건이 가득했어요. 가격표 붙은 것도요.)
8. Jiwoo: "So why do you think you bought them?" (그럼 그걸 왜 샀다고 생각해요?)
9. Chloe: "Honestly? It’s less about the things and more about the moment I click “buy.” It’s retail therapy." (솔직히요? 물건보다는 ‘구매’를 누르는 그 순간의 문제예요. 기분 전환 쇼핑이죠.)
10. Jiwoo: "Buying things feels good for a moment. But clutter weighs you down. I feel calmer with less." (물건을 사면 잠깐은 기분이 좋죠. 그래도 잡동사니는 사람을 짓눌러요. 저는 물건이 적을 때 더 편해요.)
11. Chloe: "Nice “clutter”! That soft “t” sounded so natural. But minimalism has become a trend itself. People show off “minimal” hauls." (clutter 좋았어요! 부드러운 t 소리가 자연스러웠어요. 그런데 미니멀리즘도 유행이 됐어요. ‘미니멀한’ 쇼핑을 자랑하잖아요.)
12. Jiwoo: "True. Maybe we also buy to fit in." (맞아요. 남들과 어울리려고 사는 것도 있는 것 같아요.)
13. Chloe: "Fair enough. OK, I’m emptying this cart. Well, most of it." (그렇네요. 좋아요, 이 장바구니 비울게요. 음, 거의 다요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It’s less about ___ and more about ___.
head: The thing is, …
It’s less about …
and more about …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: The thing is, ___. / It’s less about ___ and more about ___. Table (The thing is, … → It’s less about …):
- I rarely use it. → the coffee machine
- sales are hard to resist. → the discount
- all my friends have one. → the bag
- I was tired that day. → the shoes
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I love sales. *The thing is,* I don’t need most of it. 세일이 좋아요. 문제는 대부분 필요 없다는 거예요. 
앞말을 인정한 뒤 진짜 문제를 꺼내요. 글에서는 *The thing is that …*도 써요.
It’s less about A and more about B

It’s *less about* the price *and more about* the feeling. 가격보다는 기분의 문제예요. 
A·B는 같은 꼴로: 명사 + 명사, less about buying and more about having(-ing + -ing)
errors: We’re constantly tell that we need it.
We’re constantly told that we need it.
clutter는 셀 수 없는 명사(단수 취급)라 *weighs*.
I wait a week before buy.
I wait a week before buying.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- The thing is, … — 진짜 이유·문제: I love sales. The thing is, I don’t need most of it. 세일이 좋아요. 문제는 대부분 필요 없다는 거예요. / 앞말을 인정한 뒤 진짜 문제를 꺼내요. 글에서는 The thing is that …도 써요.
- It’s less about A and more about B: It’s less about the price and more about the feeling. 가격보다는 기분의 문제예요. / A·B는 같은 꼴로: 명사 + 명사, less about buying and more about having(-ing + -ing)
Common mistakes on screen:
- We’re constantly tell that we need it. → We’re constantly told that we need it. (남에게서 듣는 거라 be + told.)
- Clutter weigh you down. → Clutter weighs you down. (clutter는 셀 수 없는 명사(단수 취급)라 weighs.)
- I wait a week before buy. → I wait a week before buying. (before 뒤에 동사가 오면 -ing.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) the price / the feeling → A: Why did you buy it? B: The thing is, it’s less about the price and more about the feeling.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) the price / the feeling → A: Why did you buy it? B: The thing is, it’s less about the price and more about the feeling. Items (situation → model answer): the price → the feeling | the shoes → fitting in | the discount → the excitement | the stuff → the habit.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: It’s less about ___ and more about ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "The thing is, …" (소비 습관); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "The thing is, ___." / "We’re constantly told that ___." / "It’s less about ___ and more about ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Ads create needs we didn’t have.
Buying things feels good for a moment.

사기 전에 일주일 기다려 보려고 해요.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 왜 살까: "Ads create needs we didn’t have." (광고가 없던 필요를 만들어 내요., 보통); "Online shopping is too easy." (온라인 쇼핑은 너무 쉬워요., 보통); "Buying things feels good for a moment." (물건을 사면 잠깐은 기분이 좋아요., 보통); "We buy to fit in." (우리는 남들과 어울리려고 사요., 보통); "It’s retail therapy." (기분 전환 쇼핑이에요., 친근)
- 덜 사기에 대해: "I try to wait a week before buying." (사기 전에 일주일 기다려 보려고 해요., 보통); "Clutter weighs you down." (잡동사니는 사람을 짓눌러요., 보통); "Less is more." (적을수록 더 좋아요., 친근)
- 다른 쪽 시선: "Minimalism has become a trend itself." (미니멀리즘도 그 자체로 유행이 됐어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 낱말 가족과 덩어리 표현

*consume* 소비하다 → *consumer* 소비자 → *consumption* 소비

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 낱말 가족과 덩어리 표현: consume 소비하다 → consumer 소비자 → consumption 소비 / take the lot 몽땅 사다(가져가다) · walk up and down the aisles 통로를 이리저리 오가다 / quit for good 아주(영영) 그만두다

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Why do we shop so much online? B: The ___ is, it’s too easy. / A: And we’re constantly ___ that we need more. B: True. It’s less ___ the stuff and more about the feeling. / 낱말 상자: thing · told · about
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 미니멀리즘(꼭 필요한 것만 두고 사는 방식)
지속 가능한, 환경에 부담을 덜 주는

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: consumer (소비자), advertising (광고(광고하는 일, 광고물)), minimalism (미니멀리즘(꼭 필요한 것만 두고 사는 방식)), clutter (잡동사니, 어수선하게 널린 물건), subscription (구독(정기적으로 돈을 내고 받는 것)), temptation (유혹), sustainable (지속 가능한, 환경에 부담을 덜 주는), impulse buy (충동구매(로 산 물건)), shopping cart (쇼핑 카트; (온라인) 장바구니), haul ((한 번에 잔뜩) 사 온 물건들), declutter ((안 쓰는 물건을) 정리해 치우다), possession (소유물, 가진 물건).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Is every purchase a sign of materialism?
치료, 요법 · retail therapy 기분 전환 쇼핑
Some people buy things for status.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: consumption (소비, 소비량) — "We could cut our consumption."; materialism (물질주의(돈·물건을 가장 중요하게 여기는 태도)) — "Is every purchase a sign of materialism?"; therapy (치료, 요법 · retail therapy 기분 전환 쇼핑) — "Shopping isn’t real therapy."; impulse (충동) — "I bought it on impulse."; status ((사회적) 지위) — "Some people buy things for status."; discount (할인) — "a year-end discount"; budget (예산) — "a monthly budget"; habit (습관) — "a shopping habit".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What’s something you bought but didn’t really need?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What’s something you bought but didn’t really need?" (hint on screen: I bought ___. The thing is, ___.)
- "Do ads create needs we didn’t have? Why do you think so?" (hint on screen: Yes. We’re constantly told that ___. / Not really. ___.)
- "Why do people buy things they don’t need?" (hint on screen: It’s less about ___ and more about ___.)
- "What helps you buy less?" (hint on screen: I try to ___ before buying. / I turn off ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Chloe’s Closet
steps.text: As they walked *up and down* the aisles, Chloe told Jiwoo more about her closet. When she decluttered her closet, she found a jacket with the tags still on, three phone cases, and a bread maker she had never opened. “I bought *the lot* in one late-night haul,” she laughed. Jiwoo shared her rule: put something in the cart, then wait seven days. “If I still want it, I buy it. Usually, I don’t.” Chloe agreed that habits are hard to change. We consume so much without even thinking. Still, she canceled two subscriptions right there in the checkout line. “I’m not giving up shopping *for good*,” she said, “but less is more.” With a bag of salad greens and a box of cookies, they headed to Grace’s place for the first dinner of the group.
steps.gloss: up and down 이리저리 · declutter 정리해 치우다 · the lot 전부, 몽땅 · haul (한 번에) 사 온 물건들 · consume 소비하다 · for good 아주, 영영

What is Jiwoo’s rule before buying?

We consume so much without even thinking. Still, she canceled two subscriptions right there in the checkout line. “I’m not giving up shopping for good,” she said, “but less is more.” With a bag of salad greens and a box of cookies, they headed to Grace’s place for the first dinner of the group." Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Chloe find in her closet?" / "What is Jiwoo’s rule before buying?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

steps.title: 돈과 행복
steps.scene_desc: 12월 첫 토요일 저녁, 그레이스 집. 안쪽 거실 식탁에 대니얼·클로이·벤·마야가 둘러앉아 있고 음식 접시 여섯 개가 놓여 있음. 앞쪽 부엌에서 그레이스가 냄비의 수프를 그릇에 담고, 지우가 샐러드 그릇을 든 채 이야기함. 창밖은 겨울밤, 작은 연말 전구 장식(글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Can money buy happiness?" (돈과 행복). Goal: 정도를 나눠 말하고 초점을 바꾸기. Today's scene: 12월 첫 토요일 저녁, 그레이스 집. 안쪽 거실 식탁에 대니얼·클로이·벤·마야가 둘러앉아 있고 음식 접시 여섯 개가 놓여 있음. 앞쪽 부엌에서 그레이스가 냄비의 수프를 그릇에 담고, 지우가 샐러드 그릇을 든 채 이야기함. 창밖은 겨울밤, 작은 연말 전구 장식(글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Up to a point, ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 생각이 *일정한 선까지만* 맞다고 인정해요.
steps.extra: Up to a point, money does make life easier.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Up to a point, ___." (어느 정도까지는 ~). When to use it: 어떤 생각이 일정한 선까지만 맞다고 인정해요. Note: Up to a point, money does make life easier.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Beyond that, ___.".

steps.when: *Up to a point* 뒤에 이어서, 그다음은 다르다고 말해요.
steps.extra: Beyond that, more money doesn’t help much.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Beyond that, ___." (그 선을 넘으면 ~). When to use it: Up to a point 뒤에 이어서, 그다음은 다르다고 말해요. Note: Beyond that, more money doesn’t help much.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s not so much ___ as ___.".

steps.when: 초점을 바꿔요. 앞은 덜 중요한 것, *as* 뒤가 진짜 중요한 것.
steps.extra: It’s not so much the money as the freedom.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s not so much ___ as ___." (~라기보다는 ~예요.). When to use it: 초점을 바꿔요. 앞은 덜 중요한 것, as 뒤가 진짜 중요한 것. Note: It’s not so much the money as the freedom.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Beyond that, …

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Up to a point, ___. / It’s not so much ___ as ___. Table (Up to a point, … → Beyond that, …):
- money brings freedom. → the extra matters less.
- a bigger home is nice. → it’s just more to clean.
- a raise feels great. → you get used to it.
- nice things are fun. → they turn into clutter.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: Up to a point / Beyond that — 정도 나누기

*Up to a point*, money helps. 어느 정도까지는 돈이 도움이 돼요. 
*Beyond that*, it matters less. 그 선을 넘으면 덜 중요해요.
not so much A as B — A라기보다는 B

It’s *not so much* the money *as* the freedom. 돈이라기보다는 자유예요. 
A와 B는 같은 꼴로: not so much saving *as* spending wisely(-ing + -ing)
errors: It’s not so much the money than the time.
It’s not so much the money as the time.
Money is a mean, not an end.
Money is a means, not an end.
It depends how do you spend it.
It depends how you spend it.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Up to a point / Beyond that — 정도 나누기: Up to a point, money helps. 어느 정도까지는 돈이 도움이 돼요. / Beyond that, it matters less. 그 선을 넘으면 덜 중요해요.
- not so much A as B — A라기보다는 B: It’s not so much the money as the freedom. 돈이라기보다는 자유예요. / A와 B는 같은 꼴로: not so much saving as spending wisely(-ing + -ing)
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s not so much the money than the time. → It’s not so much the money as the time. (not so much A as B(than ×).)
- Money is a mean, not an end. → Money is a means, not an end. (‘수단’은 하나여도 means(-s 그대로).)
- It depends how do you spend it. → It depends how you spend it. (how 뒤에는 주어 + 동사 순서.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

mistakes: It’s not so much the money than the time. → It’s not so much the money as the time.
Money is a mean, not an end. → Money is a means, not an end.
It depends how do you spend it. → It depends how you spend it.

steps.note: 예) money / freedom → A: Is it about money? B: Up to a point. But it’s not so much money as freedom.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) money / freedom → A: Is it about money? B: Up to a point. But it’s not so much money as freedom. Items (situation → model answer): money → freedom | a big house → a happy home | the price → the memory | a high salary → free time.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "Can money buy happiness?" (돈과 행복); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Up to a point, ___." / "Beyond that, ___." / "It’s not so much ___ as ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: It can’t buy time with loved ones.
It’s relative to those around you.
Money is a means, not an end.
It depends how you spend it.
A newer study found it keeps rising for most people.
새 연구는 대부분 계속 오른다고 봤어요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 돈이 주는 것: "Money buys freedom." (돈은 자유를 사 줘요., 보통); "Financial stress is real." (돈 걱정은 실제로 힘들어요., 보통); "Security matters more than luxury." (사치보다 안정이 더 중요해요., 보통)
- 돈이 못 하는 것: "It can’t buy time with loved ones." (소중한 사람들과의 시간은 못 사요., 보통); "Experiences beat possessions." (경험이 물건보다 나아요., 친근); "It’s relative to those around you." (주변과 비교해서 느끼는 거예요., 보통)
- 정리하기: "Money is a means, not an end." (돈은 수단이지 목적이 아니에요., 보통); "It depends how you spend it." (어떻게 쓰느냐에 달렸어요., 친근); "A newer study found it keeps rising for most people." (새 연구는 대부분 계속 오른다고 봤어요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 연구는 뭐라고 했나

연구 — 당시 미국에서 연간 가구 소득 약 7만 5천 달러를 넘으면 일상의 기분은 더 좋아지지 않았지만, 삶에 대한 평가는 계속 올랐어요(Kahneman·Deaton, 2010). 새 연구에서는 대부분 소득이 높을수록 일상의 행복도 계속 올랐고, 가장 덜 행복한 약 20%만 어느 선 뒤로 거의 오르지 않았어요(Killingsworth 외, 2023). 재정 조언이 아니에요.
돈에 관한 말

*poverty* 가난, 빈곤 · enough to *go round* 모두에게 돌아갈 만큼 
the other *way round* 그 반대 · a *wealth of* stories 아주 많은 이야기 
*wellbeing* 몸과 마음의 행복(이 책의 표기) · 같은 낱말의 다른 표기: well-being, well being

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Can money buy happiness? B: I’d say up to a ___, yes. ___ that, it matters less. / A: So it’s not so ___ the money as the freedom? B: Exactly. Money is a ___, not an end. / 낱말 상자: point · Beyond · much · means
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: wealth (부, 재산), luxury (사치, 사치품), threshold (문턱; 기준점(넘으면 달라지는 선)), gratitude (감사하는 마음), inequality (불평등), comfort (편안함; 위안), affluence (풍요, 넉넉한 살림), frugal (검소한, 알뜰한), splurge ((기분 내며) 돈을 펑펑 쓰다), standard of living (생활 수준), income (소득, 수입), contentment (만족감(가진 것에 만족하는 마음)).

Word list on screen: financial (돈의, 재정의) — "financial stress"; relative (상대적인 · relative to ~와 비교해서) — "Wealth is relative."; freedom (자유) — "Money buys freedom."; security ((생활의) 안정, 안전) — "financial security"; wellbeing ((몸과 마음의) 행복, 안녕) — "Sleep matters for our wellbeing."; means (수단(하나여도 means)) — "a means, not an end"; materialism (물질주의) — "Is buying gifts materialism?"; possession (소유물, 가진 물건) — "Experiences beat possessions.".

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Can money buy happiness? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: Up to a point, ___. Beyond that, ___.)
- "What’s something money can’t buy?" (hint on screen: Money can’t buy ___.)
- "Would you rather splurge on a trip or a thing? Why?" (hint on screen: I’d rather ___. It’s not so much ___ as ___.)
- "What small thing are you grateful for these days?" (hint on screen: I’m grateful for ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Six Dishes, Six Views
steps.text: Back at the table, there were six dishes: Grace’s soup, Jiwoo’s salad, Chloe’s cookies, Ben’s bread, Maya’s kimchi pancakes, and Daniel’s pasta. Everyone had a view on Daniel’s question. Maya, who has *a wealth of* stories from work, said money matters most when it removes stress. Ben wondered if it was the other *way round*: maybe happier people make calmer money choices. Chloe admitted that her late-night hauls had never made her happier. By dessert, they agreed on one thing. When there isn’t enough time *to go round*, friends often come last. So Daniel suggested a rule: dinner on the first Saturday of every month, at someone’s home or a local restaurant. Everyone raised a glass. “Time with good people,” Grace said. “Money can’t buy that.”
steps.gloss: a wealth of 아주 많은 · the other way round 그 반대 · haul (한 번에) 사 온 물건들 · enough to go round 모두에게 돌아갈 만큼 · raise a glass 건배하다
questions: What did Ben wonder?
What rule did Daniel suggest?

Everyone raised a glass. “Time with good people,” Grace said. “Money can’t buy that.”" Words: a wealth of 아주 많은 · the other way round 그 반대 · haul (한 번에) 사 온 물건들 · enough to go round 모두에게 돌아갈 만큼 · raise a glass 건배하다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Ben wonder?" / "What rule did Daniel suggest?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

steps.title: 패스트 패션
steps.scene_desc: 12월 마지막 토요일 오후, 동네 공원 광장의 중고 옷 장터(플리마켓). 클로이가 옷걸이 행거와 접이식 탁자에 옷을 늘어놓은 자기 자리 뒤에서 웃으며 손짓하고, 바로 옆 자리 앞에서 지우가 갈색 울 코트를 입어 보며 작은 거울을 봄. 옆 자리 주인(나이 든 남자)이 미소 지음. 겨울옷 차림의 사람들, 입김(가격표·간판에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Who’s really paying the price?" (패스트 패션). Goal: 숨은 비용을 짚고 책임을 나누기. Today's scene: 12월 마지막 토요일 오후, 동네 공원 광장의 중고 옷 장터(플리마켓). 클로이가 옷걸이 행거와 접이식 탁자에 옷을 늘어놓은 자기 자리 뒤에서 웃으며 손짓하고, 바로 옆 자리 앞에서 지우가 갈색 울 코트를 입어 보며 작은 거울을 봄. 옆 자리 주인(나이 든 남자)이 미소 지음. 겨울옷 차림의 사람들, 입김(가격표·간판에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It comes at the expense of ___.".

steps.en: It comes at the expense of ___.
steps.when: 겉으로는 이득이지만 *누군가·무언가가 손해를 본다*고 짚어요. 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: Cheap fashion comes at the expense of workers.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It comes at the expense of ___." (~을 희생해서 얻는 거예요.). When to use it: 겉으로는 이득이지만 누군가·무언가가 손해를 본다고 짚어요. 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: Cheap fashion comes at the expense of workers.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Who’s really paying the price?".

steps.when: 숨은 비용을 누가 떠안는지 물어요. *pay the price* = 대가를 치르다.
steps.extra: The shirt was cheap, but who’s really paying the price?
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Who’s really paying the price?" (진짜 대가를 치르는 건 누구일까요?). When to use it: 숨은 비용을 누가 떠안는지 물어요. pay the price = 대가를 치르다. Note: The shirt was cheap, but who’s really paying the price?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "The responsibility lies with ___.".

steps.when: 책임이 누구에게 있는지 차분하게 말해요. 여럿이면 *A and B*로.
steps.extra: The responsibility lies with brands and shoppers.

Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). steps.title: The Flea Market · 12월 마지막 토요일 오후, 동네 중고 옷 장터에서

lines.en: Welcome to my stall! Everything’s five thousand won. I bought the bulk of these this year.
lines.ko: 제 자리에 온 걸 환영해요! 전부 5천 원이에요. 거의 다 올해 산 거예요.

lines.en: This year? They look brand-new. Why are you selling them?
lines.ko: 올해요? 새것 같은데요. 왜 팔아요?

lines.en: I bought most of them because they were cheap. Then I wore them once or twice.
lines.ko: 대부분 싸서 샀어요. 그러고는 한두 번 입었죠.

lines.en: Well, it’s cheap for a reason. A price that low {{comes at the expense of}} someone.
lines.ko: 음, 싼 데는 이유가 있어요. 그렇게 싼 가격은 누군가를 희생해서 나오는 거예요.

lines.en: You mean the workers?
lines.ko: 노동자들 말이에요?

lines.en: Partly. Some people say workers are paid next to nothing. And unwanted clothes end up in landfills.
lines.ko: 그것도 있어요. 노동자들이 쥐꼬리만 한 돈을 받는다고들 하잖아요. 그리고 안 입는 옷은 결국 쓰레기 매립지로 가요.

lines.en: So {{who’s really paying the price?}} Not me, that’s for sure.
lines.ko: 그러니까 진짜 대가를 치르는 건 누굴까요? 제가 아닌 건 확실하네요.

lines.en: So is it the shoppers’ fault?
lines.ko: 그럼 사는 사람 잘못일까요?

lines.en: Partly. But not everyone can afford sustainable brands. I think {{the responsibility lies with}} companies, too. It’s a systemic problem.
lines.ko: 일부는요. 하지만 누구나 친환경 브랜드를 살 여유가 있는 건 아니에요. 저는 책임이 회사에도 있다고 봐요. 구조 전체의 문제예요.

lines.en: Agreed. And some companies greenwash their image.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 게다가 어떤 회사들은 친환경인 척 이미지를 꾸며요.

lines.en: Like a drama villain with a perfect smile! Still, consumers have power too.
lines.ko: 완벽한 미소를 짓는 드라마 악역처럼요! 그래도 소비자에게도 힘이 있어요.

lines.en: True. For me, buying less is the real solution.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 저는 덜 사는 게 진짜 해결책이라고 생각해요.

lines.en: Or buying second-hand! Second-hand is getting popular. Look at you in that coat from the next stall.
lines.ko: 아니면 중고로 사거나요! 중고가 인기를 얻고 있어요. 옆 자리 코트 입은 지우 씨 좀 봐요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Flea Market · 12월 마지막 토요일 오후, 동네 중고 옷 장터에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Welcome to my stall! Everything’s five thousand won. I bought the bulk of these this year." (제 자리에 온 걸 환영해요! 전부 5천 원이에요. 거의 다 올해 산 거예요.)
2. Jiwoo: "This year? They look brand-new. Why are you selling them?" (올해요? 새것 같은데요. 왜 팔아요?)
3. Chloe: "I bought most of them because they were cheap. Then I wore them once or twice." (대부분 싸서 샀어요. 그러고는 한두 번 입었죠.)
4. Jiwoo: "Well, it’s cheap for a reason. A price that low comes at the expense of someone." (음, 싼 데는 이유가 있어요. 그렇게 싼 가격은 누군가를 희생해서 나오는 거예요.)
5. Chloe: "You mean the workers?" (노동자들 말이에요?)
6. Jiwoo: "Partly. Some people say workers are paid next to nothing. And unwanted clothes end up in landfills." (그것도 있어요. 노동자들이 쥐꼬리만 한 돈을 받는다고들 하잖아요. 그리고 안 입는 옷은 결국 쓰레기 매립지로 가요.)
7. Chloe: "So who’s really paying the price? Not me, that’s for sure." (그러니까 진짜 대가를 치르는 건 누굴까요? 제가 아닌 건 확실하네요.)
8. Jiwoo: "So is it the shoppers’ fault?" (그럼 사는 사람 잘못일까요?)
9. Chloe: "Partly. But not everyone can afford sustainable brands. I think the responsibility lies with companies, too. It’s a systemic problem." (일부는요. 하지만 누구나 친환경 브랜드를 살 여유가 있는 건 아니에요. 저는 책임이 회사에도 있다고 봐요. 구조 전체의 문제예요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Agreed. And some companies greenwash their image." (맞아요. 게다가 어떤 회사들은 친환경인 척 이미지를 꾸며요.)
11. Chloe: "Like a drama villain with a perfect smile! Still, consumers have power too." (완벽한 미소를 짓는 드라마 악역처럼요! 그래도 소비자에게도 힘이 있어요.)
12. Jiwoo: "True. For me, buying less is the real solution." (맞아요. 저는 덜 사는 게 진짜 해결책이라고 생각해요.)
13. Chloe: "Or buying second-hand! Second-hand is getting popular. Look at you in that coat from the next stall." (아니면 중고로 사거나요! 중고가 인기를 얻고 있어요. 옆 자리 코트 입은 지우 씨 좀 봐요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It’s cheap, but it comes at the expense of ___.
head: 싸고 편한 것
It comes at the expense of …
The responsibility lies with …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It’s cheap, but it comes at the expense of ___. / The responsibility lies with ___. Table (싸고 편한 것 → It comes at the expense of …):
- a cheap T-shirt → the workers who make it.
- a new trend every week → the environment.
- next-day delivery → workers’ rest time.
- a very low price → quality.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Low prices *come at the expense of* workers. 싼 가격은 노동자를 희생해서 얻는 거예요. 
뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*: at the expense of quality

The responsibility *lies with* brands. 책임은 브랜드에 있어요. 
Who’s *paying the price*? 누가 대가를 치르나요?
errors: It comes at expense of workers.
It comes at the expense of workers.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- at the expense of — 희생·대가: Low prices come at the expense of workers. 싼 가격은 노동자를 희생해서 얻는 거예요. / 뒤에는 명사나 -ing: at the expense of quality
- lie with · pay the price: The responsibility lies with brands. 책임은 브랜드에 있어요. / Who’s paying the price? 누가 대가를 치르나요?
Common mistakes on screen:
- It comes at expense of workers. → It comes at the expense of workers. (the를 빼지 않아요(at the expense of).)
- The responsibility lie with brands. → The responsibility lies with brands. (responsibility는 단수라 lies.)
- Who’s really pay the price? → Who’s really paying the price? (Who’s = Who is라서 -ing.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: at the expense of — 희생·대가: Low prices come at the expense of workers. 싼 가격은 노동자를 희생해서 얻는 거예요. 뒤에는 명사나 -ing: at the expense of quality
lie with · pay the price: The responsibility lies with brands. 책임은 브랜드에 있어요. Who’s paying the price? 누가 대가를 치르나요?
mistakes: It comes at expense of workers. → It comes at the expense of workers.
The responsibility lie with brands. → The responsibility lies with brands.
Who’s really pay the price? → Who’s really paying the price?

steps.note: 예) cheap clothes / workers → A: Cheap clothes are great! B: Maybe, but they come at the expense of workers.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) cheap clothes / workers → A: Cheap clothes are great! B: Maybe, but they come at the expense of workers. Items (situation → model answer): cheap clothes → workers | fast trends → the planet | low prices → quality | fast delivery → workers’ rest.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: It comes at the expense of ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Who’s really paying the price?" (패스트 패션); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It comes at the expense of ___." / "Who’s really paying the price?" / "The responsibility lies with ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Workers are paid next to nothing.
Not everyone can afford sustainable brands.
누구나 친환경 브랜드를 살 수 있는 건 아니에요.
Buying less is the real solution.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 숨은 비용: "It’s cheap for a reason." (싼 데는 이유가 있어요., 친근); "Workers are paid next to nothing." (노동자들이 쥐꼬리만 한 돈을 받아요., 보통); "Clothes end up in landfills." (옷이 결국 쓰레기 매립지로 가요., 보통); "Companies greenwash their image." (회사들이 친환경인 척 이미지를 꾸며요., 보통)
- 책임은 누구에게: "It’s a systemic problem." (구조 전체의 문제예요., 정중); "Consumers have power too." (소비자에게도 힘이 있어요., 보통); "Not everyone can afford sustainable brands." (누구나 친환경 브랜드를 살 수 있는 건 아니에요., 보통)
- 해결책: "Buying less is the real solution." (덜 사는 게 진짜 해결책이에요., 보통); "Second-hand is getting popular." (중고가 인기를 얻고 있어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 옷이 오기까지

*textile* 옷감 → a *garment* *factory* 의류 공장 → a *brand* 브랜드 
the *supply chain* 공급망(원료부터 가게까지 이어지는 과정) 
*the bulk of* 대부분 · *with a view to* -ing ~할 생각으로(격식)
(참고) 조심해서 쓰는 말

*exploitation* 착취(남의 노동을 부당하게 이용함) 
*a case of* … ~인 경우, ~의 문제 
이 과의 말은 사람들이 흔히 하는 의견이에요. 회사·나라·공장마다 사정이 달라요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 옷이 오기까지: textile 옷감 → a garment factory 의류 공장 → a brand 브랜드 / the supply chain 공급망(원료부터 가게까지 이어지는 과정) / the bulk of 대부분 · with a view to -ing ~할 생각으로(격식)

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: This shirt was so cheap! B: It’s cheap for a ___. It comes at the ___ of workers. / A: So who’s really paying the ___? B: I think the responsibility ___ with brands and buyers. / 낱말 상자: reason · expense · price · lies
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: fashion (패션, (옷의) 유행), landfill (쓰레기 매립지), sustainability (지속 가능성), garment ((한 벌의) 옷, 의류), factory (공장), greenwashing (그린워싱(친환경인 척 꾸미기)), brand (브랜드, 상표), second-hand (중고의), textile (직물, 옷감), ethical (윤리적인(사람·환경에 떳떳한)), supply (공급; 공급하다), chain (사슬; 연결 · supply chain 공급망).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: 지속 가능한, 환경에 부담을 덜 주는
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: exploitation (착취(남의 노동을 부당하게 이용함)) — "the exploitation of workers"; systemic ((한 부분이 아니라) 체계 전체의, 구조적인) — "a systemic problem"; sustainable (지속 가능한, 환경에 부담을 덜 주는) — "sustainable brands"; wage (임금(일한 대가로 정기적으로 받는 돈)) — "a fair wage"; consumer (소비자) — "Consumers have power too."; afford ((돈·여유가 있어) ~할 수 있다) — "I can’t afford it."; price (가격; 대가) — "pay the price"; quality (품질) — "good quality".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Where do you usually buy clothes? Why?
Have you ever bought second-hand clothes?
Yes, I bought ___. / Not yet. The thing is, ___.
Who should be responsible for the hidden costs of fashion?
What’s something cheap or convenient that has a hidden cost?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Where do you usually buy clothes? Why?" (hint on screen: I usually buy clothes ___ because ___.)
- "Have you ever bought second-hand clothes?" (hint on screen: Yes, I bought ___. / Not yet. The thing is, ___.)
- "Who should be responsible for the hidden costs of fashion?" (hint on screen: The responsibility lies with ___.)
- "What’s something cheap or convenient that has a hidden cost?" (hint on screen: ___ comes at the expense of ___.)

steps.title: A Coat with a Story
steps.text: By four o’clock, Chloe had sold most of her clothes. “I bought many of them *with a view to* wearing them at one party,” she admitted. “Then I forgot about them.” The rest went into a donation box. Meanwhile, Jiwoo was wearing her “new” coat. The man at the next stall said it had been his father’s, and his father had worn it every winter for twenty years. “That’s the opposite of fast fashion,” Jiwoo said. On the walk home, they talked about who should change first. Chloe thought it was *a case of* shared responsibility. Brands need to be honest about their supply chains, and shoppers need to slow down. Her goal for next year? One new item a month, and second-hand first.
steps.gloss: with a view to ~할 생각으로(격식) · donation box 기부함 · stall 장터의 자리, 가판 · a case of ~의 문제, ~인 경우 · supply chain 공급망
questions: What did Chloe do with the clothes she didn’t sell?
What is Chloe’s goal for next year?

React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. steps.title: The Walk to the Station · 1월 첫 토요일 밤, 지하철역으로 걸어가는 길에서

lines.en: That was a great dinner. But you were quiet when Daniel asked about our biggest failures last year.
lines.ko: 저녁 정말 좋았어요. 그런데 대니얼이 작년의 가장 큰 실패를 물었을 때 조용하더라고요.

lines.en: I was thinking about the “ride together” feature. We spent three months on it, and almost nobody used it.
lines.ko: ‘같이 타기’ 기능 생각을 했어요. 석 달을 들였는데 쓰는 사람이 거의 없었잖아요.

lines.en: I remember. It stings at the time, doesn’t it?
lines.ko: 기억나요. 그때는 쓰라리죠?

lines.en: It did. We shut it down in October. {{Looking back,}} I fell in love with my own idea and never tested it with real riders.
lines.ko: 정말요. 10월에 접었잖아요. 돌이켜 보면 제 아이디어에 푹 빠져서 실제 이용자에게 시험해 보지 않았어요.

lines.en: That’s a big lesson. Failure is a great teacher.
lines.ko: 큰 교훈이네요. 실패는 좋은 스승이에요.

lines.en: Maybe. But it’s easy to say in hindsight. And not every failure teaches something.
lines.ko: 그럴지도요. 하지만 지나고 나서야 쉽게 하는 말이죠. 그리고 모든 실패가 뭔가를 가르쳐 주는 건 아니에요.

lines.en: Fair point. A few years ago, I managed a project that was canceled after eight months. I had doubts from the start, but I stayed quiet.
lines.ko: 맞는 말이에요. 몇 년 전에 제가 맡은 프로젝트가 여덟 달 만에 중단됐어요. 처음부터 의심이 들었는데 말을 안 했어요.

lines.en: That must have been hard.
lines.ko: 힘드셨겠어요.

lines.en: It was. But {{if I hadn’t}} gone through that, {{I wouldn’t have}} learned to speak up early. It shaped who I am.
lines.ko: 힘들었죠. 하지만 그 일을 겪지 않았다면 일찍 말하는 법을 배우지 못했을 거예요. 그 일이 지금의 저를 만들었어요.

lines.en: So {{it was a blessing in disguise.}}
lines.ko: 그러니까 전화위복이었네요.

lines.en: In a way. Resilience comes from setbacks. Now, say it like you mean it. What will you do differently this year?
lines.ko: 어떤 면에서는요. 회복력은 좌절을 겪으며 생겨요. 자, 진심을 담아 말해 봐요. 올해는 뭘 다르게 할 거예요?

lines.en: Test small ideas with real riders before we build anything. Fail fast, learn fast!
lines.ko: 뭘 만들기 전에 실제 이용자와 작은 아이디어부터 시험해 볼 거예요. 빨리 실패하고 빨리 배우기!

The app has just played this scene, "The Walk to the Station · 1월 첫 토요일 밤, 지하철역으로 걸어가는 길에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "That was a great dinner. But you were quiet when Daniel asked about our biggest failures last year." (저녁 정말 좋았어요. 그런데 대니얼이 작년의 가장 큰 실패를 물었을 때 조용하더라고요.)
2. Jiwoo: "I was thinking about the “ride together” feature. We spent three months on it, and almost nobody used it." (‘같이 타기’ 기능 생각을 했어요. 석 달을 들였는데 쓰는 사람이 거의 없었잖아요.)
3. Maya: "I remember. It stings at the time, doesn’t it?" (기억나요. 그때는 쓰라리죠?)
4. Jiwoo: "It did. We shut it down in October. Looking back, I fell in love with my own idea and never tested it with real riders." (정말요. 10월에 접었잖아요. 돌이켜 보면 제 아이디어에 푹 빠져서 실제 이용자에게 시험해 보지 않았어요.)
5. Maya: "That’s a big lesson. Failure is a great teacher." (큰 교훈이네요. 실패는 좋은 스승이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Maybe. But it’s easy to say in hindsight. And not every failure teaches something." (그럴지도요. 하지만 지나고 나서야 쉽게 하는 말이죠. 그리고 모든 실패가 뭔가를 가르쳐 주는 건 아니에요.)
7. Maya: "Fair point. A few years ago, I managed a project that was canceled after eight months. I had doubts from the start, but I stayed quiet." (맞는 말이에요. 몇 년 전에 제가 맡은 프로젝트가 여덟 달 만에 중단됐어요. 처음부터 의심이 들었는데 말을 안 했어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "That must have been hard." (힘드셨겠어요.)
9. Maya: "It was. But if I hadn’t gone through that, I wouldn’t have learned to speak up early. It shaped who I am." (힘들었죠. 하지만 그 일을 겪지 않았다면 일찍 말하는 법을 배우지 못했을 거예요. 그 일이 지금의 저를 만들었어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "So it was a blessing in disguise." (그러니까 전화위복이었네요.)
11. Maya: "In a way. Resilience comes from setbacks. Now, say it like you mean it. What will you do differently this year?" (어떤 면에서는요. 회복력은 좌절을 겪으며 생겨요. 자, 진심을 담아 말해 봐요. 올해는 뭘 다르게 할 거예요?)
12. Jiwoo: "Test small ideas with real riders before we build anything. Fail fast, learn fast!" (뭘 만들기 전에 실제 이용자와 작은 아이디어부터 시험해 볼 거예요. 빨리 실패하고 빨리 배우기!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Almost nobody used Jiwoo’s “ride together” feature.
Maya’s project was canceled after two years.
Jiwoo wants to test small ideas with real riders this year.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Almost nobody used Jiwoo’s “ride together” feature.
2. Maya’s project was canceled after two years.
3. Jiwoo wants to test small ideas with real riders this year.
The scene they are about:
1. Maya: "That was a great dinner. But you were quiet when Daniel asked about our biggest failures last year." (저녁 정말 좋았어요. 그런데 대니얼이 작년의 가장 큰 실패를 물었을 때 조용하더라고요.)
2. Jiwoo: "I was thinking about the “ride together” feature. We spent three months on it, and almost nobody used it." (‘같이 타기’ 기능 생각을 했어요. 석 달을 들였는데 쓰는 사람이 거의 없었잖아요.)
3. Maya: "I remember. It stings at the time, doesn’t it?" (기억나요. 그때는 쓰라리죠?)
4. Jiwoo: "It did. We shut it down in October. Looking back, I fell in love with my own idea and never tested it with real riders." (정말요. 10월에 접었잖아요. 돌이켜 보면 제 아이디어에 푹 빠져서 실제 이용자에게 시험해 보지 않았어요.)
5. Maya: "That’s a big lesson. Failure is a great teacher." (큰 교훈이네요. 실패는 좋은 스승이에요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Maybe. But it’s easy to say in hindsight. And not every failure teaches something." (그럴지도요. 하지만 지나고 나서야 쉽게 하는 말이죠. 그리고 모든 실패가 뭔가를 가르쳐 주는 건 아니에요.)
7. Maya: "Fair point. A few years ago, I managed a project that was canceled after eight months. I had doubts from the start, but I stayed quiet." (맞는 말이에요. 몇 년 전에 제가 맡은 프로젝트가 여덟 달 만에 중단됐어요. 처음부터 의심이 들었는데 말을 안 했어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "That must have been hard." (힘드셨겠어요.)
9. Maya: "It was. But if I hadn’t gone through that, I wouldn’t have learned to speak up early. It shaped who I am." (힘들었죠. 하지만 그 일을 겪지 않았다면 일찍 말하는 법을 배우지 못했을 거예요. 그 일이 지금의 저를 만들었어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "So it was a blessing in disguise." (그러니까 전화위복이었네요.)
11. Maya: "In a way. Resilience comes from setbacks. Now, say it like you mean it. What will you do differently this year?" (어떤 면에서는요. 회복력은 좌절을 겪으며 생겨요. 자, 진심을 담아 말해 봐요. 올해는 뭘 다르게 할 거예요?)
12. Jiwoo: "Test small ideas with real riders before we build anything. Fail fast, learn fast!" (뭘 만들기 전에 실제 이용자와 작은 아이디어부터 시험해 볼 거예요. 빨리 실패하고 빨리 배우기!)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___.
head: Looking back, …
If I hadn’t …,
I wouldn’t have …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Looking back, ___. / If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___. Table (Looking back, … → If I hadn’t …,):
- it was a good lesson. → failed that test,
- it was the right call. → quit that job,
- it hurt, but it helped. → lost that project,
- I needed that push. → missed the bus,
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*If I hadn’t failed*, *I wouldn’t have learned* so much. 실패하지 않았다면 그렇게 많이 배우지 못했을 거예요. 
if + had(n’t) + p.p. → would(n’t) have + p.p. (실제로는 실패했어요.)
Looking back · a blessing in disguise

*Looking back*, it was *a blessing in disguise*. 돌이켜 보면 전화위복이었어요. 
Looking back = 지금 그때를 돌아보면
errors: If I didn’t fail, I wouldn’t have learned.
If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned.
지난 일을 가정하면 if 쪽도 *had + p.p.*
If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t learned.
If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 지난 일을 반대로 가정하기: If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned so much. 실패하지 않았다면 그렇게 많이 배우지 못했을 거예요. / if + had(n’t) + p.p. → would(n’t) have + p.p. (실제로는 실패했어요.)
- Looking back · a blessing in disguise: Looking back, it was a blessing in disguise. 돌이켜 보면 전화위복이었어요. / Looking back = 지금 그때를 돌아보면
Common mistakes on screen:
- If I didn’t fail, I wouldn’t have learned. → If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned. (지난 일을 가정하면 if 쪽도 had + p.p.)
- If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t learned. → If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned. (would 뒤에 have + p.p.)
- It stinged at the time. → It stung at the time. (sting–stung–stung(불규칙).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 지난 일을 반대로 가정하기: If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned so much. 실패하지 않았다면 그렇게 많이 배우지 못했을 거예요. if + had(n’t) + p.p. → would(n’t) have + p.p. (실제로는 실패했어요.)
Looking back · a blessing in disguise: Looking back, it was a blessing in disguise. 돌이켜 보면 전화위복이었어요. Looking back = 지금 그때를 돌아보면
mistakes: If I didn’t fail, I wouldn’t have learned. → If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned.
If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t learned. → If I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned.
It stinged at the time. → It stung at the time.

steps.note: 예) failed / learned so much → Looking back, if I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned so much.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) failed / learned so much → Looking back, if I hadn’t failed, I wouldn’t have learned so much. Items (situation → model answer): failed → learned so much | lost that job → found this one | missed the train → met my neighbor | made that mistake → asked for help.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___.
It was a blessing in disguise.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It was a blessing in disguise." (실패의 가치); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Looking back, ___." / "If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___." / "It was a blessing in disguise.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: You learn more from failure than success.
It’s easy to say in hindsight.
모든 실패가 뭔가를 가르쳐 주는 건 아니에요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 실패에서 배우기: "Failure is a great teacher." (실패는 좋은 스승이에요., 보통); "You learn more from failure than success." (성공보다 실패에서 더 많이 배워요., 보통); "Resilience comes from setbacks." (회복력은 좌절을 겪으며 생겨요., 정중); "It shaped who I am." (그 일이 지금의 나를 만들었어요., 보통); "Fail fast, learn fast." (빨리 실패하고 빨리 배워요., 친근)
- 다른 쪽 시선: "It stings at the time." (그때는 쓰라려요., 친근); "It’s easy to say in hindsight." (지나고 나서야 쉽게 하는 말이에요., 보통); "Not every failure teaches something." (모든 실패가 뭔가를 가르쳐 주는 건 아니에요., 보통); "Schools punish mistakes." (학교는 실수를 벌해요(점수를 깎는 식으로)., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 실패를 넘어서

*overcome* a fear 두려움을 이겨 내다 · *make up your mind* 마음을 정하다 
*back up* an idea with data 생각을 자료로 뒷받침하다 
*a degree of* risk 어느 정도의 위험 · *look to* the future 앞날을 내다보다
느낌을 말하는 말

It *stings*. (벌에 쏘인 듯) 따끔해요 → 마음이 쓰릴 때도 써요. 
*in hindsight* 지나고 나서 보니 · a *setback* 차질 
지우의 기능과 마야의 프로젝트는 수업용 가상 이야기예요.
steps.blank:
A: How do you feel about that failure now?   B: ___ back, it was a blessing in ___. 
A: Really?   B: Yes. If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___ so much. 
낱말 상자: Looking · disguise · failed · learned
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 실패를 넘어서: overcome a fear 두려움을 이겨 내다 · make up your mind 마음을 정하다 / back up an idea with data 생각을 자료로 뒷받침하다 / a degree of risk 어느 정도의 위험 · look to the future 앞날을 내다보다
- 느낌을 말하는 말: It stings. (벌에 쏘인 듯) 따끔해요 → 마음이 쓰릴 때도 써요. / in hindsight 지나고 나서 보니 · a setback 차질 / 지우의 기능과 마야의 프로젝트는 수업용 가상 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: How do you feel about that failure now? B: ___ back, it was a blessing in ___. / A: Really? B: Yes. If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___ so much. / 낱말 상자: Looking · disguise · failed · learned
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 회복력(힘든 일 뒤에 다시 일어서는 힘)
지나고 나서 깨달음 · in hindsight 돌이켜 보니

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: failure (실패), setback (차질, (일이 잠시) 뒤로 밀림), resilience (회복력(힘든 일 뒤에 다시 일어서는 힘)), hindsight (지나고 나서 깨달음 · in hindsight 돌이켜 보니), recover (회복하다, (원래대로) 되찾다), persevere ((힘들어도) 끈기 있게 계속하다), perseverance (끈기, 인내), fear (두려움), sting ((벌 등이) 쏘다; (마음이) 쓰리다), punish (벌주다, 처벌하다), shape (모양; (사람·생각을) 만들어 가다), mindset (사고방식, 마음가짐).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: 위험, 좋지 않은 일이 생길 가능성
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: mistake (실수) — "I learned from my mistake."; lesson (교훈) — "That’s a big lesson."; growth (성장) — "Failure can lead to growth."; risk (위험, 좋지 않은 일이 생길 가능성) — "take a risk"; overcome (이겨 내다, 극복하다) — "overcome a fear"; blessing (축복, 고마운 일) — "a blessing in disguise"; feature ((앱·기기의) 기능) — "a new feature"; cancel (취소하다, 중단하다) — "The project was canceled.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Looking back, what’s a mistake you learned from?
Can you think of a blessing in disguise in your life?
When ___, it felt bad. But it was a blessing in disguise.
Finish this sentence about your own life.
If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___.
Do you agree that failure is a great teacher? Why?
Up to a point. ___. / Not every failure teaches something.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Looking back, what’s a mistake you learned from?" (hint on screen: Looking back, ___. I learned ___.)
- "Can you think of a blessing in disguise in your life?" (hint on screen: When ___, it felt bad. But it was a blessing in disguise.)
- "Finish this sentence about your own life." (hint on screen: If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___.)
- "Do you agree that failure is a great teacher? Why?" (hint on screen: Up to a point. ___. / Not every failure teaches something.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Looking back, what’s a mistake you learned from?
Can you think of a blessing in disguise in your life?
Finish this sentence about your own life.
Do you agree that failure is a great teacher? Why?

steps.title: Maya’s Story
steps.text: On the subway platform, Maya told Jiwoo the rest of her story. Years ago, she managed a booking app for a client. From the start, she had doubts about the plan, but she stayed quiet. Eight months later, the client canceled the project. “I felt like a failure for weeks,” she said. It took her a while to *make up her mind* to lead a project again, and she had to *overcome* her fear of speaking up. Now she asks her team to raise problems early and *back up* their concerns with data. “Every project has *a degree of* risk,” she said. “Silence makes it bigger.” Jiwoo thought about her own feature. It still stung a little, but she was ready to *look to* the year ahead. Her first goal: test with real riders before designing a single screen.
steps.gloss: make up one’s mind 마음을 정하다 · overcome 이겨 내다 · back up 뒷받침하다 · a degree of 어느 정도의 · look to (앞날을) 내다보다
questions: What did Maya do when she had doubts about the plan?
What does Maya ask her team to do now?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Maya’s Story". Text: "On the subway platform, Maya told Jiwoo the rest of her story. Years ago, she managed a booking app for a client. From the start, she had doubts about the plan, but she stayed quiet. Eight months later, the client canceled the project. “I felt like a failure for weeks,” she said. It took her a while to make up her mind to lead a project again, and she had to overcome her fear of speaking up. Now she asks her team to raise problems early and back up their concerns with data. “Every project has a degree of risk,” she said. “Silence makes it bigger.” Jiwoo thought about her own feature. It still stung a little, but she was ready to look to the year ahead. Her first goal: test with real riders before designing a single screen." Words: make up one’s mind 마음을 정하다 · overcome 이겨 내다 · back up 뒷받침하다 · a degree of 어느 정도의 · look to (앞날을) 내다보다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Maya do when she had doubts about the plan?" / "What does Maya ask her team to do now?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Looking back, ___.’으로 지난 일을 돌아보며 말할 수 있어요.
‘If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___.’로 지난 일을 반대로 가정할 수 있어요.
‘It was a blessing in disguise.’로 나빴던 일이 좋은 일이 되었다고 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Looking back, ___.’으로 지난 일을 돌아보며 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘If I hadn’t ___, I wouldn’t have ___.’로 지난 일을 반대로 가정할 수 있어요.
- ‘It was a blessing in disguise.’로 나빴던 일이 좋은 일이 되었다고 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 전문가 vs 다재다능
steps.scene_desc: 2월 첫 토요일 저녁, 대니얼 단골 동네 카페를 저녁에 빌린 모임. 긴 나무 테이블에 여섯 명분 음식 접시와 찻잔, 테이블에서 벤·클로이·마야가 웃으며 이야기 중. 앞쪽 카운터에서 그레이스가 찻주전자를 들고 지우와 이야기하고, 대니얼이 찻잔을 들고 다가옴(간판·메뉴판 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s not either-or." (전문가 vs 다재다능). Goal: 한쪽을 인정하고 이분법을 넘기. Today's scene: 2월 첫 토요일 저녁, 대니얼 단골 동네 카페를 저녁에 빌린 모임. 긴 나무 테이블에 여섯 명분 음식 접시와 찻잔, 테이블에서 벤·클로이·마야가 웃으며 이야기 중. 앞쪽 카운터에서 그레이스가 찻주전자를 들고 지우와 이야기하고, 대니얼이 찻잔을 들고 다가옴(간판·메뉴판 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "There’s a lot to be said for ___.".

steps.en: There’s a lot to be said for ___.
steps.when: 어떤 쪽의 장점을 먼저 인정해요. *for* 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: There’s a lot to be said for trying different jobs.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "There’s a lot to be said for ___." (~에는 좋은 점이 많아요.). When to use it: 어떤 쪽의 장점을 먼저 인정해요. for 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: There’s a lot to be said for trying different jobs.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "That said, ___.".

steps.when: 앞에서 인정한 말에 단서나 다른 면을 붙여요. but보다 차분하고 무게 있게 들려요.
steps.extra: Generalists adapt fast. That said, depth takes years.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "That said, ___." (그렇긴 해도, ~.). When to use it: 앞에서 인정한 말에 단서나 다른 면을 붙여요. but보다 차분하고 무게 있게 들려요. Note: Generalists adapt fast. That said, depth takes years.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

lines.en: A generalist! Travel consultant, a summer at a hotel front desk, now an English teacher.

lines.en: Guilty! But {{there’s a lot to be said for}} trying different jobs. Planning trips taught me to listen for what people really want. That’s half of teaching.

lines.en: Depth matters in my field, too. A senior designer once spotted a problem on my screen in ten seconds. That kind of mastery takes years.
lines.ko: 제 분야에서도 깊이는 중요해요. 선배 디자이너가 제 화면의 문제를 10초 만에 찾아낸 적이 있어요. 그런 경지는 몇 년이 걸려요.

lines.en: So, you mean depth beats breadth?

8. Jiwoo: "In some fields, yes. But specialists can get stuck if their niche disappears. Honestly, it’s not either-or. The best designers I know have one deep skill and many shallow ones." (어떤 분야에선요. 하지만 전문가는 자기 분야가 사라지면 막힐 수 있어요. 솔직히 둘 중 하나를 고를 문제가 아니에요. 최고의 디자이너들은 깊은 기술 하나에 얕은 기술 여럿을 갖췄어요.)

11. Daniel: "Fair enough. For me, it depends on the stage of your career." (일리 있네요. 저는 경력 단계에 따라 다르다고 봐요.)
12. Grace: "And on the person. Both have their place." (사람에 따라서도요. 둘 다 쓸모가 있어요.)
