frame: There’s a lot to be said for ___.
head: There’s a lot to be said for …
That said, …
정리하기
rows: it takes a lot of time.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: There’s a lot to be said for ___. / That said, ___. / It’s not either-or. Table (There’s a lot to be said for … → That said, …):
- trying different jobs. → you might never go deep.
- staying in one field. → you can get stuck.
- learning a second skill. → it takes a lot of time.
- working on your own. → you miss other perspectives.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Generalists adapt fast. *That said*, they may not go deep. 
앞 말을 인정한 뒤 문장 맨 앞에 쓰고 쉼표를 찍어요. (Having said that도 같은 뜻)
There’s a lot to be said for + 명사 / -ing

There’s a lot to be said for *experience*. (명사) 
There’s a lot to be said for *staying* in one field. (-ing, 동사원형 stay는 ×)
errors: She has a lot of expertise.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- That said, … = 그렇긴 해도: Generalists adapt fast. That said, they may not go deep. / 앞 말을 인정한 뒤 문장 맨 앞에 쓰고 쉼표를 찍어요. (Having said that도 같은 뜻)
- There’s a lot to be said for + 명사 / -ing: There’s a lot to be said for experience. (명사) / There’s a lot to be said for staying in one field. (-ing, 동사원형 stay는 ×)
Common mistakes on screen:
- That said, but it’s hard. → That said, it’s hard. (That said에 ‘그렇긴 해도’가 있어 but은 빼요.)
- She has many expertises. → She has a lot of expertise. (expertise는 셀 수 없어요(-s ×).)
- Generalists adapts faster. → Generalists adapt faster. (주어가 복수라 -s 없이 adapt.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: That said, … = 그렇긴 해도: Generalists adapt fast. That said, they may not go deep. 앞 말을 인정한 뒤 문장 맨 앞에 쓰고 쉼표를 찍어요. (Having said that도 같은 뜻)
There’s a lot to be said for + 명사 / -ing: There’s a lot to be said for experience. (명사) There’s a lot to be said for staying in one field. (-ing, 동사원형 stay는 ×)
mistakes: That said, but it’s hard. → That said, it’s hard.
She has many expertises. → She has a lot of expertise.
Generalists adapts faster. → Generalists adapt faster.

steps.note: 예) changing jobs / it’s risky → A: There’s a lot to be said for changing jobs. B: That said, it’s risky.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) changing jobs / it’s risky → A: There’s a lot to be said for changing jobs. B: That said, it’s risky. Items (situation → model answer): changing jobs → it’s risky | staying put → you can get stuck | working alone → it gets lonely | learning online → it’s easy to quit.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: There’s a lot to be said for ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It’s not either-or." (전문가 vs 다재다능); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "There’s a lot to be said for ___." / "That said, ___." / "It’s not either-or.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Depth beats breadth in some fields.
A jack of all trades, master of none.
이것저것 다 하지만 제대로 하는 건 없다(속담).
두루 잘하는 사람이 더 빨리 적응해요.
The best people have one deep skill and many shallow ones.
최고인 사람들은 깊은 기술 하나와 얕은 기술 여럿을 갖고 있어요.
It depends on the stage of your career.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 깊이 쪽: "Depth beats breadth in some fields." (어떤 분야에서는 넓이보다 깊이가 이겨요., 보통); "A jack of all trades, master of none." (이것저것 다 하지만 제대로 하는 건 없다(속담)., 보통)
- 넓이 쪽: "Generalists adapt faster." (두루 잘하는 사람이 더 빨리 적응해요., 보통); "Specialists can get stuck." (전문가는 막힐 수 있어요., 보통); "Curiosity is underrated." (호기심은 과소평가돼 있어요., 친근)
- 둘을 넘어서기: "The best people have one deep skill and many shallow ones." (최고인 사람들은 깊은 기술 하나와 얕은 기술 여럿을 갖고 있어요., 보통); "It depends on the stage of your career." (경력 단계에 따라 달라요., 보통); "Both have their place." (둘 다 쓸모가 있어요., 보통); "It’s a false choice." (애초에 잘못된 양자택일이에요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 덩어리 표현

*head to* the subway 지하철역으로 향하다 · *in the interest of* time 시간을 아끼려고 
useful to a few people *at best* 잘해야 몇 사람에게나 쓸모 있는 
*go deep* (한 가지를) 깊이 파고들다
(참고) 일과 경력을 말하는 낱말

a *T-shaped* person 한 분야는 깊게, 여러 분야는 넓게 아는 사람 
a *jack of all trades* 이것저것 다 할 줄 아는 사람(‘master of none’을 붙이면 깎아내리는 말) 
모임과 인물의 경력은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.

A: Specialist or generalist?   B: Well, there’s a lot to be ___ for both. 
A: Generalists adapt faster.   B: That ___, depth matters in some fields.

낱말 상자: said · said · either · place
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 덩어리 표현: head to the subway 지하철역으로 향하다 · in the interest of time 시간을 아끼려고 / useful to a few people at best 잘해야 몇 사람에게나 쓸모 있는 / go deep (한 가지를) 깊이 파고들다
- (참고) 일과 경력을 말하는 낱말: a T-shaped person 한 분야는 깊게, 여러 분야는 넓게 아는 사람 / a jack of all trades 이것저것 다 할 줄 아는 사람(‘master of none’을 붙이면 깎아내리는 말) / 모임과 인물의 경력은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Specialist or generalist? B: Well, there’s a lot to be ___ for both. / A: Generalists adapt faster. B: That ___, depth matters in some fields. / A: So which one? B: It’s not ___-or. Both have their ___. / 낱말 상자: said · said · either · place
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: specialist (전문가(한 분야를 깊이 아는 사람)), generalist (여러 분야를 두루 아는 사람), depth (깊이), breadth (폭, 넓이), versatile (다재다능한; 여러 용도로 쓰이는), adaptable (적응을 잘하는), niche (틈새(분야), 꼭 맞는 자리), curiosity (호기심), mastery (숙달, 통달), perspective (관점, 시각), stuck (꼼짝 못 하는, 막힌), competitive (경쟁이 치열한; 경쟁심이 강한).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: expertise (전문 지식, 전문 기술) — "His expertise is amazing."; transferable ((다른 일에) 옮겨 쓸 수 있는) — "a transferable skill"; discipline ((학문) 분야 (‘규율’이라는 뜻도 있어요)) — "other disciplines"; adapt (적응하다) — "Generalists adapt faster."; field ((일·공부의) 분야) — "Depth matters in my field."; shallow (얕은) — "many shallow skills"; career (경력, 직업 생활) — "the stage of your career"; underrated (과소평가된) — "Curiosity is underrated.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Are you more of a specialist or a generalist? Why?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Are you more of a specialist or a generalist? Why?" (hint on screen: I’m more of a ___ because ___.)
- "What’s a skill from one job or hobby that you use somewhere else?" (hint on screen: ___ taught me ___. It’s a transferable skill.)
- "Name a field where depth beats breadth." (hint on screen: In ___, depth beats breadth. That said, ___.)
- "Someone asks, “Specialist or generalist?” Go beyond the choice." (hint on screen: It’s not either-or. ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Grace’s Napkin
steps.text: Before everyone *headed to* the subway, Daniel asked Grace to sum up the evening. *In the interest of* time, she grabbed a napkin and drew a big letter T. “The top line is breadth, and the long line is depth,” she said. Chloe said video design is so competitive that you have to be versatile. Ben joked that he’s a specialist in only one thing, good coffee. Daniel admitted that his research is a narrow niche. “Without other disciplines, it would be useful to a few experts *at best*.” Grace added that curiosity is underrated. “If you love learning, you can always adapt.” Jiwoo folded the napkin and put it in her bag. Maybe the question itself was a false choice.
steps.gloss: head to ~로 향하다 · in the interest of ~을 위해서 · competitive 경쟁이 치열한 · niche 틈새 분야 · at best 잘해야, 기껏해야 · false choice 잘못된 양자택일
questions: What did Grace draw on the napkin?
What does Grace say is underrated?

steps.title: 일과 의미
steps.scene_desc: 2월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 작은 식당 창가 자리. 마야와 지우가 마주 앉아 국수와 덮밥을 먹으며 이야기하고, 지우가 휴대폰 화면(글자 없이)을 마야에게 보여 주며 웃음. 창밖은 늦겨울 거리(간판 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s a matter of priorities." (일과 의미). Goal: 핵심 가치를 말하고 조건부로 양보하기. Today's scene: 2월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 작은 식당 창가 자리. 마야와 지우가 마주 앉아 국수와 덮밥을 먹으며 이야기하고, 지우가 휴대폰 화면(글자 없이)을 마야에게 보여 주며 웃음. 창밖은 늦겨울 거리(간판 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "For me, it boils down to ___.".

steps.en: For me, it boils down to ___.
steps.when: 여러 이유를 줄이고 줄여 가장 중요한 하나를 말해요. 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: For me, it boils down to helping real people.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "For me, it boils down to ___." (저한테는 결국 ~예요.). When to use it: 여러 이유를 줄이고 줄여 가장 중요한 하나를 말해요. 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: For me, it boils down to helping real people.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’d be willing to ___ if ___.".

steps.when: 조건을 달고 양보할 수 있는 것을 말해요. if 뒤에는 *과거형*(가정).
steps.extra: I’d be willing to take a pay cut if I believed in the work.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’d be willing to ___ if ___." (~라면 ~할 의향이 있어요.). When to use it: 조건을 달고 양보할 수 있는 것을 말해요. if 뒤에는 과거형(가정). Note: I’d be willing to take a pay cut if I believed in the work.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s a matter of priorities.".

steps.extra: Money or meaning? It’s a matter of priorities.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s a matter of priorities." (우선순위의 문제예요.). When to use it: 맞고 틀림이 아니라 무엇을 먼저 두느냐의 차이라고 정리해요. Note: Money or meaning? It’s a matter of priorities.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("What Keeps You Going? · 2월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: What Keeps You Going? · 2월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, I ask everyone on my team this sooner or later. What keeps you going at work?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 우리 팀 모두에게 언젠가는 묻는 질문이에요. 일할 때 뭐가 계속 힘이 돼요?

lines.en: Honestly? Last week, an older user wrote that she could finally return a bike on her own, thanks to our redesigned screen.
lines.ko: 솔직히요? 지난주에 나이 든 이용자 한 분이 우리가 고친 화면 덕분에 드디어 혼자 자전거를 반납했다고 쓰셨어요.

lines.en: Lovely. Tell me more. Why did that one comment matter so much?
lines.ko: 좋네요. 더 얘기해 봐요. 그 댓글 하나가 왜 그렇게 중요했어요?

lines.en: Because it’s real. {{For me, it boils down to}} helping actual people. When my design makes someone’s day easier, the work feels meaningful.
lines.ko: 진짜니까요. 저한테는 결국 실제 사람을 돕는 거예요. 제 디자인이 누군가의 하루를 편하게 해 주면 일이 의미 있게 느껴져요.

lines.en: I get that. For me, it’s watching my team grow. You were nervous in meetings at first. Now you run them.
lines.ko: 알아요. 저는 팀이 성장하는 걸 보는 거예요. 처음엔 회의 때 긴장했었죠. 지금은 회의를 진행하잖아요.

lines.en: Thanks. But honestly, meaning doesn’t pay the rent.
lines.ko: 고마워요. 그래도 솔직히, 의미가 월세를 내 주진 않잖아요.

lines.en: True. Money isn’t everything, but it helps. Would you ever take a pay cut for a more meaningful job?
lines.ko: 맞아요. 돈이 전부는 아니지만 도움은 되죠. 더 의미 있는 일을 위해 급여가 줄어도 괜찮겠어요?

lines.en: Hmm. {{I’d be willing to}} take a small one {{if}} I really believed in the work. But not a big one. I have bills like everyone else.
lines.ko: 음. 그 일을 정말 믿는다면 조금 줄어드는 건 괜찮아요. 많이는 말고요. 저도 다른 사람들처럼 낼 돈이 있으니까요.

lines.en: Fair. And not everyone can afford to choose.
lines.ko: 그렇죠. 그리고 모두가 고를 수 있는 형편은 아니에요.

lines.en: Exactly. So I don’t think there’s one right answer. {{It’s a matter of priorities}}, and priorities change at different stages of life.
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 그래서 정답은 하나가 아니라고 봐요. 우선순위의 문제고, 우선순위는 삶의 시기마다 바뀌어요.

lines.en: Mine did. In my twenties, I only wanted a big title, and I came close to burnout. Now I know a sense of purpose keeps you going longer.
lines.ko: 제 건 바뀌었어요. 20대에는 높은 직함만 원했고, 번아웃 직전까지 갔어요. 이제는 목적의식이 더 오래 버티게 해 준다는 걸 알아요.

lines.en: It sounds simple, but people forget it. In a sense, we do the same job. We help people, users for me and teammates for you.
lines.ko: 간단해 보여도 다들 잊죠. 어떤 의미에서는 우리 둘 다 같은 일을 해요. 사람을 돕는 거요. 저는 사용자를, 마야는 팀원을요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "What Keeps You Going? · 2월 말 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "Jiwoo, I ask everyone on my team this sooner or later. What keeps you going at work?" (지우 씨, 우리 팀 모두에게 언젠가는 묻는 질문이에요. 일할 때 뭐가 계속 힘이 돼요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Honestly? Last week, an older user wrote that she could finally return a bike on her own, thanks to our redesigned screen." (솔직히요? 지난주에 나이 든 이용자 한 분이 우리가 고친 화면 덕분에 드디어 혼자 자전거를 반납했다고 쓰셨어요.)
3. Maya: "Lovely. Tell me more. Why did that one comment matter so much?" (좋네요. 더 얘기해 봐요. 그 댓글 하나가 왜 그렇게 중요했어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Because it’s real. For me, it boils down to helping actual people. When my design makes someone’s day easier, the work feels meaningful." (진짜니까요. 저한테는 결국 실제 사람을 돕는 거예요. 제 디자인이 누군가의 하루를 편하게 해 주면 일이 의미 있게 느껴져요.)
5. Maya: "I get that. For me, it’s watching my team grow. You were nervous in meetings at first. Now you run them." (알아요. 저는 팀이 성장하는 걸 보는 거예요. 처음엔 회의 때 긴장했었죠. 지금은 회의를 진행하잖아요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Thanks. But honestly, meaning doesn’t pay the rent." (고마워요. 그래도 솔직히, 의미가 월세를 내 주진 않잖아요.)
7. Maya: "True. Money isn’t everything, but it helps. Would you ever take a pay cut for a more meaningful job?" (맞아요. 돈이 전부는 아니지만 도움은 되죠. 더 의미 있는 일을 위해 급여가 줄어도 괜찮겠어요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Hmm. I’d be willing to take a small one if I really believed in the work. But not a big one. I have bills like everyone else." (음. 그 일을 정말 믿는다면 조금 줄어드는 건 괜찮아요. 많이는 말고요. 저도 다른 사람들처럼 낼 돈이 있으니까요.)
9. Maya: "Fair. And not everyone can afford to choose." (그렇죠. 그리고 모두가 고를 수 있는 형편은 아니에요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Exactly. So I don’t think there’s one right answer. It’s a matter of priorities, and priorities change at different stages of life." (바로 그거예요. 그래서 정답은 하나가 아니라고 봐요. 우선순위의 문제고, 우선순위는 삶의 시기마다 바뀌어요.)
11. Maya: "Mine did. In my twenties, I only wanted a big title, and I came close to burnout. Now I know a sense of purpose keeps you going longer." (제 건 바뀌었어요. 20대에는 높은 직함만 원했고, 번아웃 직전까지 갔어요. 이제는 목적의식이 더 오래 버티게 해 준다는 걸 알아요.)
12. Jiwoo: "It sounds simple, but people forget it. In a sense, we do the same job. We help people, users for me and teammates for you." (간단해 보여도 다들 잊죠. 어떤 의미에서는 우리 둘 다 같은 일을 해요. 사람을 돕는 거요. 저는 사용자를, 마야는 팀원을요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

frame: For me, it boils down to ___.
head: For me, it boils down to …
I’d be willing to …
if …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: For me, it boils down to ___. / I’d be willing to ___ if ___. Table (For me, it boils down to … → I’d be willing to …):
- helping real people. → take a pay cut
- learning new things. → work longer hours
- a good team. → change jobs
- having free time. → earn a bit less
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I’m *willing to* learn. 배울 의향이 있어요. 
I’d *be willing to* move *if* the job *was* right. (가정 — if 뒤는 과거형) 
I’m *not willing to* work every weekend. ~할 생각은 없어요.

It *boils down to* people. 결국 사람 문제예요. 
It boils down to *helping* others. (to 뒤 -ing) 
boil down = 끓여 졸이다 → 줄이고 줄여 핵심만 남다
errors: I’m willing take a pay cut.
I’m willing to take a pay cut.
It boils down to help people.
It boils down to helping people.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- be willing to + 동사원형: I’m willing to learn. 배울 의향이 있어요. / I’d be willing to move if the job was right. (가정 — if 뒤는 과거형) / I’m not willing to work every weekend. ~할 생각은 없어요.
- boil down to + 명사 / -ing: It boils down to people. 결국 사람 문제예요. / It boils down to helping others. (to 뒤 -ing) / boil down = 끓여 졸이다 → 줄이고 줄여 핵심만 남다
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m willing take a pay cut. → I’m willing to take a pay cut. (willing 뒤에 to가 꼭 있어야 해요.)
- It boils down to help people. → It boils down to helping people. (여기 to는 전치사라 -ing.)
- Meaning don’t pay the rent. → Meaning doesn’t pay the rent. (meaning은 단수라 doesn’t.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: be willing to + 동사원형: I’m willing to learn. 배울 의향이 있어요. I’d be willing to move if the job was right. (가정 — if 뒤는 과거형) I’m not willing to work every weekend. ~할 생각은 없어요.
boil down to + 명사 / -ing: It boils down to people. 결국 사람 문제예요. It boils down to helping others. (to 뒤 -ing) boil down = 끓여 졸이다 → 줄이고 줄여 핵심만 남다
mistakes: I’m willing take a pay cut. → I’m willing to take a pay cut.
It boils down to help people. → It boils down to helping people.
Meaning don’t pay the rent. → Meaning doesn’t pay the rent.

steps.note: 예) take a pay cut / I believed in it → A: Would you take a pay cut? B: I’d be willing to take a pay cut if I believed in it.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) take a pay cut / I believed in it → A: Would you take a pay cut? B: I’d be willing to take a pay cut if I believed in it. Items (situation → model answer): take a pay cut → I believed in it | work weekends → it was short-term | move cities → the team was great | learn to code → I had more time.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: For me, it boils down to ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It’s a matter of priorities." (일과 의미); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "For me, it boils down to ___." / "I’d be willing to ___ if ___." / "It’s a matter of priorities.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.title: Three Questions on the Whiteboard
steps.text: That afternoon, Maya *laid out* three questions on the whiteboard for a short team chat. What gives your work meaning? What would you sacrifice for it? What wouldn’t you sacrifice? One teammate said his motivation was simple, a stable livelihood for his family. Another said she finds her fulfillment in music, outside work, so a calm job is the right fit for her. A third designer said she would love to work for a purpose-driven company, but idealism alone wouldn’t fulfill her if the team was unkind. Jiwoo shared the user’s comment from last week. Maya listened and smiled. “It’s *common sense*, but we often forget it,” she said. “Everyone’s contribution matters, and everyone’s reasons are different. No answer is wrong.”

steps.title: 긱 경제
steps.scene_desc: 3월 첫 토요일 저녁, 아파트 3층 벤의 집 현관. 헬멧을 쓴 배달 기사(로고 없는 큰 보온 가방)가 음식 봉투를 건네고, 벤이 고맙다며 받음. 뒤쪽 거실 식탁에 지우·그레이스·클로이·마야·대니얼이 앉아 있음(간판·로고·글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s a double-edged sword." (긱 경제). Goal: 위험과 자유를 저울질하기. Today's scene: 3월 첫 토요일 저녁, 아파트 3층 벤의 집 현관. 헬멧을 쓴 배달 기사(로고 없는 큰 보온 가방)가 음식 봉투를 건네고, 벤이 고맙다며 받음. 뒤쪽 거실 식탁에 지우·그레이스·클로이·마야·대니얼이 앉아 있음(간판·로고·글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "You have to weigh up ___ against ___.".

steps.en: You have to weigh up ___ against ___.
steps.when: 좋은 점과 나쁜 점을 나란히 놓고 따져 봐요. *weigh up A against B*.
steps.extra: You have to weigh up the freedom against the risk.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "You have to weigh up ___ against ___." (~와 ~를 저울질해 봐야 해요.). When to use it: 좋은 점과 나쁜 점을 나란히 놓고 따져 봐요. weigh up A against B. Note: You have to weigh up the freedom against the risk.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "On paper, ___, but in reality ___.".

steps.title: Your Own Boss? · 3월 첫 토요일 저녁, 벤의 집에서

lines.en: Delivery for Ben? Two chicken dishes, rice, and a big salad.
lines.ko: 벤 씨 배달이요? 치킨 요리 두 개, 밥, 큰 샐러드예요.

lines.en: That’s us. Thanks so much! It must be freezing out there.
lines.ko: 저희예요. 정말 고마워요! 밖에 엄청 춥죠.

lines.en: It’s OK. I have five more orders before nine, so I’d better run. Enjoy!
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 9시 전에 주문이 다섯 건 더 있어서 서둘러야 해요. 맛있게 드세요!

lines.en: He was in such a hurry. I wonder if he likes the work.
lines.ko: 정말 바빠 보이네요. 그 일을 좋아하실까요?

lines.en: Hard to say. Some couriers love the flexibility. You’re your own boss, and you can log off whenever you want.
lines.ko: 모르죠. 유연해서 좋아하는 배달 기사도 있어요. 내가 내 사장이고, 원할 때 언제든 앱을 끌 수 있으니까요.

lines.en: {{On paper}}, you choose your hours, {{but in reality}} the orders decide. It can feel like platforms hold all the power.
lines.ko: 서류상으로는 시간을 고르지만, 실제로는 주문이 정하죠. 플랫폼이 모든 힘을 쥔 것처럼 느껴질 수 있어요.

lines.en: Really? How is it?

lines.en: Right. If the orders stop, income can be unpredictable.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 주문이 끊기면 수입을 예측할 수 없죠.

lines.en: So {{you have to weigh up}} the freedom {{against}} the risk. It suits some lifestyles, but not others.
lines.ko: 그래서 자유와 위험을 저울질해 봐야 해요. 어떤 생활 방식에는 맞고, 어떤 데는 안 맞아요.

lines.en: I see both sides. The flexibility is real, but so is the pressure. Some people even call it precarious work.
lines.ko: 양쪽 다 이해돼요. 유연함도 진짜지만 압박도 진짜예요. 불안정한 일이라고까지 말하는 사람도 있어요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Your Own Boss? · 3월 첫 토요일 저녁, 벤의 집에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Courier: "Delivery for Ben? Two chicken dishes, rice, and a big salad." (벤 씨 배달이요? 치킨 요리 두 개, 밥, 큰 샐러드예요.)
2. Ben: "That’s us. Thanks so much! It must be freezing out there." (저희예요. 정말 고마워요! 밖에 엄청 춥죠.)
3. Courier: "It’s OK. I have five more orders before nine, so I’d better run. Enjoy!" (괜찮아요. 9시 전에 주문이 다섯 건 더 있어서 서둘러야 해요. 맛있게 드세요!)
4. Jiwoo: "He was in such a hurry. I wonder if he likes the work." (정말 바빠 보이네요. 그 일을 좋아하실까요?)
5. Ben: "Hard to say. Some couriers love the flexibility. You’re your own boss, and you can log off whenever you want." (모르죠. 유연해서 좋아하는 배달 기사도 있어요. 내가 내 사장이고, 원할 때 언제든 앱을 끌 수 있으니까요.)
6. Jiwoo: "On paper, you choose your hours, but in reality the orders decide. It can feel like platforms hold all the power." (서류상으로는 시간을 고르지만, 실제로는 주문이 정하죠. 플랫폼이 모든 힘을 쥔 것처럼 느껴질 수 있어요.)
7. Ben: "That’s fair. I do a bit of freelance work myself, you know. I proofread English texts on some weekends." (일리 있어요. 사실 저도 프리랜서 일을 조금 해요. 주말에 가끔 영어 글을 교정하거든요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Really? How is it?" (정말요? 어때요?)
9. Ben: "It works as a side hustle. I send an invoice after each job. But I have a full-time job with benefits. People who rely on gigs may have no safety net." (부업으로는 괜찮아요. 일이 끝날 때마다 청구서를 보내요. 하지만 저는 복리 후생이 있는 정규직이 있잖아요. 건별 일에만 기대는 사람에겐 안전망이 없을 수도 있어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Right. If the orders stop, income can be unpredictable." (맞아요. 주문이 끊기면 수입을 예측할 수 없죠.)
11. Ben: "So you have to weigh up the freedom against the risk. It suits some lifestyles, but not others." (그래서 자유와 위험을 저울질해 봐야 해요. 어떤 생활 방식에는 맞고, 어떤 데는 안 맞아요.)
12. Jiwoo: "I see both sides. The flexibility is real, but so is the pressure. Some people even call it precarious work." (양쪽 다 이해돼요. 유연함도 진짜지만 압박도 진짜예요. 불안정한 일이라고까지 말하는 사람도 있어요.)
13. Ben: "Exactly. It’s a double-edged sword. Now, let’s eat before our own delivery gets cold!" (그렇죠. 양날의 칼이에요. 자, 우리 배달 음식이 식기 전에 먹읍시다!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

7. Ben (you): "That’s fair. I do a bit of freelance work myself, you know. I proofread English texts on some weekends." (일리 있어요. 사실 저도 프리랜서 일을 조금 해요. 주말에 가끔 영어 글을 교정하거든요.)

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Courier and Ben. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: You have to weigh up ___ against ___. / On paper, ___, but in reality ___. Table (You have to weigh up … → against …):
- the freedom → the risk.
- extra money → your free time.
- being your own boss → having no safety net.
- flexible hours → unpredictable income.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

up 없이 weigh A against B라고도 해요.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- weigh up A against B: You have to weigh up the freedom against the risk. / I’m still weighing it up. 아직 따져 보는 중이에요. (대명사는 weigh와 up 사이) / up 없이 weigh A against B라고도 해요.
- On paper, …, but in reality …: On paper, it’s a great deal. 조건·서류상으로는 / In reality, it’s hard work. 실제로는 / on paper = 이론상·겉보기에는(진짜 종이 이야기가 아니에요)
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m weighing up it. → I’m weighing it up. (대명사(it)는 weigh와 up 사이.)
- On the paper, it looks easy. → On paper, it looks easy. (이 뜻일 때는 the 없이.)
- It’s a double-edge sword. → It’s a double-edged sword. (double-edged(-ed)로 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

steps.title: Ben’s Side Gig
steps.text: After dinner, the group kept talking. Ben explained how his side gig works. As an independent contractor, he sends an invoice for each job. *On average*, he gets two proofreading jobs a month. “That’s fine for me, because my full-time job gives me insurance and other benefits,” he said. Maya pointed out that many delivery and rideshare apps are *on the market*, so they compete for workers, too. 2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "There’s a fine line." (야망). Goal: 장단점을 사례로 따지고 선을 긋기. steps.title: At What Cost? · 4월 저녁, 퇴근 후 회사 옥상 정원에서

lines.en: You’ve been quiet all day, Maya. Everything OK?
lines.ko: 오늘 하루 종일 조용하던데요, 마야. 괜찮아요?

lines.en: This morning, I was asked to lead a bigger project with an overseas client.
lines.ko: 오늘 아침에 해외 고객과 하는 더 큰 프로젝트를 맡아 달라는 제안을 받았어요.

lines.en: Congratulations! So why the long face?
lines.ko: 축하해요! 그런데 왜 그렇게 시무룩해요?

lines.en: Because {{it comes at a cost}}. Late calls, more travel, less time with the team. I’m not sure I’m that ambitious anymore.
lines.ko: 대가가 따르니까요. 늦은 통화, 더 많은 출장, 팀과 보낼 시간은 줄고요. 제가 아직 그렇게 야망이 큰지 모르겠어요.

lines.en: But {{ambition can be}} a good thing. Without ambition, nothing changes.
lines.ko: 하지만 야망은 좋은 것일 수 있어요. 야망이 없으면 아무것도 안 바뀌잖아요.

lines.en: True. But I’ve seen the other side. My old boss was relentless, a real workaholic. He expected us to answer emails at midnight.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그런데 반대쪽도 봤어요. 예전 상사는 쉴 줄 모르는 일 중독자였어요. 한밤중에도 이메일에 답하길 바랐죠.

lines.en: That sounds toxic.
lines.ko: 해로운 분위기였겠네요.

lines.en: It was. {{There’s a fine line between}} ambition {{and}} greed.
lines.ko: 그랬어요. 야망과 탐욕은 종이 한 장 차이예요.

lines.en: But ambition isn’t greed. Healthy ambition is about growth, for you and for the team.
lines.ko: 그래도 야망이 탐욕은 아니에요. 건강한 야망은 성장에 관한 거예요. 마야에게도, 팀에게도요.

lines.en: Say it like you mean it, Jiwoo. Why should I take it?
lines.ko: 진심을 담아 말해 봐요, 지우 씨. 제가 왜 맡아야 해요?

lines.en: Because you’re the best person for it, and we’re ready. If you turn it down, we all miss the chance to work with overseas clients.
lines.ko: 마야가 가장 적임자고, 저희도 준비됐으니까요. 마야가 거절하면 우리 모두 해외 고객과 일할 기회를 놓쳐요.

lines.en: That was convincing! But a project like this can strain relationships, too.
lines.ko: 설득력 있네요! 그래도 이런 프로젝트는 관계에도 부담을 줄 수 있어요.

lines.en: Then take it, on one condition. Protect the team’s hours, and yours.
lines.ko: 그럼 조건 하나를 걸고 맡아요. 팀 근무 시간을 지키기. 마야 시간도요.

lines.en: No calls after seven, except real emergencies? I like that. I’ll say yes on that condition.
lines.ko: 저녁 7시 이후엔 진짜 급한 일 말고는 통화 없음? 좋아요. 그 조건으로 하겠다고 할게요.

7. Jiwoo: "That sounds toxic." (해로운 분위기였겠네요.)
8. Maya: "It was. There’s a fine line between ambition and greed." (그랬어요. 야망과 탐욕은 종이 한 장 차이예요.)
9. Jiwoo: "But ambition isn’t greed. Healthy ambition is about growth, for you and for the team." (그래도 야망이 탐욕은 아니에요. 건강한 야망은 성장에 관한 거예요. 마야에게도, 팀에게도요.)
10. Maya: "Say it like you mean it, Jiwoo. Why should I take it?" (진심을 담아 말해 봐요, 지우 씨. 제가 왜 맡아야 해요?)
11. Jiwoo: "Because you’re the best person for it, and we’re ready. If you turn it down, we all miss the chance to work with overseas clients." (마야가 가장 적임자고, 저희도 준비됐으니까요. 마야가 거절하면 우리 모두 해외 고객과 일할 기회를 놓쳐요.)
12. Maya: "That was convincing! But a project like this can strain relationships, too." (설득력 있네요! 그래도 이런 프로젝트는 관계에도 부담을 줄 수 있어요.)
13. Jiwoo: "Then take it, on one condition. Protect the team’s hours, and yours." (그럼 조건 하나를 걸고 맡아요. 팀 근무 시간을 지키기. 마야 시간도요.)
14. Maya: "No calls after seven, except real emergencies? I like that. I’ll say yes on that condition." (저녁 7시 이후엔 진짜 급한 일 말고는 통화 없음? 좋아요. 그 조건으로 하겠다고 할게요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. The learner speaks first: call highlight_line with 1 and invite them to start. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Maya got the offer this morning.
Maya’s old boss never contacted the team late at night.
Maya will say yes if the team’s working hours are protected.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Maya got the offer this morning.
2. Maya’s old boss never contacted the team late at night.
3. Maya will say yes if the team’s working hours are protected.
The scene they are about:
1. Jiwoo: "You’ve been quiet all day, Maya. Everything OK?" (오늘 하루 종일 조용하던데요, 마야. 괜찮아요?)
2. Maya: "This morning, I was asked to lead a bigger project with an overseas client." (오늘 아침에 해외 고객과 하는 더 큰 프로젝트를 맡아 달라는 제안을 받았어요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Congratulations! So why the long face?" (축하해요! 그런데 왜 그렇게 시무룩해요?)
4. Maya: "Because it comes at a cost. Late calls, more travel, less time with the team. I’m not sure I’m that ambitious anymore." (대가가 따르니까요. 늦은 통화, 더 많은 출장, 팀과 보낼 시간은 줄고요. 제가 아직 그렇게 야망이 큰지 모르겠어요.)
5. Jiwoo: "But ambition can be a good thing. Without ambition, nothing changes." (하지만 야망은 좋은 것일 수 있어요. 야망이 없으면 아무것도 안 바뀌잖아요.)
6. Maya: "True. But I’ve seen the other side. My old boss was relentless, a real workaholic. He expected us to answer emails at midnight." (맞아요. 그런데 반대쪽도 봤어요. 예전 상사는 쉴 줄 모르는 일 중독자였어요. 한밤중에도 이메일에 답하길 바랐죠.)
7. Jiwoo: "That sounds toxic." (해로운 분위기였겠네요.)
8. Maya: "It was. There’s a fine line between ambition and greed." (그랬어요. 야망과 탐욕은 종이 한 장 차이예요.)
9. Jiwoo: "But ambition isn’t greed. Healthy ambition is about growth, for you and for the team." (그래도 야망이 탐욕은 아니에요. 건강한 야망은 성장에 관한 거예요. 마야에게도, 팀에게도요.)
10. Maya: "Say it like you mean it, Jiwoo. Why should I take it?" (진심을 담아 말해 봐요, 지우 씨. 제가 왜 맡아야 해요?)
11. Jiwoo: "Because you’re the best person for it, and we’re ready. If you turn it down, we all miss the chance to work with overseas clients." (마야가 가장 적임자고, 저희도 준비됐으니까요. 마야가 거절하면 우리 모두 해외 고객과 일할 기회를 놓쳐요.)
12. Maya: "That was convincing! But a project like this can strain relationships, too." (설득력 있네요! 그래도 이런 프로젝트는 관계에도 부담을 줄 수 있어요.)
13. Jiwoo: "Then take it, on one condition. Protect the team’s hours, and yours." (그럼 조건 하나를 걸고 맡아요. 팀 근무 시간을 지키기. 마야 시간도요.)
14. Maya: "No calls after seven, except real emergencies? I like that. I’ll say yes on that condition." (저녁 7시 이후엔 진짜 급한 일 말고는 통화 없음? 좋아요. 그 조건으로 하겠다고 할게요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: There’s a fine line between ___ and ___.
head: Ambition can be …
There’s a fine line between …
and …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Ambition can be ___. / It can ___. / There’s a fine line between ___ and ___. Table (Ambition can be … → There’s a fine line between …):
- a good thing. → ambition
- healthy. → hard work
- exhausting. → confidence
- a great motivator. → high standards
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Ambition *can be* healthy. 야망은 건강할 수 있어요. 
It *can strain* relationships. 관계에 부담을 줄 수도 있어요. 
‘할 줄 안다’(능력)가 아니라 ‘그런 경우가 있다’는 뜻이에요.

Big projects *can* be stressful. 큰 프로젝트는 (대개) 힘들 수 있어요. 
This project *could* help the team. 이번 프로젝트는 팀에 도움이 될지도 몰라요.
errors: There’s a fine line between love or hate.
There’s a fine line between love and hate.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- can + 동사원형 = ~일 수 있다(가능성): Ambition can be healthy. 야망은 건강할 수 있어요. / It can strain relationships. 관계에 부담을 줄 수도 있어요. / ‘할 줄 안다’(능력)가 아니라 ‘그런 경우가 있다’는 뜻이에요.
- can(일반적으로) · could(이번 일은): Big projects can be stressful. 큰 프로젝트는 (대개) 힘들 수 있어요. / This project could help the team. 이번 프로젝트는 팀에 도움이 될지도 몰라요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Ambition can is good. → Ambition can be good. (can 뒤에는 동사원형 be.)
- It can strains relationships. → It can strain relationships. (can 뒤 동사에는 -s를 붙이지 않아요.)
- There’s a fine line between love or hate. → There’s a fine line between love and hate. (between A and B로 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: can + 동사원형 = ~일 수 있다(가능성): Ambition can be healthy. 야망은 건강할 수 있어요. It can strain relationships. 관계에 부담을 줄 수도 있어요. ‘할 줄 안다’(능력)가 아니라 ‘그런 경우가 있다’는 뜻이에요.
can(일반적으로) · could(이번 일은): Big projects can be stressful. 큰 프로젝트는 (대개) 힘들 수 있어요. This project could help the team. 이번 프로젝트는 팀에 도움이 될지도 몰라요.
mistakes: Ambition can is good. → Ambition can be good.
It can strains relationships. → It can strain relationships.
There’s a fine line between love or hate. → There’s a fine line between love and hate.

steps.note: 예) ambition / greed → A: Ambition can be healthy. B: True, but there’s a fine line between ambition and greed.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) ambition / greed → A: Ambition can be healthy. B: True, but there’s a fine line between ambition and greed. Items (situation → model answer): ambition → greed | confidence → arrogance | hard work → overwork | high standards → perfectionism.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: There’s a fine line between ___ and ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "There’s a fine line." (야망); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Ambition can be ___." / "There’s a fine line between ___ and ___." / "It comes at a cost.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Some people burn out chasing it.
야망을 좇다 지쳐 버리는 사람도 있어요.
Success means different things to different people.
만족할 줄 아는 마음은 과소평가돼 있어요.
It depends on what drives you.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 야망의 좋은 점: "Without ambition, nothing changes." (야망이 없으면 아무것도 바뀌지 않아요., 보통); "Healthy ambition is about growth." (건강한 야망은 성장에 관한 거예요., 보통); "Ambition isn’t greed." (야망은 탐욕이 아니에요., 친근)
- 야망의 그늘: "Some people burn out chasing it." (야망을 좇다 지쳐 버리는 사람도 있어요., 보통); "It can strain relationships." (관계에 부담을 줄 수 있어요., 보통); "It turns toxic when ___." (~하면 해로워져요., 보통)
- 사람마다 달라요: "Success means different things to different people." (성공의 뜻은 사람마다 달라요., 정중); "Contentment is underrated." (만족할 줄 아는 마음은 과소평가돼 있어요., 보통); "It depends on what drives you." (무엇이 나를 움직이느냐에 달렸어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 덩어리 표현

How did it *come about*? 어떻게 그렇게 됐어요? · *turn down* an offer 제안을 거절하다 
*come to terms with* the past 지난 일을 받아들이다 · a *touch of* surprise 약간의 놀라움
(참고) 일과 야망을 말하는 말

*aim high* 목표를 높게 잡다 · *climb the ladder* (회사에서) 승진해 올라가다 
*work-life balance* 일과 삶의 균형 · say yes *on one condition* 조건 하나를 걸고 승낙하다 
마야의 제안과 해외 고객은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
steps.blank:
A: Is ambition a good thing?   B: It ___ be. But there’s a fine ___ between ambition and greed. 
A: And a big job comes ___ a cost.   B: True. It depends on what ___ you. 
낱말 상자: can · line · at · drives
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 덩어리 표현: How did it come about? 어떻게 그렇게 됐어요? · turn down an offer 제안을 거절하다 / come to terms with the past 지난 일을 받아들이다 · a touch of surprise 약간의 놀라움
- (참고) 일과 야망을 말하는 말: aim high 목표를 높게 잡다 · climb the ladder (회사에서) 승진해 올라가다 / work-life balance 일과 삶의 균형 · say yes on one condition 조건 하나를 걸고 승낙하다 / 마야의 제안과 해외 고객은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Is ambition a good thing? B: It ___ be. But there’s a fine ___ between ambition and greed. / A: And a big job comes ___ a cost. B: True. It depends on what ___ you. / 낱말 상자: can · line · at · drives
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: ambitious (야망 있는, 포부가 큰), greed (탐욕), toxic (유독한; (분위기·관계가) 해로운), strain (부담을 주다; 부담, 무리), relentless (끈질긴, 쉬지 않는), recognition (인정(받음), 알아줌), competition (경쟁; 대회), perfectionism (완벽주의), workaholic (일 중독자(일만 하는 사람)), rat race (끝없는 출세 경쟁), achievement (성취, 업적), success (성공).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: 자존감, 스스로 가치 있다고 느끼는 마음
She has a lot of drive.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: self-worth (자존감, 스스로 가치 있다고 느끼는 마음) — "My self-worth depended on recognition."; ambition (야망, 포부) — "Without ambition, nothing changes."; drive (추진력, 해내려는 의욕) — "She has a lot of drive."; sacrifice (희생) — "It takes some sacrifice."; status ((사회적) 지위) — "a job with high status"; fulfillment (성취감, 보람) — "Growth brings fulfillment."; cost (비용; 대가) — "It comes at a cost."; contentment (만족(가진 것에 만족하는 마음)) — "Contentment is underrated.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Would you call yourself ambitious? Why or why not?
Name two things with a fine line between them.
There’s a fine line between ___ and ___.
Think of something good that came at a cost. What was the cost?
___ was great, but it came at a cost. ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Would you call yourself ambitious? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: I’m (not) very ambitious because ___.)
- "When can ambition turn toxic?" (hint on screen: It turns toxic when ___.)
- "Name two things with a fine line between them." (hint on screen: There’s a fine line between ___ and ___.)
- "Think of something good that came at a cost. What was the cost?" (hint on screen: ___ was great, but it came at a cost. ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Would you call yourself ambitious? Why or why not?
When can ambition turn toxic?
Name two things with a fine line between them.
Think of something good that came at a cost. What was the cost?

steps.title: How the Offer Came About
steps.text: The next day, Maya told Jiwoo how the offer had *come about*. An overseas client had seen the team’s bike-sharing app and wanted something similar for their own city. There was some competition for the role, but the client asked for Maya by name. At first, she almost *turned* it *down*. “In my twenties, I was stuck in the rat race,” she admitted. “My self-worth depended on recognition, and my perfectionism made it worse.” It took her years to *come to terms with* that. Now she believes success means different things to different people. So she put her condition in a short email: no team calls after 7 p.m., except in real emergencies. Her manager agreed, with a *touch of* surprise. Then Maya smiled at Jiwoo. “Next year, you might lead some of these client meetings yourself.”
steps.gloss: come about 생기다, 일어나다 · turn down 거절하다 · rat race 끝없는 출세 경쟁 · come to terms with (힘든 일을) 받아들이다 · a touch of 약간의
questions: Who asked for Maya by name?
What was Maya’s condition?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "How the Offer Came About". Text: "The next day, Maya told Jiwoo how the offer had come about. An overseas client had seen the team’s bike-sharing app and wanted something similar for their own city. There was some competition for the role, but the client asked for Maya by name. At first, she almost turned it down. “In my twenties, I was stuck in the rat race,” she admitted. “My self-worth depended on recognition, and my perfectionism made it worse.” It took her years to come to terms with that. Now she believes success means different things to different people. So she put her condition in a short email: no team calls after 7 p.m., except in real emergencies. Her manager agreed, with a touch of surprise. Then Maya smiled at Jiwoo. “Next year, you might lead some of these client meetings yourself.”" Words: come about 생기다, 일어나다 · turn down 거절하다 · rat race 끝없는 출세 경쟁 · come to terms with (힘든 일을) 받아들이다 · a touch of 약간의.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Who asked for Maya by name?" / "What was Maya’s condition?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Ambition can be ___.’로 야망의 여러 가능성을 말할 수 있어요.
‘There’s a fine line between ___ and ___.’로 비슷한 두 가지의 경계를 짚을 수 있어요.
‘It comes at a cost.’로 좋은 일에 따르는 대가를 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Ambition can be ___.’로 야망의 여러 가능성을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘There’s a fine line between ___ and ___.’로 비슷한 두 가지의 경계를 짚을 수 있어요.
- ‘It comes at a cost.’로 좋은 일에 따르는 대가를 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 세대 차이
steps.scene_desc: 5월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당의 긴 식탁. 지우·그레이스·대니얼·클로이·마야·벤과 보스턴에서 온 벤의 부모님(60대)이 함께 앉아 있음. 벤의 어머니가 지우 쪽으로 몸을 기울여 웃으며 이야기하고, 벤은 부침개 접시를 건네며 웃음. 식탁 위에 여러 반찬과 찌개(간판·메뉴·화면에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s a two-way street." (세대 차이). Goal: 흔한 가정을 짚고 공정하게 덧붙이기. Today's scene: 5월 첫 토요일 저녁, 동네 식당의 긴 식탁. 지우·그레이스·대니얼·클로이·마야·벤과 보스턴에서 온 벤의 부모님(60대)이 함께 앉아 있음. 벤의 어머니가 지우 쪽으로 몸을 기울여 웃으며 이야기하고, 벤은 부침개 접시를 건네며 웃음. 식탁 위에 여러 반찬과 찌개(간판·메뉴·화면에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "People often assume that ___.".

steps.when: 확인 없이 널리 퍼진 생각을 짚어요. 뒤에 반박이나 다른 면을 이어 말해요.
steps.extra: People often assume that young people are always on their phones.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "People often assume that ___." (사람들은 흔히 ~라고 생각해요.). When to use it: 확인 없이 널리 퍼진 생각을 짚어요. 뒤에 반박이나 다른 면을 이어 말해요. Note: People often assume that young people are always on their phones.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "To be fair, ___.".

steps.when: 앞에서 한 비판이나 흔한 생각에 *공정한 사실*을 덧붙여요. 누구 편을 드는 게 아니라 균형을 맞춰요.
steps.extra: To be fair, the circumstances were very different.
steps.teach:

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: People often assume that ___. / To be fair, ___. Table (People often assume that … → To be fair, …):
- young people are lazy. → they work in new ways.
- older people hate apps. → many learn fast.
- young people job-hop. → they build new skills.
- older people fear change. → many try new things.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*To be fair*, times were different. 공정하게 말하면, 그때는 달랐어요. 
He’s often late. *To be fair*, he always calls. 그래도 늘 전화는 해요.
to be fair to + 사람 · partly because

*To be fair to* Mom, … 엄마 입장에서 공정하게 말하면 … 
It’s *partly because* jobs changed. 일자리가 바뀐 탓도 있어요. (여러 이유 중 하나)
errors: It’s partly because of prices rose.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- To be fair, … = 공정하게 말하면: To be fair, times were different. 공정하게 말하면, 그때는 달랐어요. / He’s often late. To be fair, he always calls. 그래도 늘 전화는 해요.
- to be fair to + 사람 · partly because: To be fair to Mom, … 엄마 입장에서 공정하게 말하면 … / It’s partly because jobs changed. 일자리가 바뀐 탓도 있어요. (여러 이유 중 하나)
Common mistakes on screen:
- The circumstances was different. → The circumstances were different. (복수 주어라 were.)
- Young people is not lazy. → Young people are not lazy. (people은 복수라 are.)
- It’s partly because of prices rose. → It’s partly because prices rose. (문장 앞에는 because(of ×).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: To be fair, … = 공정하게 말하면: To be fair, times were different. 공정하게 말하면, 그때는 달랐어요. He’s often late. To be fair, he always calls. 그래도 늘 전화는 해요.
to be fair to + 사람 · partly because: To be fair to Mom, … 엄마 입장에서 공정하게 말하면 … It’s partly because jobs changed. 일자리가 바뀐 탓도 있어요. (여러 이유 중 하나)
mistakes: The circumstances was different. → The circumstances were different.
Young people is not lazy. → Young people are not lazy.
It’s partly because of prices rose. → It’s partly because prices rose.

steps.note: 예) young people are lazy / they work differently → A: People often assume that young people are lazy. B: To be fair, they just work differently.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) young people are lazy / they work differently → A: People often assume that young people are lazy. B: To be fair, they just work differently. Items (situation → model answer): young people are lazy → they work differently | older people hate apps → many learn fast | teens never read → they read online | retirees get bored → many are very busy.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "It’s a two-way street." (세대 차이); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "People often assume that ___." / "To be fair, ___." / "It’s partly because ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Every generation complains about the next one.
어느 세대나 다음 세대를 두고 불평해요.
Young people aren’t lazy, just different.
젊은 사람들은 게으른 게 아니라 다를 뿐이에요.
We have more in common than we think.
잘 들어 주기만 해도 큰 도움이 돼요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 흔한 생각 짚기: "Every generation complains about the next one." (어느 세대나 다음 세대를 두고 불평해요., 보통); "Stereotypes cut both ways." (고정관념은 양쪽 다 있어요., 보통); "Young people aren’t lazy, just different." (젊은 사람들은 게으른 게 아니라 다를 뿐이에요., 친근)
- 공정하게 덧붙이기: "The circumstances were very different." (상황이 많이 달랐어요., 보통); "Housing prices changed everything." (집값이 모든 걸 바꿔 놨어요., 보통); "Older people have hard-earned wisdom." (어르신들에게는 힘들게 얻은 지혜가 있어요., 정중)
- 서로 이해하기: "We have more in common than we think." (우리는 생각보다 공통점이 많아요., 보통); "It’s a two-way street." (양쪽이 함께 노력해야 해요., 친근); "Listening goes a long way." (잘 들어 주기만 해도 큰 도움이 돼요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 세대 이름 (대략 태어난 시기)

a *baby boomer* (*boomer*) 대략 1946~1964년생 
a *millennial* 대략 1981~1996년생 · *Gen Z* 대략 1997~2012년생 
나누는 기준은 조금씩 달라요. 세대 이름으로 한 사람을 판단하지 않아요.
(참고) 조심해서 쓰는 낱말

a *conservative* dress code 보수적인(전통을 지키는) 복장 규정 · a *liberal* dress code 자유로운 복장 규정 
정치 이야기에도 쓰는 낱말이지만 여기서는 규칙·방식에 쓰는 일반 뜻이에요. 
*prejudice* 편견 · be *entitled* to ~할 권리가 있다 (사람을 ‘entitled’라고 하면 ‘특권 의식이 있는’이라는 비난이 돼요)

A: People often ___ that young people are lazy.   B: To be ___, they work hard in new ways. 
A: True. It’s ___ because jobs have changed.   B: Right. It’s a two-way ___.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 세대 이름 (대략 태어난 시기): a baby boomer (boomer) 대략 1946~1964년생 / a millennial 대략 1981~1996년생 · Gen Z 대략 1997~2012년생 / 나누는 기준은 조금씩 달라요. 세대 이름으로 한 사람을 판단하지 않아요.
- (참고) 조심해서 쓰는 낱말: a conservative dress code 보수적인(전통을 지키는) 복장 규정 · a liberal dress code 자유로운 복장 규정 / 정치 이야기에도 쓰는 낱말이지만 여기서는 규칙·방식에 쓰는 일반 뜻이에요. / prejudice 편견 · be entitled to ~할 권리가 있다 (사람을 ‘entitled’라고 하면 ‘특권 의식이 있는’이라는 비난이 돼요)
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: People often ___ that young people are lazy. B: To be ___, they work hard in new ways. / A: True. It’s ___ because jobs have changed. B: Right. It’s a two-way ___. / 낱말 상자: assume · fair · partly · street
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: stereotype (고정관념), assumption (가정, 넘겨짚음), circumstance ((주로 -s) 상황, 형편), wisdom (지혜), attitude (태도, 사고방식), gap (차이, 틈), prejudice (편견), resilient (회복력이 강한, 잘 이겨 내는), boomer (베이비붐 세대), millennial (밀레니얼 세대), Gen Z (Z세대), upbringing (자라 온 환경, 양육).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Everyone is entitled to their opinion.
(-s) 가치관, 중요하게 여기는 것(앞에서는 ‘가치; 소중히 여기다’)
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: entitled ((be entitled to) ~할 권리가 있다) — "Everyone is entitled to their opinion."; generation (세대) — "the generation gap"; perspective (관점, 시각) — "a new perspective"; value ((-s) 가치관, 중요하게 여기는 것(앞에서는 ‘가치; 소중히 여기다’)) — "We share the same values."; housing (주거, 집) — "housing prices"; opportunity (기회) — "new opportunities"; understanding (이해) — "Listening builds understanding."; respect (존중) — "Respect goes both ways.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What do people often assume about your generation? Is it fair?
People often assume that ___. To be fair, ___.
What’s one thing you learned from an older person?
I learned ___ from ___. Older people have hard-earned wisdom.
Why do you think generations see things differently?
What do you have in common with someone from another generation?
We both ___. We have more in common than we think.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do people often assume about your generation? Is it fair?" (hint on screen: People often assume that ___. To be fair, ___.)
- "What’s one thing you learned from an older person?" (hint on screen: I learned ___ from ___. Older people have hard-earned wisdom.)
- "Why do you think generations see things differently?" (hint on screen: It’s partly because ___.)
- "What do you have in common with someone from another generation?" (hint on screen: We both ___. We have more in common than we think.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Different Times, Different Rules
steps.text: After dinner, Ben’s mother told the group about her first office job in Boston. The dress code was very conservative, with suits every day. Ben laughed. His academy in Seoul has a much more liberal dress code, and he sometimes teaches in sneakers. “Different times, different rules,” she said. “My upbringing taught me to stay with one company. Ben had to get used to constant change.” Jiwoo said both generations were resilient in their own way. Her parents learned to use smartphones in their fifties, and her friends keep learning new skills. Soon the dinner turned into a small classroom, *as it were*. In the end, everyone agreed on one thing. The generation gap is real, but it’s smaller than people think, and even *more so* when you sit down and talk.
steps.gloss: conservative (방식이) 보수적인 · liberal (규칙이) 자유로운 · upbringing 자라 온 환경 · as it were 말하자면 · more so 더욱 그런
questions: What was the dress code like at Ben’s mother’s first job?
What did everyone agree on in the end?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Different Times, Different Rules". Text: "After dinner, Ben’s mother told the group about her first office job in Boston. The dress code was very conservative, with suits every day. Ben laughed. His academy in Seoul has a much more liberal dress code, and he sometimes teaches in sneakers. “Different times, different rules,” she said. “My upbringing taught me to stay with one company. Ben had to get used to constant change.” Jiwoo said both generations were resilient in their own way. Her parents learned to use smartphones in their fifties, and her friends keep learning new skills. Soon the dinner turned into a small classroom, as it were. In the end, everyone agreed on one thing. The generation gap is real, but it’s smaller than people think, and even more so when you sit down and talk." Words: conservative (방식이) 보수적인 · liberal (규칙이) 자유로운 · upbringing 자라 온 환경 · as it were 말하자면 · more so 더욱 그런.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was the dress code like at Ben’s mother’s first job?" / "What did everyone agree on in the end?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘People often assume that ___.’으로 흔한 가정을 짚을 수 있어요.
‘To be fair, ___.’로 공정하게 다른 면을 덧붙일 수 있어요.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

- ‘To be fair, ___.’로 공정하게 다른 면을 덧붙일 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s partly because ___.’로 여러 이유 가운데 하나를 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 온라인 수업
steps.goal: 조건을 붙여 비교하고 장점을 살리는 방법 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 5월 말 평일 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실 식탁. 노트북 한 대와 헤드셋, 메모 공책이 놓여 있음(화면·공책에 글자 없이). 그레이스가 헤드셋을 목에 걸고 공책에 메모하고, 맞은편의 지우가 웃으며 엄지를 들어 보임. 창밖은 해 질 녘
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It works best when …" (온라인 수업). Goal: 조건을 붙여 비교하고 장점을 살리는 방법 말하기. Today's scene: 5월 말 평일 저녁, 그레이스 집 거실 식탁. 노트북 한 대와 헤드셋, 메모 공책이 놓여 있음(화면·공책에 글자 없이). 그레이스가 헤드셋을 목에 걸고 공책에 메모하고, 맞은편의 지우가 웃으며 엄지를 들어 보임. 창밖은 해 질 녘. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Provided that ___, ___.".

steps.when: 조건을 분명히 붙여요. *if*보다 ‘그 조건이 꼭 맞아야’라는 느낌이 강하고 조금 격식 있어요.
steps.extra: Provided that the class is short, people will stay focused.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Provided that ___, ___." (~하기만 하면, ~해요.). When to use it: 조건을 분명히 붙여요. if보다 ‘그 조건이 꼭 맞아야’라는 느낌이 강하고 조금 격식 있어요. Note: Provided that the class is short, people will stay focused.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "What gets lost is ___.".

steps.when: 새 방식의 좋은 점을 인정하면서 *사라지는 것*을 짚어요.
steps.extra: What gets lost is the small talk before class.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "What gets lost is ___." (잃게 되는 건 ~예요.). When to use it: 새 방식의 좋은 점을 인정하면서 사라지는 것을 짚어요. Note: What gets lost is the small talk before class.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It works best when ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 방식이 가장 효과 있는 *때·조건*을 말해요.
steps.extra: It works best when students talk more than the teacher.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It works best when ___." (~할 때 가장 잘돼요.). When to use it: 어떤 방식이 가장 효과 있는 때·조건을 말해요. Note: It works best when students talk more than the teacher.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The Test Class · 5월 말 평일 저녁, 시험 수업을 마치고 그레이스 집에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: The Test Class · 5월 말 평일 저녁, 시험 수업을 마치고 그레이스 집에서

lines.en: Thanks for being my test student! So, how was it from the student side?
lines.ko: 시험 수강생이 돼 줘서 고마워요! 그래서 학생 쪽에서는 어땠어요?

lines.en: Mostly great. But at first, I couldn’t make out what you said. Your sound kept cutting out.
lines.ko: 대체로 좋았어요. 그런데 처음엔 잘 안 들렸어요. 소리가 계속 끊겼거든요.

lines.en: Oh no. It’s my first online class, with breakout rooms, polls and all that.
lines.ko: 아이고. 온라인 수업은 이번이 처음이거든요. 소그룹 방에 투표 같은 기능도 쓰고요.

lines.en: It got better after you changed headsets. And honestly, {{it opened up access for many people}}.
lines.ko: 헤드셋을 바꾸고 나서는 나아졌어요. 그리고 솔직히 많은 사람에게 배울 기회가 열렸잖아요.

lines.en: That’s my hope. But {{what gets lost is}} the chat before class. {{You miss the hallway conversations.}}
lines.ko: 저도 그러길 바라요. 그런데 잃게 되는 건 수업 전 수다예요. 복도에서 나누던 대화가 없잖아요.

lines.en: True. And {{screen fatigue is real}}. After a day of video calls, it’s tough.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그리고 화면 피로는 진짜예요. 하루 종일 화상 회의를 하고 나면 힘들어요.

lines.en: So, you mean it might be too much for office workers?
lines.ko: 그러니까 직장인에게는 너무 벅찰 수도 있다는 거죠?

lines.en: Not necessarily. {{Provided that}} the class is short and active, people will stay. {{It works best when}} students talk more than the teacher.
lines.ko: 꼭 그렇지는 않아요. 수업이 짧고 활동적이기만 하면 사람들이 남을 거예요. 선생님보다 학생이 더 많이 말할 때 가장 잘돼요.

lines.en: Good point. Some students might have weak internet, in which case they can watch the recording.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Test Class · 5월 말 평일 저녁, 시험 수업을 마치고 그레이스 집에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Grace: "Thanks for being my test student! So, how was it from the student side?" (시험 수강생이 돼 줘서 고마워요! 그래서 학생 쪽에서는 어땠어요?)

9. Grace: "Good point. Some students might have weak internet, in which case they can watch the recording." (좋은 지적이에요. 인터넷이 약한 학생도 있을 텐데, 그럴 땐 녹화본을 보면 되겠네요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Right. You can learn at your own pace with recordings. But it takes a lot of self-discipline." (맞아요. 녹화본으로는 자기 속도대로 배울 수 있죠. 하지만 자기 관리가 정말 많이 필요해요.)
11. Grace: "That’s why I’m adding one in-person class a month. A blended approach works well." (그래서 한 달에 한 번은 대면 수업을 넣으려고요. 섞어서 하는 방식이 잘 맞거든요.)

What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: Provided that …
→ 그러면 (결과)
What gets lost is …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Provided that ___, ___. / What gets lost is ___. Table (Provided that … → → 그러면 (결과)):
- the class is short, → people stay focused.
- cameras are on, → it feels more real.
- the sound is clear, → everyone joins in.
- there’s a recording, → no one falls behind.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Provided that* the class *is* short, I’ll join. 수업이 짧기만 하면 들을게요. 
조건 부분은 미래 일이어도 현재형. *as long as*와 뜻이 거의 같아요.
What gets lost · It works best when

*What gets lost is* the small talk. 잃게 되는 건 잡담이에요. 
It *works best when* it’s short. 짧을 때 가장 잘돼요.
errors: Provided that it will be short, I’ll join.
Provided that it’s short, I’ll join.
What get lost is the small talk.
What gets lost is the small talk.
It works best when students talks.
It works best when students talk.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Provided that … = ~하기만 하면: Provided that the class is short, I’ll join. 수업이 짧기만 하면 들을게요. / 조건 부분은 미래 일이어도 현재형. as long as와 뜻이 거의 같아요.
- What gets lost · It works best when: What gets lost is the small talk. 잃게 되는 건 잡담이에요. / It works best when it’s short. 짧을 때 가장 잘돼요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Provided that it will be short, I’ll join. → Provided that it’s short, I’ll join. (조건 부분은 현재형(will ×).)
- What get lost is the small talk. → What gets lost is the small talk. (What은 하나로 봐서 gets.)
- It works best when students talks. → It works best when students talk. (복수 주어라 -s 없이 talk.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: Provided that … = ~하기만 하면: Provided that the class is short, I’ll join. 수업이 짧기만 하면 들을게요. 조건 부분은 미래 일이어도 현재형. as long as와 뜻이 거의 같아요.
What gets lost · It works best when: What gets lost is the small talk. 잃게 되는 건 잡담이에요. It works best when it’s short. 짧을 때 가장 잘돼요.
mistakes: Provided that it will be short, I’ll join. → Provided that it’s short, I’ll join.
What get lost is the small talk. → What gets lost is the small talk.
It works best when students talks. → It works best when students talk.

steps.note: 예) the class is short / stay focused → Provided that the class is short, people will stay focused.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) the class is short / stay focused → Provided that the class is short, people will stay focused. Items (situation → model answer): the class is short → stay focused | cameras are on → feel connected | the sound is clear → join in | there’s a recording → catch up.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "It works best when …" (온라인 수업); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Provided that ___, ___." / "What gets lost is ___." / "It works best when ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 좋은 점: "You can learn at your own pace." (자기 속도대로 배울 수 있어요., 보통); "It opened up access for many people." (많은 사람에게 배울 기회를 열어 줬어요., 보통); "It’s here to stay." (앞으로도 계속 있을 거예요., 친근)
- 어려운 점: "It takes a lot of self-discipline." (자기 관리가 많이 필요해요., 보통); "You miss the hallway conversations." (복도에서 나누던 대화가 없어요., 보통); "Screen fatigue is real." (화면 피로는 진짜예요., 친근); "Some subjects need hands-on practice." (직접 해 봐야 하는 과목도 있어요., 보통)
- 잘하려면: "A blended approach works well." (섞어서 하는 방식이 잘 맞아요., 보통); "The teacher still makes the difference." (그래도 차이를 만드는 건 선생님이에요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 온라인 수업에서 쓰는 말

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on.
