steps.title: Grace’s New Plan
steps.text: That night, Grace rewrote her plan for the evening class. It starts in June as a trial, with twelve students. She made three changes. First, each class will be fifty minutes, not ninety, because screen fatigue is real. Second, students will talk in small breakout rooms every ten minutes, so they stay active. Third, she’ll test her sound before every class, so no one struggles to *make out* a word. Every class will be recorded. Students may miss one, *in which case* they can watch it later and send her a short voice message. Once a month, the class will meet in person for coffee, games, *and all that*. Jiwoo read the plan and smiled. “Provided that you keep it short,” she said, “I’d sign up.”
steps.gloss: trial 시범 · breakout room 소그룹 방 · make out 알아듣다 · in which case 그런 경우에는 · and all that 그런 것들
questions: Why will each class be fifty minutes?
What can students do if they miss a class?

steps.title: 학교가 가르쳐야 할 것
steps.scene_desc: 6월 첫 토요일 밤, 지우의 아파트(5층) 부엌. 저녁 모임이 끝난 뒤 그레이스가 고무장갑을 끼고 설거지하고, 지우가 행주로 그릇을 닦으며 이야기함. 뒤쪽 거실에는 빈 접시가 놓인 식탁과 소파에서 이야기하는 벤·마야·클로이·대니얼이 흐릿하게 보임. 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It should have been taught." (학교가 가르쳐야 할 것). Goal: 빠진 것을 짚고 우선순위를 주장하기. Today's scene: 6월 첫 토요일 밤, 지우의 아파트(5층) 부엌. 저녁 모임이 끝난 뒤 그레이스가 고무장갑을 끼고 설거지하고, 지우가 행주로 그릇을 닦으며 이야기함. 뒤쪽 거실에는 빈 접시가 놓인 식탁과 소파에서 이야기하는 벤·마야·클로이·대니얼이 흐릿하게 보임. 글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It should have been taught ___.".

Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

steps.title: After the Dinner · 6월 첫 토요일 밤, 지우 집 부엌에서

lines.en: Dinner was amazing, Jiwoo. Let me wash, and you dry.
lines.ko: 저녁 정말 맛있었어요, 지우 씨. 제가 씻을 테니 지우 씨가 닦아요.

lines.en: Deal. I keep thinking about Maya. She said she learned to budget from online videos.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 마야 씨 말이 계속 생각나요. 예산 짜는 법을 인터넷 영상으로 배웠다고 했잖아요.

lines.en: We didn’t learn much about that at school, either.
lines.ko: 학교에서도 그걸 많이 배우지는 않았어요.

lines.en: Right! {{It should have been taught}} in high school. I couldn’t even read my first rental contract.
lines.ko: 맞아요! 그건 고등학교 때 가르쳤어야 했어요. 저는 첫 임대 계약서도 제대로 못 읽었어요.

lines.en: So, you mean school should be more practical?
lines.ko: 그러니까 학교가 더 실용적이어야 한다는 거죠?

lines.en: Partly. {{Far too much emphasis is placed on}} memorization. {{Schools teach to the test.}} But {{critical thinking is essential now}}.
lines.ko: 어느 정도는요. 암기에 지나치게 비중을 둬요. 학교가 시험에 맞춰 가르치잖아요. 하지만 요즘은 비판적 사고가 꼭 필요해요.

lines.en: I hear you. But as a teacher, I’ll push back a little. {{The curriculum is overloaded}}, and {{teachers are already stretched thin}}.
lines.ko: 무슨 말인지 알아요. 그래도 선생님으로서 조금 반박할게요. 교육과정은 이미 꽉 찼고, 선생님들도 이미 여유가 없어요.

lines.en: That’s fair. {{It’s easy to criticize}} from the outside.
lines.ko: 맞는 말이에요. 밖에서 비판하기는 쉽죠.

lines.en: And {{parents have a role as well}}. My dad taught me to budget with a little notebook.
lines.ko: 그리고 부모도 할 몫이 있어요. 저는 아빠가 작은 공책으로 예산 짜는 법을 가르쳐 주셨어요.

lines.en: Lucky you! But not every parent is in a position to do that. That’s why school matters.
lines.ko: 운이 좋았네요! 하지만 모든 부모가 그럴 수 있는 형편은 아니잖아요. 그래서 학교가 중요해요.

lines.en: Good point. So what would you add?
lines.ko: 좋은 지적이에요. 그럼 뭘 더하고 싶어요?

lines.en: {{If I could add one subject,}} it would be life skills: money, cooking, and handling stress. {{Emotional skills matter too.}}
lines.ko: 과목 하나를 더할 수 있다면 ‘생활 기술’이요. 돈 관리, 요리, 그리고 스트레스 다루기요. 감정을 다루는 능력도 중요하니까요.

lines.en: I’d take that class! But the big question is, {{who gets to decide?}}
lines.ko: 그 수업은 저도 듣고 싶네요! 그런데 큰 문제는, 그걸 누가 정하느냐예요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "After the Dinner · 6월 첫 토요일 밤, 지우 집 부엌에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Grace: "Dinner was amazing, Jiwoo. Let me wash, and you dry." (저녁 정말 맛있었어요, 지우 씨. 제가 씻을 테니 지우 씨가 닦아요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Deal. I keep thinking about Maya. She said she learned to budget from online videos." (좋아요. 마야 씨 말이 계속 생각나요. 예산 짜는 법을 인터넷 영상으로 배웠다고 했잖아요.)
3. Grace: "We didn’t learn much about that at school, either." (학교에서도 그걸 많이 배우지는 않았어요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Right! It should have been taught in high school. I couldn’t even read my first rental contract." (맞아요! 그건 고등학교 때 가르쳤어야 했어요. 저는 첫 임대 계약서도 제대로 못 읽었어요.)
5. Grace: "So, you mean school should be more practical?" (그러니까 학교가 더 실용적이어야 한다는 거죠?)
6. Jiwoo: "Partly. Far too much emphasis is placed on memorization. Schools teach to the test. But critical thinking is essential now." (어느 정도는요. 암기에 지나치게 비중을 둬요. 학교가 시험에 맞춰 가르치잖아요. 하지만 요즘은 비판적 사고가 꼭 필요해요.)
7. Grace: "I hear you. But as a teacher, I’ll push back a little. The curriculum is overloaded, and teachers are already stretched thin." (무슨 말인지 알아요. 그래도 선생님으로서 조금 반박할게요. 교육과정은 이미 꽉 찼고, 선생님들도 이미 여유가 없어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "That’s fair. It’s easy to criticize from the outside." (맞는 말이에요. 밖에서 비판하기는 쉽죠.)
9. Grace: "And parents have a role as well. My dad taught me to budget with a little notebook." (그리고 부모도 할 몫이 있어요. 저는 아빠가 작은 공책으로 예산 짜는 법을 가르쳐 주셨어요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Lucky you! But not every parent is in a position to do that. That’s why school matters." (운이 좋았네요! 하지만 모든 부모가 그럴 수 있는 형편은 아니잖아요. 그래서 학교가 중요해요.)
11. Grace: "Good point. So what would you add?" (좋은 지적이에요. 그럼 뭘 더하고 싶어요?)
12. Jiwoo: "If I could add one subject, it would be life skills: money, cooking, and handling stress. Emotional skills matter too." (과목 하나를 더할 수 있다면 ‘생활 기술’이요. 돈 관리, 요리, 그리고 스트레스 다루기요. 감정을 다루는 능력도 중요하니까요.)
13. Grace: "I’d take that class! But the big question is, who gets to decide?" (그 수업은 저도 듣고 싶네요! 그런데 큰 문제는, 그걸 누가 정하느냐예요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Grace exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Grace (you): "Dinner was amazing, Jiwoo. Let me wash, and you dry." (저녁 정말 맛있었어요, 지우 씨. 제가 씻을 테니 지우 씨가 닦아요.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Deal. I keep thinking about Maya. She said she learned to budget from online videos." (좋아요. 마야 씨 말이 계속 생각나요. 예산 짜는 법을 인터넷 영상으로 배웠다고 했잖아요.)
3. Grace (you): "We didn’t learn much about that at school, either." (학교에서도 그걸 많이 배우지는 않았어요.)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Right! It should have been taught in high school. I couldn’t even read my first rental contract." (맞아요! 그건 고등학교 때 가르쳤어야 했어요. 저는 첫 임대 계약서도 제대로 못 읽었어요.)
5. Grace (you): "So, you mean school should be more practical?" (그러니까 학교가 더 실용적이어야 한다는 거죠?)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Partly. Far too much emphasis is placed on memorization. Schools teach to the test. But critical thinking is essential now." (어느 정도는요. 암기에 지나치게 비중을 둬요. 학교가 시험에 맞춰 가르치잖아요. 하지만 요즘은 비판적 사고가 꼭 필요해요.)
7. Grace (you): "I hear you. But as a teacher, I’ll push back a little. The curriculum is overloaded, and teachers are already stretched thin." (무슨 말인지 알아요. 그래도 선생님으로서 조금 반박할게요. 교육과정은 이미 꽉 찼고, 선생님들도 이미 여유가 없어요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s fair. It’s easy to criticize from the outside." (맞는 말이에요. 밖에서 비판하기는 쉽죠.)
9. Grace (you): "And parents have a role as well. My dad taught me to budget with a little notebook." (그리고 부모도 할 몫이 있어요. 저는 아빠가 작은 공책으로 예산 짜는 법을 가르쳐 주셨어요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Lucky you! But not every parent is in a position to do that. That’s why school matters." (운이 좋았네요! 하지만 모든 부모가 그럴 수 있는 형편은 아니잖아요. 그래서 학교가 중요해요.)
11. Grace (you): "Good point. So what would you add?" (좋은 지적이에요. 그럼 뭘 더하고 싶어요?)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "If I could add one subject, it would be life skills: money, cooking, and handling stress. Emotional skills matter too." (과목 하나를 더할 수 있다면 ‘생활 기술’이요. 돈 관리, 요리, 그리고 스트레스 다루기요. 감정을 다루는 능력도 중요하니까요.)
13. Grace (you): "I’d take that class! But the big question is, who gets to decide?" (그 수업은 저도 듣고 싶네요! 그런데 큰 문제는, 그걸 누가 정하느냐예요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Grace. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

frame: Far too much emphasis is placed on ___.
head: 배우지 못한 것
It should have been taught …
대신 너무 비중을 둔 것
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It should have been taught ___. / Far too much emphasis is placed on ___. Table (배우지 못한 것 → It should have been taught …):
- money skills → in high school.
- critical thinking → from an early age.
- cooking → in middle school.
- writing emails → before graduation.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
Cooking *should have been taught*. 요리를 가르쳤어야 했어요(그런데 안 가르쳤어요). 
We *should have been told*. 우리가 들었어야 했어요.
be placed on · If I could …

Emphasis *is placed on* tests. 시험에 비중을 둬요. 
*If I could* add one, it *would* be art. (지금 사실이 아닌 가정)
errors: If I could add one, it will be art.
If I could add one, it would be art.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- should have been + p.p.: Cooking should have been taught. 요리를 가르쳤어야 했어요(그런데 안 가르쳤어요). / We should have been told. 우리가 들었어야 했어요.
- be placed on · If I could …: Emphasis is placed on tests. 시험에 비중을 둬요. / If I could add one, it would be art. (지금 사실이 아닌 가정)
Common mistakes on screen:
- Cooking should have taught. → Cooking should have been taught. (요리는 ‘가르쳐지는’ 쪽이라 been taught.)
- Emphasis are placed on tests. → Emphasis is placed on tests. (emphasis는 단수라 is.)
- If I could add one, it will be art. → If I could add one, it would be art. (could와 짝을 맞춰 would.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: should have been + p.p.: Cooking should have been taught. 요리를 가르쳤어야 했어요(그런데 안 가르쳤어요). We should have been told. 우리가 들었어야 했어요.
be placed on · If I could …: Emphasis is placed on tests. 시험에 비중을 둬요. If I could add one, it would be art. (지금 사실이 아닌 가정)
mistakes: Cooking should have taught. → Cooking should have been taught.
Emphasis are placed on tests. → Emphasis is placed on tests.
If I could add one, it will be art. → If I could add one, it would be art.

steps.note: 예) money skills / in high school → Money skills should have been taught in high school.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) money skills / in high school → Money skills should have been taught in high school. Items (situation → model answer): money skills → in high school | critical thinking → early on | cooking → in middle school | coding → in elementary school.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: Far too much emphasis is placed on ___.
If I could add one subject, ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It should have been taught." (학교가 가르쳐야 할 것); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It should have been taught ___." / "Far too much emphasis is placed on ___." / "If I could add one subject, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Nobody taught us how to manage money.
돈 관리하는 법은 아무도 안 가르쳐 줬어요.
Parents have a role as well.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 빠진 것 짚기: "Nobody taught us how to manage money." (돈 관리하는 법은 아무도 안 가르쳐 줬어요., 친근); "Critical thinking is essential now." (요즘은 비판적 사고가 꼭 필요해요., 보통); "Emotional skills matter too." (감정을 다루는 능력도 중요해요., 보통)
- 문제점: "Schools teach to the test." (학교가 시험에 맞춰 가르쳐요., 보통); "The curriculum is overloaded." (교육과정이 너무 꽉 차 있어요., 보통)
- 다른 쪽 생각: "Teachers are already stretched thin." (선생님들도 이미 여유가 없어요., 보통); "Parents have a role as well." (부모도 할 몫이 있어요., 보통); "It’s easy to criticize." (비판하기는 쉬워요., 친근); "Who gets to decide?" (누가 정하죠?, 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 학교·배움에 관한 말: financial literacy 돈 관리 지식 · media literacy 정보를 따져 읽는 능력 / teach to the test 시험에 나오는 것만 가르치다 / stretched thin (사람·시간이) 빠듯한, 여유 없는

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Money skills should have ___ taught in school. B: I agree. Far too much ___ is placed on tests. / A: If I ___ add one subject, it would be cooking. B: Nice! Who gets to ___, though? / 낱말 상자: been · emphasis · could · decide
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: curriculum (교육과정), critical (비판적인 (critical thinking 비판적 사고)), literacy (읽고 쓰는 능력; (분야를) 다루는 능력), emotional (감정의, 정서적인), test (시험, 테스트), memorization (암기), subject (과목), reform (개혁), essential (꼭 필요한, 필수적인), coding (코딩, 프로그래밍), citizenship (시민권; 시민으로서의 자세), creativity (창의성).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Life skills should be a priority.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: emphasis (강조, 중점) — "Emphasis is placed on tests."; thinking (사고, 생각) — "critical thinking"; financial (돈의, 금융의) — "financial skills"; exam (시험) — "a big exam"; priority (우선순위, 먼저 할 일) — "Life skills should be a priority."; practical (실용적인) — "practical skills"; contract (계약(서)) — "read a rental contract".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What should have been taught at your school?
___ should have been taught at school.
In school, where is too much emphasis placed?
Far too much emphasis is placed on ___.
If you could add one subject, what would it be?
If I could add one subject, it would be ___.
Who should decide what schools teach?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What should have been taught at your school?" (hint on screen: ___ should have been taught at school.)
- "In school, where is too much emphasis placed?" (hint on screen: Far too much emphasis is placed on ___.)
- "If you could add one subject, what would it be?" (hint on screen: If I could add one subject, it would be ___.)
- "Who should decide what schools teach?" (hint on screen: I think ___ should decide, because ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The Fridge List
steps.text: It was Jiwoo’s first time hosting the group in her apartment. She was nervous, but her bibimbap was a hit. After dinner, everyone named one thing that should have been taught at school. For Maya, it was financial literacy. Daniel chose citizenship: how a city makes decisions. Chloe said she had only *a handful of* art classes in high school, so creativity got very little time. Ben joked that he should have tried coding “before my brain got lazy.” Grace listened, then reminded everyone that teachers aren’t always *in a position to* change the curriculum. Reform takes time, and many people need to agree. “Still,” she said, “it’s a good list.” Jiwoo wrote it on a sticky note and put it on her fridge.
steps.gloss: host (모임을) 열다 · a hit 대성공 · financial literacy 돈 관리 지식 · a handful of 몇 안 되는 · in a position to ~할 수 있는 입장인 · reform 개혁
questions: What did Maya choose?
Where did Jiwoo put the list?

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Maya choose?" / "Where did Jiwoo put the list?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘It should have been taught ___.’로 배웠어야 했던 것을 짚을 수 있어요.
- ‘Far too much emphasis is placed on ___.’로 치우친 우선순위를 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘If I could add one subject, ___.’로 내 우선순위를 주장할 수 있어요.

steps.teach:

Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It’s how we use it." (기술과 외로움). Goal: 역설을 말하고 원인을 다시 짚기. steps.title: An Evening Walk · 7월 평일 저녁, 동네 공원 산책길에서

lines.en: Thanks for coming out, Jiwoo. I really needed this walk.
lines.ko: 나와 줘서 고마워요, 지우 씨. 이 산책이 정말 필요했어요.

lines.en: Of course. You sounded a bit down in your message.
lines.ko: 당연하죠. 메시지가 좀 처져 보이던데요.

lines.en: I’m OK. My team is almost fully remote now. {{I’ve noticed that}} some days, I don’t say a word out loud until dinner.
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 우리 팀이 이제 거의 다 재택이에요. 어떤 날은 저녁때까지 소리 내서 한마디도 안 한다는 걸 알게 됐어요.

lines.en: Really? But you’re on team chat all day.
lines.ko: 정말요? 그래도 하루 종일 팀 메신저에 있잖아요.

lines.en: Exactly. {{Ironically}}, I’m in touch with more people than ever. Ooh, “i-RON-ically.” I love that word!
lines.ko: 바로 그거예요. 아이러니하게도, 그 어느 때보다 많은 사람과 연락해요. 오, ‘아이러니컬리’, 소리가 참 좋은 낱말이죠!

lines.en: I get it. {{Notifications constantly interrupt us}}, but none of them is a real conversation.
lines.ko: 알아요. 알림은 끊임없이 우리를 방해하는데, 진짜 대화는 하나도 없죠.

lines.en: Right. {{Online friends aren’t the same.}} You can’t share a snack through a screen.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 온라인 친구는 달라요. 화면으로 간식을 나눠 먹을 수는 없잖아요.

lines.en: True. But {{it’s not}} the phone {{itself, it’s how we}} use it. For people far from family, {{it can be a lifeline}}.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그래도 문제는 휴대폰 자체가 아니라 우리가 쓰는 방식이에요. 가족과 멀리 사는 사람들에게는 생명줄이 될 수도 있고요.

lines.en: That’s fair. But {{it’s easy to hide behind a screen}}. I text “Let’s meet soon!” and then never do.
lines.ko: 맞는 말이에요. 그래도 화면 뒤에 숨기 쉬워요. ‘곧 만나요!’ 하고 보내 놓고 정작 안 만나요.

lines.en: Me too. At one time, I saw my college friends every weekend. Now we just send emojis. {{We need to be more intentional.}}
lines.ko: 저도요. 한때는 대학 친구들을 주말마다 만났는데, 지금은 이모티콘만 보내요. 좀 더 의식적으로 노력해야 해요.

lines.en: Like our first-Saturday dinners! {{Face-to-face time is precious.}}
lines.ko: 우리 첫 토요일 저녁 모임처럼요! 얼굴 보는 시간은 소중해요.

lines.en: So let’s make this walk a weekly thing. Every Wednesday?
lines.ko: 그럼 이 산책을 매주 해요. 수요일마다 어때요?

lines.en: Deal! Phones stay in our pockets. Well, maybe one sunset photo.
lines.ko: 좋아요! 휴대폰은 주머니에 넣어 두기. 음, 노을 사진 한 장 정도는 괜찮겠죠.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "An Evening Walk · 7월 평일 저녁, 동네 공원 산책길에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Thanks for coming out, Jiwoo. I really needed this walk." (나와 줘서 고마워요, 지우 씨. 이 산책이 정말 필요했어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Of course. You sounded a bit down in your message." (당연하죠. 메시지가 좀 처져 보이던데요.)
3. Chloe: "I’m OK. My team is almost fully remote now. I’ve noticed that some days, I don’t say a word out loud until dinner." (괜찮아요. 우리 팀이 이제 거의 다 재택이에요. 어떤 날은 저녁때까지 소리 내서 한마디도 안 한다는 걸 알게 됐어요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Really? But you’re on team chat all day." (정말요? 그래도 하루 종일 팀 메신저에 있잖아요.)
5. Chloe: "Exactly. Ironically, I’m in touch with more people than ever. Ooh, “i-RON-ically.” I love that word!" (바로 그거예요. 아이러니하게도, 그 어느 때보다 많은 사람과 연락해요. 오, ‘아이러니컬리’, 소리가 참 좋은 낱말이죠!)
6. Jiwoo: "I get it. Notifications constantly interrupt us, but none of them is a real conversation." (알아요. 알림은 끊임없이 우리를 방해하는데, 진짜 대화는 하나도 없죠.)
7. Chloe: "Right. Online friends aren’t the same. You can’t share a snack through a screen." (맞아요. 온라인 친구는 달라요. 화면으로 간식을 나눠 먹을 수는 없잖아요.)
8. Jiwoo: "True. But it’s not the phone itself, it’s how we use it. For people far from family, it can be a lifeline." (맞아요. 그래도 문제는 휴대폰 자체가 아니라 우리가 쓰는 방식이에요. 가족과 멀리 사는 사람들에게는 생명줄이 될 수도 있고요.)
9. Chloe: "That’s fair. But it’s easy to hide behind a screen. I text “Let’s meet soon!” and then never do." (맞는 말이에요. 그래도 화면 뒤에 숨기 쉬워요. ‘곧 만나요!’ 하고 보내 놓고 정작 안 만나요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Me too. At one time, I saw my college friends every weekend. Now we just send emojis. We need to be more intentional." (저도요. 한때는 대학 친구들을 주말마다 만났는데, 지금은 이모티콘만 보내요. 좀 더 의식적으로 노력해야 해요.)
11. Chloe: "Like our first-Saturday dinners! Face-to-face time is precious." (우리 첫 토요일 저녁 모임처럼요! 얼굴 보는 시간은 소중해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "So let’s make this walk a weekly thing. Every Wednesday?" (그럼 이 산책을 매주 해요. 수요일마다 어때요?)
13. Chloe: "Deal! Phones stay in our pockets. Well, maybe one sunset photo." (좋아요! 휴대폰은 주머니에 넣어 두기. 음, 노을 사진 한 장 정도는 괜찮겠죠.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

5. Chloe: "Exactly. Ironically, I’m in touch with more people than ever. Ooh, “i-RON-ically.” I love that word!" (바로 그거예요. 아이러니하게도, 그 어느 때보다 많은 사람과 연락해요. 오, ‘아이러니컬리’, 소리가 참 좋은 낱말이죠!)
6. Jiwoo: "I get it. Notifications constantly interrupt us, but none of them is a real conversation." (알아요. 알림은 끊임없이 우리를 방해하는데, 진짜 대화는 하나도 없죠.)
7. Chloe: "Right. Online friends aren’t the same. You can’t share a snack through a screen." (맞아요. 온라인 친구는 달라요. 화면으로 간식을 나눠 먹을 수는 없잖아요.)
8. Jiwoo: "True. But it’s not the phone itself, it’s how we use it. For people far from family, it can be a lifeline." (맞아요. 그래도 문제는 휴대폰 자체가 아니라 우리가 쓰는 방식이에요. 가족과 멀리 사는 사람들에게는 생명줄이 될 수도 있고요.)
9. Chloe: "That’s fair. But it’s easy to hide behind a screen. I text “Let’s meet soon!” and then never do." (맞는 말이에요. 그래도 화면 뒤에 숨기 쉬워요. ‘곧 만나요!’ 하고 보내 놓고 정작 안 만나요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Me too. At one time, I saw my college friends every weekend. Now we just send emojis. We need to be more intentional." (저도요. 한때는 대학 친구들을 주말마다 만났는데, 지금은 이모티콘만 보내요. 좀 더 의식적으로 노력해야 해요.)
11. Chloe: "Like our first-Saturday dinners! Face-to-face time is precious." (우리 첫 토요일 저녁 모임처럼요! 얼굴 보는 시간은 소중해요.)
12. Jiwoo: "So let’s make this walk a weekly thing. Every Wednesday?" (그럼 이 산책을 매주 해요. 수요일마다 어때요?)
13. Chloe: "Deal! Phones stay in our pockets. Well, maybe one sunset photo." (좋아요! 휴대폰은 주머니에 넣어 두기. 음, 노을 사진 한 장 정도는 괜찮겠죠.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___.
head: Ironically, …
It’s not … itself,
it’s how we …
rows: we have many followers but feel alone.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Ironically, ___. / It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___. Table (Ironically, … → It’s not … itself,):
- we’re online but feel alone. → the phone
- we have many followers but feel alone. → social media
- chat apps make us quieter. → chatting
- remote work feels lonely. → working from home
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: It’s not A itself, it’s B

*It’s not* the phone *itself*, *it’s* how we use it. 문제는 휴대폰 자체가 아니라 쓰는 방식이에요. 
A를 탓하지 않고 진짜 원인 B에 힘을 줘요.
I miss face-to-face time. → *It’s* face-to-face time *that* I miss. 내가 그리운 건 바로 얼굴 보는 시간이에요.
errors: It’s my friends what I miss.
It’s my friends that I miss.
I’ve notice that I rarely call.
I’ve noticed that I rarely call.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- It’s not A itself, it’s B: It’s not the phone itself, it’s how we use it. 문제는 휴대폰 자체가 아니라 쓰는 방식이에요. / A를 탓하지 않고 진짜 원인 B에 힘을 줘요.
- It’s … that … (강조): I miss face-to-face time. → It’s face-to-face time that I miss. 내가 그리운 건 바로 얼굴 보는 시간이에요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Ironic, I feel lonelier online. → Ironically, I feel lonelier online. (문장 앞 꾸밈말은 -ly.)
- It’s my friends what I miss. → It’s my friends that I miss. (강조 구문은 It’s … that.)
- I’ve notice that I rarely call. → I’ve noticed that I rarely call. (have 뒤에는 과거분사 noticed.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: It’s not A itself, it’s B: It’s not the phone itself, it’s how we use it. 문제는 휴대폰 자체가 아니라 쓰는 방식이에요. A를 탓하지 않고 진짜 원인 B에 힘을 줘요.
It’s … that … (강조): I miss face-to-face time. → It’s face-to-face time that I miss. 내가 그리운 건 바로 얼굴 보는 시간이에요.
mistakes: Ironic, I feel lonelier online. → Ironically, I feel lonelier online.
It’s my friends what I miss. → It’s my friends that I miss.
I’ve notice that I rarely call. → I’ve noticed that I rarely call.

steps.note: 예) the phone / use it → It’s not the phone itself, it’s how we use it.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) the phone / use it → It’s not the phone itself, it’s how we use it. Items (situation → model answer): the phone → use it | social media → compare ourselves | the internet → spend our time | gaming → balance it with other things.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "It’s how we use it." (기술과 외로움); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Ironically, ___." / "It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___." / "I’ve noticed that ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: We’re more connected than ever, yet lonelier.
그 어느 때보다 연결돼 있는데 더 외로워요.
We’ve lost the art of small talk.
It can be a lifeline for isolated people.
고립된 사람들에게는 생명줄이 될 수 있어요.
It depends on how you use it.
It’s easy to hide behind a screen.
We need to be more intentional.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 역설 말하기: "We’re more connected than ever, yet lonelier." (그 어느 때보다 연결돼 있는데 더 외로워요., 보통); "Online friends aren’t the same." (온라인 친구는 달라요., 친근); "Notifications constantly interrupt us." (알림이 끊임없이 우리를 방해해요., 보통); "We’ve lost the art of small talk." (가벼운 잡담을 나누는 법을 잊었어요., 보통)
- 다른 면 보기: "It can be a lifeline for isolated people." (고립된 사람들에게는 생명줄이 될 수 있어요., 보통); "It depends on how you use it." (어떻게 쓰느냐에 달렸어요., 보통); "It’s easy to hide behind a screen." (화면 뒤에 숨기 쉬워요., 친근)
- 다시 이어지기: "Face-to-face time is precious." (얼굴 보는 시간은 소중해요., 보통); "We need to be more intentional." (좀 더 의식적으로 노력해야 해요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: loneliness · solitude

*loneliness* 외로움(함께하고 싶은데 혼자라 힘든 마음) 
*solitude* 혼자만의 시간(스스로 고른 편안한 혼자) 
I enjoy my *solitude*, but *loneliness* is different.
(참고) 일상에서 해 볼 수 있는 것

a weekly walk 매주 산책 · a phone-free dinner 휴대폰 없는 저녁 
turn off notifications 알림 끄기 
일상 이야기예요. 상담·건강 조언이 아니에요.
steps.blank:
A: ___, I chat online all day but feel alone.   B: Hmm. It’s not the phone ___, it’s how we use it. 
A: True. I’ve ___ that I rarely meet friends.   B: Let’s be more ___. Coffee on Friday? 
낱말 상자: Ironically · itself · noticed · intentional
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- loneliness · solitude: loneliness 외로움(함께하고 싶은데 혼자라 힘든 마음) / solitude 혼자만의 시간(스스로 고른 편안한 혼자) / I enjoy my solitude, but loneliness is different.
- (참고) 일상에서 해 볼 수 있는 것: a weekly walk 매주 산책 · a phone-free dinner 휴대폰 없는 저녁 / turn off notifications 알림 끄기 / 일상 이야기예요. 상담·건강 조언이 아니에요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: ___, I chat online all day but feel alone. B: Hmm. It’s not the phone ___, it’s how we use it. / A: True. I’ve ___ that I rarely meet friends. B: Let’s be more ___. Coffee on Friday? / 낱말 상자: Ironically · itself · noticed · intentional
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: loneliness (외로움), irony (아이러니, 역설), ironically (아이러니하게도, 역설적이게도), notification ((휴대폰) 알림), lifeline (생명줄, 꼭 필요한 연결), intentional (의도적인, 일부러 하는), superficial (겉핥기의, 피상적인), belonging (소속감), presence ((그 자리에) 함께 있음, 존재감), solitude (혼자만의 시간, 고독), bond (유대, 끈끈한 관계), community (공동체, (동네) 모임).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: isolation (고립, 혼자 떨어짐) — "Isolation can creep in slowly."; connection (연결, (사람 사이의) 유대) — "a real connection"; interaction (상호 작용, 교류) — "face-to-face interaction"; digital (디지털의) — "a digital detox"; remote (원격의) — "a remote team"; small talk (가벼운 잡담) — "the art of small talk".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What’s something ironic about technology in your life?
Have you noticed any changes in how people talk to each other?
Some say phones make people lonely. What do you think?
It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___.
What helps you stay close to people?
I try to ___. Face-to-face time is precious.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What’s something ironic about technology in your life?" (hint on screen: Ironically, ___.)
- "Have you noticed any changes in how people talk to each other?" (hint on screen: I’ve noticed that ___.)
- "Some say phones make people lonely. What do you think?" (hint on screen: It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___.)
- "What helps you stay close to people?" (hint on screen: I try to ___. Face-to-face time is precious.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The Wednesday Walk
steps.text: Chloe and Jiwoo kept their promise. Every Wednesday at eight, they met at the park gate and walked for an hour, phones in their pockets. *At one time*, Chloe thought small talk was a waste of time. Now she enjoys it, with the man who walks three dogs or the kids on scooters. Their talks aren’t superficial, either. They talk about work, books, and their families. Soon, a neighbor started joining them. Chloe also made a small change at work. She suggested a ten-minute video coffee break for her remote team every Friday, with cameras on and no work talk. The idea was *backed by* her manager, and most of the team joins now. Chloe still enjoys her solitude, but those small moments of presence help her feel a sense of belonging.
steps.gloss: at one time 한때 · small talk 가벼운 잡담 · superficial 겉핥기의 · backed by ~의 지지를 받는 · solitude 혼자만의 시간 · presence 함께 있음 · belonging 소속감
questions: When do Chloe and Jiwoo walk together?
What did Chloe suggest for her team?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "The Wednesday Walk". Text: "Chloe and Jiwoo kept their promise. Every Wednesday at eight, they met at the park gate and walked for an hour, phones in their pockets. At one time, Chloe thought small talk was a waste of time. Now she enjoys it, with the man who walks three dogs or the kids on scooters. Their talks aren’t superficial, either. They talk about work, books, and their families. Soon, a neighbor started joining them. Chloe also made a small change at work. She suggested a ten-minute video coffee break for her remote team every Friday, with cameras on and no work talk. The idea was backed by her manager, and most of the team joins now. Chloe still enjoys her solitude, but those small moments of presence help her feel a sense of belonging." Words: at one time 한때 · small talk 가벼운 잡담 · superficial 겉핥기의 · backed by ~의 지지를 받는 · solitude 혼자만의 시간 · presence 함께 있음 · belonging 소속감.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "When do Chloe and Jiwoo walk together?" / "What did Chloe suggest for her team?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Ironically, ___.’로 기대와 반대되는 결과를 말할 수 있어요.
‘It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___.’로 진짜 원인을 짚을 수 있어요.
‘I’ve noticed that ___.’으로 내가 본 변화를 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Ironically, ___.’로 기대와 반대되는 결과를 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s not ___ itself, it’s how we ___.’로 진짜 원인을 짚을 수 있어요.
- ‘I’ve noticed that ___.’으로 내가 본 변화를 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: AI가 만든 그림도 예술일까
steps.title_en: Where do we draw the line?
steps.goal: 질문을 던지고 경계를 묻고 내 주장 펴기
steps.scene_desc: 7월 말 토요일 오후, 작은 동네 갤러리(가상)의 ‘AI로 만든 그림’ 전시. 흰 벽에 색이 강한 추상화 몇 점이 걸려 있고, 클로이가 큰 그림 앞에서 팔짱을 끼고 고개를 갸웃하며, 지우가 옆에서 손짓하며 열심히 이야기함. 그림 옆 작은 설명 카드·벽·간판에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Where do we draw the line?" (AI가 만든 그림도 예술일까). Goal: 질문을 던지고 경계를 묻고 내 주장 펴기. Today's scene: 7월 말 토요일 오후, 작은 동네 갤러리(가상)의 ‘AI로 만든 그림’ 전시. 흰 벽에 색이 강한 추상화 몇 점이 걸려 있고, 클로이가 큰 그림 앞에서 팔짱을 끼고 고개를 갸웃하며, 지우가 옆에서 손짓하며 열심히 이야기함. 그림 옆 작은 설명 카드·벽·간판에 글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It raises the question of ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 일이 더 큰 질문으로 이어질 때 써요. *of* 뒤에는 명사나 *who/what/how* + 문장.
steps.extra: AI art raises the question of who the real artist is.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "It raises the question of ___." (~라는 질문을 던지게 해요.). When to use it: 어떤 일이 더 큰 질문으로 이어질 때 써요. of 뒤에는 명사나 who/what/how + 문장. Note: AI art raises the question of who the real artist is.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Where do we draw the line?".

steps.en: Where do we draw the line?
steps.when: 허용과 불허, 인정과 불인정의 *경계*를 함께 따져 보자고 할 때 써요.
steps.extra: A filter is fine, but a whole picture from one sentence? Where do we draw the line?
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Where do we draw the line?" (어디까지를 괜찮다고 봐야 할까요?). When to use it: 허용과 불허, 인정과 불인정의 경계를 함께 따져 보자고 할 때 써요. Note: A filter is fine, but a whole picture from one sentence? Where do we draw the line?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’d argue that ___.".

steps.when: 내 주장을 분명하게 펴되 *would*로 조금 부드럽게 말해요. 뒤에 이유를 붙이면 좋아요.
steps.extra: I’d argue that the idea matters more than the tool.
steps.teach:

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It raises the question of ___. Where do we draw the line? / I’d argue that ___. Table (이야깃거리 → It raises the question of …):
- AI pictures in a gallery → who the real artist is.
- a song made by a program → what creativity means.
- a photo with heavy filters → how much editing is too much.
- copying a famous painting → where imitation ends.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*I’d argue that* the idea matters most. 저는 아이디어가 가장 중요하다고 봐요. 
I’d = I would. would로 단정을 조금 누그러뜨려요.

It *raises the question of* ownership. (+ 명사) 
It *raises the question of* who owns it. (+ who/what + 문장)

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I’d argue that … = 저는 ~라고 봐요: I’d argue that the idea matters most. 저는 아이디어가 가장 중요하다고 봐요. / I’d = I would. would로 단정을 조금 누그러뜨려요.
- It raises the question of …: It raises the question of ownership. (+ 명사) / It raises the question of who owns it. (+ who/what + 문장)
Common mistakes on screen:
- It rises the question of ownership. → It raises the question of ownership. (질문을 ‘제기하다’는 목적어를 받는 raise.)
- AI art are real art. → AI art is real art. (art는 셀 수 없는 명사라 is.)
- It all hinges in how you define art. → It all hinges on how you define art. (hinge는 on과 함께 써요(~에 달려 있다).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) AI art / the idea matters most → A: What do you think about AI art? B: It raises the question of what art is. I’d argue that the idea matters most.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) AI art / the idea matters most → A: What do you think about AI art? B: It raises the question of what art is. I’d argue that the idea matters most. Items (situation → model answer): AI art → the idea matters most | an edited photo → it’s still a photo | a copied painting → it’s good practice | a song made by AI → something is missing.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: Where do we draw the line?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Where do we draw the line?" (AI가 만든 그림도 예술일까); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It raises the question of ___." / "Where do we draw the line?" / "I’d argue that ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: It all hinges on how you define art.
Creativity isn’t just about the final product.
Artists have always borrowed from each other.
It’s a tool like any other.
아직 아무도 가 보지 않은 영역이에요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 예술이란 뭘까: "It all hinges on how you define art." (결국 예술을 어떻게 정의하느냐에 달렸어요., 보통); "Creativity isn’t just about the final product." (창의성은 결과물만의 문제가 아니에요., 보통); "That’s a slippery definition." (딱 잘라 정하기 어려운 정의예요., 보통); "Artists have always borrowed from each other." (예술가들은 늘 서로에게서 빌려 왔어요., 보통)
- 도구로 보는 쪽: "The intent behind it matters." (그 뒤에 있는 의도가 중요해요., 보통); "It’s a tool like any other." (다른 도구와 다를 게 없어요., 친근)
- 아직 모르는 것: "Who owns the copyright?" (저작권은 누구 거예요?, 보통); "It’s uncharted territory." (아직 아무도 가 보지 않은 영역이에요., 보통); "The jury’s still out." (아직 결론이 나지 않았어요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 미술 낱말

*contemporary* art 현대 미술 · an *abstract* painting 추상화

an *algorithm* 컴퓨터가 따르는 계산 절차
(참고) 저작권은 아직 논의 중

AI로 만든 작품의 저작권은 나라와 사람의 창작 기여 정도에 따라 달라지고, 일부 쟁점은 아직 논의 중이에요. 법률 조언이 아니에요.

Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: masterpiece (걸작, 명작), imitation (모방, 흉내 낸 것), generate ((컴퓨터 등이) 만들어 내다, 생성하다), inspiration (영감(무언가를 만들고 싶게 하는 자극)), controversy (논란, 논쟁), artistic (예술적인, 예술의), copyright (저작권), ownership (소유, 소유권), authenticity (진짜임, 진품임; 진정성), originality (독창성), aesthetic (미적인; (n.) 미적 스타일), define ((뜻을) 정의하다, 분명히 밝히다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The algorithm learned from old paintings.
Is it her creation or the machine’s?
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: intent (의도, 목적) — "The intent behind it matters."; definition (정의, 뜻풀이) — "That’s a slippery definition."; creativity (창의성) — "Creativity takes practice."; algorithm (알고리즘(컴퓨터가 따르는 계산 절차)) — "The algorithm learned from old paintings."; contemporary (현대의, 동시대의) — "a contemporary art gallery"; creation (창작물; 만들어 냄) — "Is it her creation or the machine’s?"; abstract (추상적인) — "an abstract painting"; controversial (논란이 많은) — "a controversial question".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Have you ever seen pictures made with AI? What did you think?
When you edit photos, where do you draw the line?
What else raises a big question about art or creativity?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Have you ever seen pictures made with AI? What did you think?" (hint on screen: I saw ___. I thought ___.)
- "Is AI art real art?" (hint on screen: I’d argue that ___, because ___.)
- "When you edit photos, where do you draw the line?" (hint on screen: A filter is fine, but ___.)
- "What else raises a big question about art or creativity?" (hint on screen: ___ raises the question of ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: The Artist’s Talk
steps.text: Before leaving, Jiwoo and Chloe joined the artist’s short talk. For twenty years, she was *thought of as* a traditional painter. “People think making AI art is *free from* hard work,” she said. “That isn’t true. I wrote hundreds of prompts and threw most of the pictures away.” She showed two abstract works, one painted by hand and one generated by an algorithm. Most visitors couldn’t tell which was which. Someone asked a controversial question. “Is the machine an artist *in its own right*?” The artist smiled. “I’d argue that it isn’t. The creation is mine. The tool is just new.” Chloe whispered that contemporary art has always started arguments. Jiwoo still wasn’t sure, but she wrote one line in her notebook. “Art is a question, not an answer.”
steps.gloss: thought of as ~로 여겨지는 · free from ~이 없는 · prompt (AI에 넣는) 지시문 · in its own right 그 자체로, 독자적으로 · whisper 속삭이다
questions: What was the artist thought of as before she used AI?
Could most visitors tell which work was painted by hand?

Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 편리함과 개인정보
steps.scene_desc: 8월 첫 토요일 저녁, 새로 연 동네 식당(가상). 긴 나무 식탁에 여섯 명이 둘러앉아 있고 식탁 위에 작은 QR 코드 스탠드(글자 없이)가 놓여 있음. 지우가 휴대폰을 든 채 멈칫하고, 옆자리 대니얼이 지우 휴대폰 화면 속 긴 약관(글자 없이 회색 줄만)을 가리키며 이야기함. 직원이 웃으며 식탁 옆에 서 있음. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Nothing to hide?" (편리함과 개인정보). Goal: 맞바꾸는 것을 짚고 위험을 말하기. Today's scene: 8월 첫 토요일 저녁, 새로 연 동네 식당(가상). 긴 나무 식탁에 여섯 명이 둘러앉아 있고 식탁 위에 작은 QR 코드 스탠드(글자 없이)가 놓여 있음. 지우가 휴대폰을 든 채 멈칫하고, 옆자리 대니얼이 지우 휴대폰 화면 속 긴 약관(글자 없이 회색 줄만)을 가리키며 이야기함. 직원이 웃으며 식탁 옆에 서 있음. 간판·메뉴판에 글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "We tend to ___ without realizing ___.".

steps.when: 사람들이 흔히 하는 행동과 그 안에 숨은 점을 함께 짚어요. *tend to* + 동사원형.
steps.extra: We tend to tap “Agree” without realizing what we’re sharing.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "We tend to ___ without realizing ___." (우리는 ~를 모른 채 ~하곤 해요.). When to use it: 사람들이 흔히 하는 행동과 그 안에 숨은 점을 함께 짚어요. tend to + 동사원형. Note: We tend to tap “Agree” without realizing what we’re sharing.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___.".

steps.when: 하나를 얻으면 다른 하나를 조금 내줘야 하는 관계를 말해요.
steps.extra: There’s a trade-off between convenience and privacy.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___." (~와 ~ 사이에는 맞바꾸는 게 있어요.). When to use it: 하나를 얻으면 다른 하나를 조금 내줘야 하는 관계를 말해요. Note: There’s a trade-off between convenience and privacy.

The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s a slippery slope.".

What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Ten Percent Off · 8월 첫 토요일 저녁, 새로 연 동네 식당 모임에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Ten Percent Off · 8월 첫 토요일 저녁, 새로 연 동네 식당 모임에서

lines.en: Welcome! Just scan the QR code to order. And if you sign up for our app, you get ten percent off tonight.
lines.ko: 어서 오세요! QR 코드를 찍어서 주문하시면 돼요. 저희 앱에 가입하시면 오늘 10% 할인돼요.

lines.en: Great! … Oh, it wants my name, phone number, birthday, and location.
lines.ko: 좋네요! … 어, 이름, 전화번호, 생일, 위치까지 달라고 하네요.

lines.en: For a bowl of noodles? Why would a restaurant need your location?
lines.ko: 국수 한 그릇에요? 식당이 왜 위치까지 필요할까요?

lines.en: Probably for coupons. Honestly, I’ve got nothing to hide. And I tapped “Agree,” so it’s fine.
lines.ko: 아마 쿠폰 때문이겠죠. 솔직히 저는 숨길 게 없어요. 그리고 ‘동의’를 눌렀으니 괜찮아요.

lines.en: Did you read the terms? {{We tend to}} tap “Agree” {{without realizing}} what we’re sharing. Most people never read the terms.
lines.ko: 약관은 읽었어요? 우리는 뭘 넘기는지 모른 채 ‘동의’를 누르곤 해요. 대부분은 약관을 아예 안 읽죠.

lines.en: Guilty. But they’re ten pages long! Convenience wins every time. And I’m not opposed to sharing a little if I get something back.
lines.ko: 찔리네요. 그래도 열 쪽이나 되잖아요! 결국 늘 편리함이 이겨요. 그리고 뭔가 돌려받는다면 조금 나누는 건 반대하지 않아요.

lines.en: Fair. {{There’s a trade-off between}} convenience {{and}} privacy. But privacy isn’t about hiding. It’s a matter of consent, so “nothing to hide” misses the point.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 편리함과 사생활 사이에는 맞바꾸는 게 있죠. 하지만 사생활은 숨기는 문제가 아니에요. 동의의 문제라서, ‘숨길 게 없다’는 말은 요점을 벗어나요.

lines.en: Isn’t that a bit dramatic? It’s just a noodle place. What’s your evidence?
lines.ko: 좀 과장 아니에요? 그냥 국숫집인데요. 근거가 뭐예요?

lines.en: Ha, that’s my line! About this place, I have none. My point is general. First your birthday, then your location, then everything you buy. {{It’s a slippery slope.}}
lines.ko: 하, 그건 제 대사인데요! 이 가게에 대한 근거는 없어요. 일반적인 얘기예요. 처음엔 생일, 다음엔 위치, 그다음엔 사는 물건 전부. 점점 더 내주게 되죠.

lines.en: OK, I’ll turn off location. But shouldn’t there be clearer rules?
lines.ko: 알았어요, 위치는 끌게요. 그런데 더 분명한 규칙이 있어야 하지 않아요?

lines.en: In my view, regulation is lagging behind. But I’m no lawyer. Let’s get on with ordering. I’m starving!
lines.ko: 제가 보기엔 규제가 뒤처지고 있어요. 하지만 저는 법 전문가가 아니에요. 주문이나 계속해요. 배고파요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Ten Percent Off · 8월 첫 토요일 저녁, 새로 연 동네 식당 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Server: "Welcome! Just scan the QR code to order. And if you sign up for our app, you get ten percent off tonight." (어서 오세요! QR 코드를 찍어서 주문하시면 돼요. 저희 앱에 가입하시면 오늘 10% 할인돼요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Great! … Oh, it wants my name, phone number, birthday, and location." (좋네요! … 어, 이름, 전화번호, 생일, 위치까지 달라고 하네요.)
3. Daniel: "For a bowl of noodles? Why would a restaurant need your location?" (국수 한 그릇에요? 식당이 왜 위치까지 필요할까요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Probably for coupons. Honestly, I’ve got nothing to hide. And I tapped “Agree,” so it’s fine." (아마 쿠폰 때문이겠죠. 솔직히 저는 숨길 게 없어요. 그리고 ‘동의’를 눌렀으니 괜찮아요.)
5. Daniel: "Did you read the terms? We tend to tap “Agree” without realizing what we’re sharing. Most people never read the terms." (약관은 읽었어요? 우리는 뭘 넘기는지 모른 채 ‘동의’를 누르곤 해요. 대부분은 약관을 아예 안 읽죠.)
6. Jiwoo: "Guilty. But they’re ten pages long! Convenience wins every time. And I’m not opposed to sharing a little if I get something back." (찔리네요. 그래도 열 쪽이나 되잖아요! 결국 늘 편리함이 이겨요. 그리고 뭔가 돌려받는다면 조금 나누는 건 반대하지 않아요.)
7. Daniel: "Fair. There’s a trade-off between convenience and privacy. But privacy isn’t about hiding. It’s a matter of consent, so “nothing to hide” misses the point." (맞아요. 편리함과 사생활 사이에는 맞바꾸는 게 있죠. 하지만 사생활은 숨기는 문제가 아니에요. 동의의 문제라서, ‘숨길 게 없다’는 말은 요점을 벗어나요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Isn’t that a bit dramatic? It’s just a noodle place. What’s your evidence?" (좀 과장 아니에요? 그냥 국숫집인데요. 근거가 뭐예요?)
9. Daniel: "Ha, that’s my line! About this place, I have none. My point is general. First your birthday, then your location, then everything you buy. It’s a slippery slope." (하, 그건 제 대사인데요! 이 가게에 대한 근거는 없어요. 일반적인 얘기예요. 처음엔 생일, 다음엔 위치, 그다음엔 사는 물건 전부. 점점 더 내주게 되죠.)
10. Jiwoo: "OK, I’ll turn off location. But shouldn’t there be clearer rules?" (알았어요, 위치는 끌게요. 그런데 더 분명한 규칙이 있어야 하지 않아요?)
11. Daniel: "In my view, regulation is lagging behind. But I’m no lawyer. Let’s get on with ordering. I’m starving!" (제가 보기엔 규제가 뒤처지고 있어요. 하지만 저는 법 전문가가 아니에요. 주문이나 계속해요. 배고파요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: We tend to …
without realizing …
There’s a trade-off between …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: We tend to ___ without realizing ___. / There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___. Table (We tend to … → without realizing …):
- tap “Agree” → what we’re sharing.
- post vacation photos → who can see them.
- use free Wi-Fi → how unsafe it can be.
- turn on location → how much it reveals.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
We *tend to* skip the terms. 우리는 약관을 건너뛰는 편이에요. 
I *tend not to* share my location. 저는 위치를 잘 안 알려 주는 편이에요.

There’s a *trade-off between* speed *and* safety. 
We share data *without realizing* it. 우리는 모른 채 정보를 넘겨요.
errors: We tend to sharing too much.
We tend to share too much.
She tend to skip the terms.
She tends to skip the terms.
Most people never reads the terms.
Most people never read the terms.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- tend to + 동사원형 = ~하는 편이에요: We tend to skip the terms. 우리는 약관을 건너뛰는 편이에요. / I tend not to share my location. 저는 위치를 잘 안 알려 주는 편이에요.
- between A and B · without + -ing: There’s a trade-off between speed and safety. / We share data without realizing it. 우리는 모른 채 정보를 넘겨요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- We tend to sharing too much. → We tend to share too much. (tend to 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- She tend to skip the terms. → She tends to skip the terms. (주어가 she라 tends.)
- Most people never reads the terms. → Most people never read the terms. (people은 복수라 read.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: tend to + 동사원형 = ~하는 편이에요: We tend to skip the terms. 우리는 약관을 건너뛰는 편이에요. I tend not to share my location. 저는 위치를 잘 안 알려 주는 편이에요.
between A and B · without + -ing: There’s a trade-off between speed and safety. We share data without realizing it. 우리는 모른 채 정보를 넘겨요.
mistakes: We tend to sharing too much. → We tend to share too much.
She tend to skip the terms. → She tends to skip the terms.
Most people never reads the terms. → Most people never read the terms.

steps.note: 예) tap “Agree” / what we share → We tend to tap “Agree” without realizing what we share.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) tap “Agree” / what we share → We tend to tap “Agree” without realizing what we share. Items (situation → model answer): tap “Agree” → what we share | use free apps → how they make money | turn on location → how much it reveals | post photos → who can see them.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "Nothing to hide?" (편리함과 개인정보); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "We tend to ___ without realizing ___." / "There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___." / "It’s a slippery slope.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: If the product is free, you’re the product.
Once it’s out there, it’s out there.
Most people never read the terms.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 편리함 쪽: "Convenience wins every time." (결국 늘 편리함이 이겨요., 친근); "I’ve got nothing to hide." (저는 숨길 게 없어요., 친근)
- 개인정보 쪽: "If the product is free, you’re the product." (상품이 공짜면 내가 상품이에요., 보통); "Data is the new oil." (데이터는 새로운 석유예요., 보통); "Once it’s out there, it’s out there." (한번 퍼지면 되돌릴 수 없어요., 친근); "It’s a matter of consent." (동의의 문제예요., 보통)
- 규칙과 현실: "Most people never read the terms." (대부분은 약관을 아예 안 읽어요., 보통); "That argument misses the point." (그 주장은 요점을 벗어났어요., 보통); "Regulation is lagging behind." (규제가 뒤처지고 있어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 앱 가입할 때 쓰는 말

*sign up* for an app 앱에 가입하다 · *turn off* location 위치를 끄다 
*opt out* (정보 제공 등에서) 빠지겠다고 하다 
read the *fine print* 작은 글씨로 된 조건까지 읽다
(참고) 규칙은 곳마다 달라요

개인정보 규칙은 나라와 서비스마다 달라요. 가입 전에 약관과 개인정보 안내를 직접 확인하세요. 법률 조언이 아니에요. 
식당과 앱, 대학 카페 이야기는 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 앱 가입할 때 쓰는 말: sign up for an app 앱에 가입하다 · turn off location 위치를 끄다 / opt out (정보 제공 등에서) 빠지겠다고 하다 / read the fine print 작은 글씨로 된 조건까지 읽다
- (참고) 규칙은 곳마다 달라요: 개인정보 규칙은 나라와 서비스마다 달라요. 가입 전에 약관과 개인정보 안내를 직접 확인하세요. 법률 조언이 아니에요. / 식당과 앱, 대학 카페 이야기는 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.

Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: surveillance ((카메라 등으로) 감시), consent (동의, 허락; 동의하다), breach ((규칙·보안을) 깨뜨림, 위반), transparency (투명성(숨김없이 드러냄)), collect (모으다, 수집하다), anonymous (익명의, 이름을 밝히지 않은), vulnerable ((공격·피해에) 취약한, 약한), monitor ((계속) 지켜보다, 감시하다), leak (새다; (정보를) 흘리다, 유출되다), tracking (추적(움직임을 따라가며 기록함)), privacy (사생활, 개인 정보 보호), data (데이터, 자료).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Word list on screen: convenience (편리함) — "Convenience wins every time."; terms ((서비스) 약관, 조건) — "Most people never read the terms."; exploit ((사람·약점을) 부당하게 이용하다) — "Some apps can exploit our habits."; regulation (규제, 규정) — "Regulation is lagging behind."; discount (할인) — "ten percent off as a discount"; location (위치) — "I turned off my location."; permission (허락, (앱의) 접근 권한) — "The app asked for permission."; scan ((코드를) 찍다, 스캔하다) — "Scan the QR code to order.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

items: Do you usually read the terms before you sign up for an app?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Do you usually read the terms before you sign up for an app?" (hint on screen: I tend to ___. / I tend not to ___.)
- "What do people often share online without thinking?" (hint on screen: We tend to ___ without realizing ___.)
- "What trade-off do you accept for convenience?" (hint on screen: There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___. I usually choose ___.)
- "Someone says, “I’ve got nothing to hide.” What do you say?" (hint on screen: I agree, because ___. / I think that argument misses the point.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Who Was Watching?
steps.text: Walking home, Daniel told the group a story from his university. Last year, a small campus café asked students to sign up for its app. A few months later, it had a data breach, and students’ names, phone numbers, and birthdays leaked. “Nobody thought a café was vulnerable,” he said. “Names, birthdays, *that sort of thing*. It all got out.” Grace said apps should collect only what they need and be open about it. “Transparency is the least they can do.” Ben said all the cameras on the street make him feel monitored. Daniel added, “Surveillance cameras can also keep people safe. It’s a balance.” Jiwoo said, “Companies shouldn’t *get away with* collecting more than they need.” At home, she turned off every app permission she didn’t need.
steps.gloss: breach (보안이) 뚫림 · leak 유출되다 · vulnerable 취약한 · that sort of thing 그런 것들 · get away with (잘못을 하고도) 그냥 넘어가다
questions: What leaked from the campus café’s app?
What did Jiwoo do when she got home?
steps.teach:

It all got out.” Grace said apps should collect only what they need and be open about it. “Transparency is the least they can do.” Ben said all the cameras on the street make him feel monitored. Daniel added, “Surveillance cameras can also keep people safe. It’s a balance.” Jiwoo said, “Companies shouldn’t get away with collecting more than they need.” At home, she turned off every app permission she didn’t need." Words: breach (보안이) 뚫림 · leak 유출되다 · vulnerable 취약한 · that sort of thing 그런 것들 · get away with (잘못을 하고도) 그냥 넘어가다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What leaked from the campus café’s app?" / "What did Jiwoo do when she got home?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘We tend to ___ without realizing ___.’로 흔한 행동 속 숨은 점을 짚을 수 있어요.
‘There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___.’로 맞바꾸는 것을 말할 수 있어요.

steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘We tend to ___ without realizing ___.’로 흔한 행동 속 숨은 점을 짚을 수 있어요.
- ‘There’s a trade-off between ___ and ___.’로 맞바꾸는 것을 말할 수 있어요.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.scene_desc: 8월 말 일요일 오후, 동네 무인 카페(가상). 유리 칸 안에서 로봇 팔이 컵에 커피를 따르고, 벤이 신기한 듯 유리 가까이 몸을 숙여 웃으며 들여다봄. 지우는 커피 두 잔이 나오는 픽업 칸 앞에 서서 벤을 보며 웃음. 직원은 없음. 화면·간판·컵에 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Robots at Work" (자동화). Goal: 분야를 좁혀 말하고 미묘한 차이 짚기. Today's scene: 8월 말 일요일 오후, 동네 무인 카페(가상). 유리 칸 안에서 로봇 팔이 컵에 커피를 따르고, 벤이 신기한 듯 유리 가까이 몸을 숙여 웃으며 들여다봄. 지우는 커피 두 잔이 나오는 픽업 칸 앞에 서서 벤을 보며 웃음. 직원은 없음. 화면·간판·컵에 글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "When it comes to ___, ___.".

steps.when: 이야기 범위를 한 분야로 좁혀 의견을 말해요. *to* 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: When it comes to making coffee, machines are hard to beat.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "When it comes to ___, ___." (~에 관해서라면, ~). When to use it: 이야기 범위를 한 분야로 좁혀 의견을 말해요. to 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: When it comes to making coffee, machines are hard to beat.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’d feel uneasy about ___.".

steps.when: 아직 일어나지 않은 일에 대한 걱정을 부드럽게 말해요. *about* 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: I’d feel uneasy about a robot driving my bus.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’d feel uneasy about ___." (~는 좀 불안할 것 같아요.). When to use it: 아직 일어나지 않은 일에 대한 걱정을 부드럽게 말해요. about 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: I’d feel uneasy about a robot driving my bus.

What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___.".

steps.extra: It’s one thing to make coffee, but quite another to run a café.

lines.en: Look at that arm! Not a single drop spilled. No wonder there’s never a line here.

lines.ko: 무서운 생각 하나 해 볼까요. 어학원이 저 대신 로봇 영어 선생님을 쓰면 어떡해요? 적어도 수업에 늦을 일은 없겠네요!

lines.en: Then again, it’s already happening in factories. And look, nobody here even bothers to watch the robot anymore. It’s normal now.
lines.ko: 다른 한편으로, 공장에서는 이미 일어나고 있는 일이에요. 그리고 봐요, 여기서는 이제 아무도 로봇을 굳이 쳐다보지도 않아요. 이젠 평범한 일이죠.

steps.teach:

8. Jiwoo: "That worries me too. And I’d feel uneasy about a robot driving my bus. Who’s accountable when it goes wrong?" (저도 그게 걱정돼요. 그리고 로봇이 제 버스를 운전한다면 좀 불안할 것 같아요. 잘못되면 누가 책임져요?)
9. Ben: "Good question. I’d trust a machine for some things, like coffee. A spilled latte isn’t a big deal. A bus is different." (좋은 질문이에요. 저는 커피처럼 어떤 일은 기계를 믿을 것 같아요. 라테를 쏟아도 큰일은 아니잖아요. 버스는 달라요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Right. In the end, it’s a question of trust, and of what happens after an error." (맞아요. 결국 믿음의 문제예요. 그리고 오류가 난 뒤에 어떻게 되느냐의 문제고요.)
11. Ben: "Well said. Now, let’s see if it can make a second cup without me watching." (좋은 말이에요. 자, 제가 안 쳐다봐도 두 번째 잔을 만들 수 있는지 볼까요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Ben exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Ben (you): "Look at that arm! Not a single drop spilled. No wonder there’s never a line here." (저 팔 좀 봐요! 한 방울도 안 흘렸어요. 여기 줄이 한 번도 없는 게 당연하네요.)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "It’s impressive. Machines don’t get tired, and every cup tastes the same." (대단해요. 기계는 지치지 않고, 커피 맛도 매번 똑같아요.)
3. Ben (you): "Here’s a scary thought. What if the school replaced me with a robot English teacher? At least it would never be late for class!" (무서운 생각 하나 해 볼까요. 어학원이 저 대신 로봇 영어 선생님을 쓰면 어떡해요? 적어도 수업에 늦을 일은 없겠네요!)
4. Jiwoo (learner): "Ha! When it comes to grammar drills, a machine could probably help. Still, it’s one thing to correct a sentence, but quite another to notice that a student is having a bad day." (하하! 문법 연습이라면 기계가 도움이 될 수도 있겠죠. 그래도 문장을 고쳐 주는 것과 학생이 힘든 날을 보내고 있다는 걸 알아채는 건 전혀 다른 문제예요.)
5. Ben (you): "Thanks. I agree. Some jobs require empathy, and human judgment still counts." (고마워요. 동감이에요. 어떤 일에는 공감 능력이 필요하고, 사람의 판단은 여전히 중요해요.)
6. Jiwoo (learner): "Then again, it’s already happening in factories. And look, nobody here even bothers to watch the robot anymore. It’s normal now." (다른 한편으로, 공장에서는 이미 일어나고 있는 일이에요. 그리고 봐요, 여기서는 이제 아무도 로봇을 굳이 쳐다보지도 않아요. 이젠 평범한 일이죠.)
7. Ben (you): "True. People say new jobs will replace old ones. Maybe, but that transition won’t be painless for everyone." (맞아요. 새 일자리가 옛 일자리를 대신할 거라고들 하죠. 그럴지도 모르지만, 그 전환이 모두에게 쉽지는 않을 거예요.)
8. Jiwoo (learner): "That worries me too. And I’d feel uneasy about a robot driving my bus. Who’s accountable when it goes wrong?" (저도 그게 걱정돼요. 그리고 로봇이 제 버스를 운전한다면 좀 불안할 것 같아요. 잘못되면 누가 책임져요?)
9. Ben (you): "Good question. I’d trust a machine for some things, like coffee. A spilled latte isn’t a big deal. A bus is different." (좋은 질문이에요. 저는 커피처럼 어떤 일은 기계를 믿을 것 같아요. 라테를 쏟아도 큰일은 아니잖아요. 버스는 달라요.)
10. Jiwoo (learner): "Right. In the end, it’s a question of trust, and of what happens after an error." (맞아요. 결국 믿음의 문제예요. 그리고 오류가 난 뒤에 어떻게 되느냐의 문제고요.)
11. Ben (you): "Well said. Now, let’s see if it can make a second cup without me watching." (좋은 말이에요. 자, 제가 안 쳐다봐도 두 번째 잔을 만들 수 있는지 볼까요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Ben. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: A robot arm makes the coffee at the café.
