Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___.
head: When it comes to …,
it’s one thing to …
but quite another to …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: When it comes to ___, ___. / It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___. Table (When it comes to …, → it’s one thing to …):
- teaching → correct grammar,
- driving → park a car,
- cooking → make coffee,
- customer service → answer simple questions,
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*When it comes to* coffee, machines win. 커피라면 기계가 이겨요. 
*When it comes to* teach*ing*, … (to는 전치사라 -ing)

*It’s one thing to* cook, *but quite another to* teach. 요리하는 것과 가르치는 건 전혀 달라요. 
I’d feel uneasy *about* it. (+ 명사/-ing)
errors: When it comes to cook, I’m slow.
When it comes to cooking, I’m slow.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- When it comes to + 명사/-ing: When it comes to coffee, machines win. 커피라면 기계가 이겨요. / When it comes to teaching, … (to는 전치사라 -ing)
- one thing … another · uneasy about: It’s one thing to cook, but quite another to teach. 요리하는 것과 가르치는 건 전혀 달라요. / I’d feel uneasy about it. (+ 명사/-ing)
Common mistakes on screen:
- When it comes to cook, I’m slow. → When it comes to cooking, I’m slow. (여기 to는 전치사라 -ing.)
- Some jobs requires empathy. → Some jobs require empathy. (jobs는 복수라 require.)
- Machines doesn’t get tired. → Machines don’t get tired. (machines는 복수라 don’t.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: When it comes to + 명사/-ing: When it comes to coffee, machines win. 커피라면 기계가 이겨요. When it comes to teaching, … (to는 전치사라 -ing)
one thing … another · uneasy about: It’s one thing to cook, but quite another to teach. 요리하는 것과 가르치는 건 전혀 달라요. I’d feel uneasy about it. (+ 명사/-ing)
mistakes: When it comes to cook, I’m slow. → When it comes to cooking, I’m slow.
Some jobs requires empathy. → Some jobs require empathy.
Machines doesn’t get tired. → Machines don’t get tired.

steps.note: 예) coffee / machines are faster → When it comes to coffee, machines are faster.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) coffee / machines are faster → When it comes to coffee, machines are faster. Items (situation → model answer): coffee → machines are faster | teaching → I trust people | driving → I prefer a human | hiring → people should decide.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Robots at Work" (자동화); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "When it comes to ___, ___." / "I’d feel uneasy about ___." / "It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I’d trust a machine for some things.
어떤 일은 기계를 믿을 것 같아요.
Who’s accountable when it goes wrong?
New jobs will replace old ones.
새 일자리가 옛 일자리를 대신할 거예요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 기계가 잘하는 것: "Machines don’t get tired." (기계는 지치지 않아요., 친근); "It’s already happening in factories." (공장에서는 이미 일어나고 있어요., 보통); "I’d trust a machine for some things." (어떤 일은 기계를 믿을 것 같아요., 보통)
- 사람의 몫: "Some jobs require empathy." (어떤 일에는 공감 능력이 필요해요., 보통); "Human judgment still counts." (사람의 판단은 여전히 중요해요., 보통); "It’s a question of trust." (결국 믿음의 문제예요., 보통)
- 걱정과 변화: "Who’s accountable when it goes wrong?" (잘못되면 누가 책임져요?, 보통); "New jobs will replace old ones." (새 일자리가 옛 일자리를 대신할 거예요., 보통); "That transition won’t be painless." (그 전환이 쉽지는 않을 거예요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 책임에 관한 낱말

be *accountable* for ~에 책임을 지다 · *accountability* 책임(지는 것) 
*liability* (특히 법적인) 책임 · *oversight* 감독, 관리 
a *manual* 설명서 (그림 사전의 manual은 ‘손으로 하는’)
(참고) 아직 정리 중인 질문

기계가 실수했을 때 누가 책임지는지는 나라와 분야마다 논의 중이에요. 법률 조언이 아니에요. 
무인 카페와 기술자 이야기는 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
steps.blank:
A: Would you trust a robot teacher?   B: When it ___ to grammar, maybe. 
A: It’s one thing to correct a sentence, but quite ___ to understand a student.   B: True. I’d feel ___ about that. 
낱말 상자: comes · another · uneasy
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 책임에 관한 낱말: be accountable for ~에 책임을 지다 · accountability 책임(지는 것) / liability (특히 법적인) 책임 · oversight 감독, 관리 / a manual 설명서 (그림 사전의 manual은 ‘손으로 하는’)
- (참고) 아직 정리 중인 질문: 기계가 실수했을 때 누가 책임지는지는 나라와 분야마다 논의 중이에요. 법률 조언이 아니에요. / 무인 카페와 기술자 이야기는 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Would you trust a robot teacher? B: When it ___ to grammar, maybe. / A: It’s one thing to correct a sentence, but quite ___ to understand a student. B: True. I’d feel ___ about that. / 낱말 상자: comes · another · uneasy
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: robot (로봇), automation (자동화), empathy (공감(다른 사람의 마음을 알아주는 능력)), error (오류, 실수), manual (손으로 하는, 수동의), workforce ((한 회사·나라의) 전체 일하는 사람들, 인력), precision (정밀함, 정확함), replace (대신하다, 바꾸다), transition ((다른 상태로) 넘어감, 전환), displace ((원래 자리에서) 밀어내다), judgment (판단, 판단력), oversight (감독, 관리).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Who’s accountable when it goes wrong?
Liability is still a hard question.
A spilled latte isn’t a big deal.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: accountable (책임이 있는(설명할 책임을 지는)) — "Who’s accountable when it goes wrong?"; accountability (책임, 책임을 지는 것) — "We need clear accountability."; liability ((특히 법적인) 책임) — "Liability is still a hard question."; efficiency (효율, 능률) — "Robots bring efficiency."; factory (공장) — "It’s already happening in factories."; unmanned (사람이 없는, 무인의) — "an unmanned café"; technician (기술자) — "A technician checks the robot."; spill (쏟다, 흘리다) — "A spilled latte isn’t a big deal.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: In your work or daily life, what could a machine do well?
When it comes to ___, a machine could ___.
What would you feel uneasy about a machine doing?
In your opinion, which jobs require empathy?
Would you use a café with only robots? Why or why not?
I would, because ___. / It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "In your work or daily life, what could a machine do well?" (hint on screen: When it comes to ___, a machine could ___.)
- "What would you feel uneasy about a machine doing?" (hint on screen: I’d feel uneasy about ___.)
- "In your opinion, which jobs require empathy?" (hint on screen: I think ___ require(s) empathy, because ___.)
- "Would you use a café with only robots? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: I would, because ___. / It’s one thing to ___, but quite another to ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: In your work or daily life, what could a machine do well?
What would you feel uneasy about a machine doing?
In your opinion, which jobs require empathy?
Would you use a café with only robots? Why or why not?

steps.title: The Man Behind the Glass
steps.text: A week later, Ben went back to the café. This time, a young man was *at work* behind the glass, cleaning the robot arm. He was a technician who looks after six cafés like this one. “The machine makes the coffee, but someone still has to check it every day,” he said. “Precision is everything. One small error, and the whole machine stops.” Ben asked about the customers. “Some stop at *the sight of* the robot and walk out,” he said. “Others don’t even *bother to* look up from their phones.” He laughed. “I used to be a barista. Now I fix the thing that makes the coffee. *No wonder* my mom still doesn’t understand my job.” That evening, Ben told Jiwoo the story. “So his job didn’t disappear. It changed shape. But not everyone gets that chance.”
steps.gloss: at work 일하는 중인 · technician 기술자 · precision 정밀함 · the sight of ~을 보는 것, ~의 모습 · bother to 굳이 ~하다 · no wonder ~하는 게 당연하다
questions: What does the young man do now?
What was his job before?

items: ‘When it comes to ___, ___.’로 범위를 좁혀 의견을 말할 수 있어요.

steps.title: 2040년의 하루
steps.scene_desc: 9월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 거실의 저녁 모임. 뒤쪽 식탁에서 다른 사람들이 웃으며 이야기하는 동안, 창가에서 대니얼이 손바닥만 한 메모 카드 몇 장(글자 없이)을 들어 보이며 지우와 이야기하고, 지우는 턱을 괴고 생각에 잠김. 창밖은 서울 야경. 글자 없음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "A Day in 2040" (2040년의 하루). Goal: 미래 완료로 예측하고 확신을 조절하기. Today's scene: 9월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 거실의 저녁 모임. 뒤쪽 식탁에서 다른 사람들이 웃으며 이야기하는 동안, 창가에서 대니얼이 손바닥만 한 메모 카드 몇 장(글자 없이)을 들어 보이며 지우와 이야기하고, 지우는 턱을 괴고 생각에 잠김. 창밖은 서울 야경. 글자 없음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "By 2040, ___ will have ___.".

steps.when: 미래의 어느 때까지 이미 끝나 있을 변화를 예측해요. *will have* + 과거분사.
steps.extra: By 2040, my job will have changed a lot.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "By 2040, ___ will have ___." (2040년쯤이면 ~는 ~해 있을 거예요.). When to use it: 미래의 어느 때까지 이미 끝나 있을 변화를 예측해요. will have + 과거분사. Note: By 2040, my job will have changed a lot.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I wouldn’t be surprised if ___.".

steps.when: 꽤 그럴 법한 일을 조심스럽게 예측해요. if 뒤에는 흔히 *과거형*을 써서 한 걸음 물러서요.
steps.extra: I wouldn’t be surprised if most meetings happened online.
steps.teach:

steps.when: 예측의 확신을 낮출 때 써요. 의견을 말한 뒤 덧붙이면 겸손하게 들려요.

steps.title: Imagine 2040 · 9월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 모임에서

lines.en: At our lab’s workshop last week, we asked people to imagine an ordinary day in 2040. Want to try?
lines.ko: 지난주 우리 연구실 워크숍에서 사람들에게 2040년의 평범한 하루를 상상해 보라고 했어요. 해 볼래요?

lines.en: Sure. {{By 2040}}, I think my job {{will have}} changed a lot. AI will have taken over the boring parts, like resizing buttons.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 2040년쯤이면 제 일은 많이 바뀌어 있을 것 같아요. 버튼 크기 조정 같은 지루한 부분은 AI가 다 맡게 됐을 거예요.

lines.en: And how will you get to work?
lines.ko: 그럼 출근은 어떻게 해요?

lines.en: Maybe I won’t. Commuting might be a thing of the past. {{I wouldn’t be surprised if}} most meetings happened in virtual rooms.
lines.ko: 안 할지도 몰라요. 통근은 옛일이 될 수도 있어요. 회의 대부분을 가상 공간에서 해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요.

lines.en: Hmm. Can you think of a counterexample? People said the same thing about video calls, but we still crowd onto the subway.
lines.ko: 음, 반례를 떠올릴 수 있어요? 화상 통화 때도 똑같은 말을 했는데, 우리는 여전히 꽉 찬 지하철을 타요.

lines.en: Fair. I still go to the office most days. Maybe I’m overestimating it. What did people at the workshop predict?
lines.ko: 그렇네요. 저도 아직 거의 매일 출근해요. 제가 과대평가하는 건지도 몰라요. 워크숍에 온 사람들은 뭐라고 예측했어요?

lines.en: We tend to overestimate the short term. Many said we’ll probably work fewer hours. But some things will stay the same, like these dinners.
lines.ko: 우리는 가까운 미래의 변화를 크게 보곤 해요. 많은 사람이 아마 일하는 시간이 줄 거라고 했어요. 하지만 이런 저녁 모임처럼 그대로인 것도 있겠죠.

lines.en: I hope so. But the pace of change is staggering. Ten years ago, I didn’t even use a translation app.
lines.ko: 그러면 좋겠어요. 그래도 변화 속도가 정말 엄청나요. 10년 전엔 번역 앱도 안 썼거든요.

lines.en: True, but I doubt it will happen that fast everywhere. {{It’s hard to say for sure.}}
lines.ko: 맞아요, 하지만 모든 곳에서 그렇게 빨리 일어날지는 의문이에요. 확실히 말하기는 어렵죠.

lines.en: Then let me be bold. By 2040, robots will have taken over the dishes after these dinners. Mark my words.
lines.ko: 그럼 과감하게 말해 볼게요. 2040년쯤이면 이런 저녁 모임 뒤 설거지는 로봇이 맡게 됐을 거예요. 두고 보세요.

lines.en: Ha! Only time will tell.
lines.ko: 하하! 시간이 지나 봐야 알겠죠.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Imagine 2040 · 9월 첫 토요일 저녁, 클로이 집 모임에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "At our lab’s workshop last week, we asked people to imagine an ordinary day in 2040. Want to try?" (지난주 우리 연구실 워크숍에서 사람들에게 2040년의 평범한 하루를 상상해 보라고 했어요. 해 볼래요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Sure. By 2040, I think my job will have changed a lot. AI will have taken over the boring parts, like resizing buttons." (좋아요. 2040년쯤이면 제 일은 많이 바뀌어 있을 것 같아요. 버튼 크기 조정 같은 지루한 부분은 AI가 다 맡게 됐을 거예요.)
3. Daniel: "And how will you get to work?" (그럼 출근은 어떻게 해요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Maybe I won’t. Commuting might be a thing of the past. I wouldn’t be surprised if most meetings happened in virtual rooms." (안 할지도 몰라요. 통근은 옛일이 될 수도 있어요. 회의 대부분을 가상 공간에서 해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요.)
5. Daniel: "Hmm. Can you think of a counterexample? People said the same thing about video calls, but we still crowd onto the subway." (음, 반례를 떠올릴 수 있어요? 화상 통화 때도 똑같은 말을 했는데, 우리는 여전히 꽉 찬 지하철을 타요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Fair. I still go to the office most days. Maybe I’m overestimating it. What did people at the workshop predict?" (그렇네요. 저도 아직 거의 매일 출근해요. 제가 과대평가하는 건지도 몰라요. 워크숍에 온 사람들은 뭐라고 예측했어요?)
7. Daniel: "We tend to overestimate the short term. Many said we’ll probably work fewer hours. But some things will stay the same, like these dinners." (우리는 가까운 미래의 변화를 크게 보곤 해요. 많은 사람이 아마 일하는 시간이 줄 거라고 했어요. 하지만 이런 저녁 모임처럼 그대로인 것도 있겠죠.)
8. Jiwoo: "I hope so. But the pace of change is staggering. Ten years ago, I didn’t even use a translation app." (그러면 좋겠어요. 그래도 변화 속도가 정말 엄청나요. 10년 전엔 번역 앱도 안 썼거든요.)
9. Daniel: "True, but I doubt it will happen that fast everywhere. It’s hard to say for sure." (맞아요, 하지만 모든 곳에서 그렇게 빨리 일어날지는 의문이에요. 확실히 말하기는 어렵죠.)
10. Jiwoo: "Then let me be bold. By 2040, robots will have taken over the dishes after these dinners. Mark my words." (그럼 과감하게 말해 볼게요. 2040년쯤이면 이런 저녁 모임 뒤 설거지는 로봇이 맡게 됐을 거예요. 두고 보세요.)
11. Daniel: "Ha! Only time will tell." (하하! 시간이 지나 봐야 알겠죠.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

10. Jiwoo (learner): "Then let me be bold. By 2040, robots will have taken over the dishes after these dinners. Mark my words." (그럼 과감하게 말해 볼게요. 2040년쯤이면 이런 저녁 모임 뒤 설거지는 로봇이 맡게 됐을 거예요. 두고 보세요.)
11. Daniel (you): "Ha! Only time will tell." (하하! 시간이 지나 봐야 알겠죠.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Daniel. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Daniel’s lab held a workshop about the future.
Daniel is sure that everything will change fast.
Jiwoo predicts that robots will do the dishes by 2040.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Daniel’s lab held a workshop about the future.
2. Daniel is sure that everything will change fast.
3. Jiwoo predicts that robots will do the dishes by 2040.
The scene they are about:
1. Daniel: "At our lab’s workshop last week, we asked people to imagine an ordinary day in 2040. Want to try?" (지난주 우리 연구실 워크숍에서 사람들에게 2040년의 평범한 하루를 상상해 보라고 했어요. 해 볼래요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Sure. By 2040, I think my job will have changed a lot. AI will have taken over the boring parts, like resizing buttons." (좋아요. 2040년쯤이면 제 일은 많이 바뀌어 있을 것 같아요. 버튼 크기 조정 같은 지루한 부분은 AI가 다 맡게 됐을 거예요.)
3. Daniel: "And how will you get to work?" (그럼 출근은 어떻게 해요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Maybe I won’t. Commuting might be a thing of the past. I wouldn’t be surprised if most meetings happened in virtual rooms." (안 할지도 몰라요. 통근은 옛일이 될 수도 있어요. 회의 대부분을 가상 공간에서 해도 놀랍지 않을 거예요.)
5. Daniel: "Hmm. Can you think of a counterexample? People said the same thing about video calls, but we still crowd onto the subway." (음, 반례를 떠올릴 수 있어요? 화상 통화 때도 똑같은 말을 했는데, 우리는 여전히 꽉 찬 지하철을 타요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Fair. I still go to the office most days. Maybe I’m overestimating it. What did people at the workshop predict?" (그렇네요. 저도 아직 거의 매일 출근해요. 제가 과대평가하는 건지도 몰라요. 워크숍에 온 사람들은 뭐라고 예측했어요?)
7. Daniel: "We tend to overestimate the short term. Many said we’ll probably work fewer hours. But some things will stay the same, like these dinners." (우리는 가까운 미래의 변화를 크게 보곤 해요. 많은 사람이 아마 일하는 시간이 줄 거라고 했어요. 하지만 이런 저녁 모임처럼 그대로인 것도 있겠죠.)
8. Jiwoo: "I hope so. But the pace of change is staggering. Ten years ago, I didn’t even use a translation app." (그러면 좋겠어요. 그래도 변화 속도가 정말 엄청나요. 10년 전엔 번역 앱도 안 썼거든요.)
9. Daniel: "True, but I doubt it will happen that fast everywhere. It’s hard to say for sure." (맞아요, 하지만 모든 곳에서 그렇게 빨리 일어날지는 의문이에요. 확실히 말하기는 어렵죠.)
10. Jiwoo: "Then let me be bold. By 2040, robots will have taken over the dishes after these dinners. Mark my words." (그럼 과감하게 말해 볼게요. 2040년쯤이면 이런 저녁 모임 뒤 설거지는 로봇이 맡게 됐을 거예요. 두고 보세요.)
11. Daniel: "Ha! Only time will tell." (하하! 시간이 지나 봐야 알겠죠.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I wouldn’t be surprised if ___. / It’s hard to say for sure.
head: By 2040, …
will have …
I wouldn’t be surprised if …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: By 2040, ___ will have ___. / I wouldn’t be surprised if ___. / It’s hard to say for sure. Table (By 2040, … → will have …):
- my job → changed a lot.
- paper tickets → disappeared.
- our neighborhood → become greener.
- online shopping → grown even more.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
By 2040, my job *will have changed*. 2040년쯤이면 제 일은 바뀌어 있을 거예요. 
*by* + 미래 시점 = 그때쯤이면 이미 끝나 있을 일

I *wouldn’t be surprised if* we work*ed* less. (과거형으로 조심스럽게) 
강함 → 약함: will · will probably · might · It’s hard to say.
errors: By 2040, my job will have change a lot.
By 2040, my job will have changed a lot.
I wouldn’t be surprise if it happened.
I wouldn’t be surprised if it happened.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 미래완료 will have + 과거분사: By 2040, my job will have changed. 2040년쯤이면 제 일은 바뀌어 있을 거예요. / by + 미래 시점 = 그때쯤이면 이미 끝나 있을 일
- 확신을 조절하는 말: I wouldn’t be surprised if we worked less. (과거형으로 조심스럽게) / 강함 → 약함: will · will probably · might · It’s hard to say.
Common mistakes on screen:
- By 2040, my job will have change a lot. → By 2040, my job will have changed a lot. (will have 뒤에는 과거분사.)
- By 2040, we will has moved. → By 2040, we will have moved. (will 뒤에는 늘 have.)
- I wouldn’t be surprise if it happened. → I wouldn’t be surprised if it happened. (놀란 상태는 surprised.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 미래완료 will have + 과거분사: By 2040, my job will have changed. 2040년쯤이면 제 일은 바뀌어 있을 거예요. by + 미래 시점 = 그때쯤이면 이미 끝나 있을 일
확신을 조절하는 말: I wouldn’t be surprised if we worked less. (과거형으로 조심스럽게) 강함 → 약함: will · will probably · might · It’s hard to say.
mistakes: By 2040, my job will have change a lot. → By 2040, my job will have changed a lot.
By 2040, we will has moved. → By 2040, we will have moved.
I wouldn’t be surprise if it happened. → I wouldn’t be surprised if it happened.

steps.note: 예) my phone / become obsolete → By 2040, my phone will have become obsolete.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) my phone / become obsolete → By 2040, my phone will have become obsolete. Items (situation → model answer): my phone → become obsolete | our city → change a lot | buses → go electric | I → learn new skills.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: It’s hard to say for sure.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "A Day in 2040" (2040년의 하루); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "By 2040, ___ will have ___." / "I wouldn’t be surprised if ___." / "It’s hard to say for sure.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Commuting might be a thing of the past.
The pace of change is staggering.
Some things will stay the same.
People said the same thing about ___.
I doubt it will happen that fast.
We tend to overestimate the short term.
우리는 가까운 미래의 변화를 크게 보곤 해요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 바뀔 것: "Commuting might be a thing of the past." (통근은 옛일이 될지도 몰라요., 보통); "We’ll probably work fewer hours." (아마 일하는 시간이 줄 거예요., 보통); "The pace of change is staggering." (변화 속도가 엄청나요., 보통)
- 조심스럽게: "Some things will stay the same." (그대로인 것도 있을 거예요., 보통); "People said the same thing about ___." (~를 두고도 사람들이 똑같은 말을 했어요., 보통); "I doubt it will happen that fast." (그렇게 빨리 일어날지는 의문이에요., 보통); "We tend to overestimate the short term." (우리는 가까운 미래의 변화를 크게 보곤 해요., 보통)
- 맺는 말: "Mark my words." (두고 보세요., 친근); "Only time will tell." (시간이 지나 봐야 알아요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 미래를 말하는 낱말

a *plausible* *scenario* 그럴듯한 시나리오 · *speculate* about ~을 추측하다 
*emerging* tech 새로 떠오르는 기술 · on the *horizon* 곧 다가올 
*longevity* 장수, 오래 삶
(참고) 예측은 의견이에요

미래 예측에는 정답이 없어요. 사람마다 생각이 달라요. 
대니얼 연구실의 워크숍은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
steps.blank:
A: By 2040, our city ___ have changed a lot.   B: I wouldn’t be ___ if cars left small streets. 
A: Really? It’s hard to say for ___.   B: Well, only time will ___. 
낱말 상자: will · surprised · sure · tell
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 미래를 말하는 낱말: a plausible scenario 그럴듯한 시나리오 · speculate about ~을 추측하다 / emerging tech 새로 떠오르는 기술 · on the horizon 곧 다가올 / longevity 장수, 오래 삶
- (참고) 예측은 의견이에요: 미래 예측에는 정답이 없어요. 사람마다 생각이 달라요. / 대니얼 연구실의 워크숍은 수업을 위해 지어낸 이야기예요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: By 2040, our city ___ have changed a lot. B: I wouldn’t be ___ if cars left small streets. / A: Really? It’s hard to say for ___. B: Well, only time will ___. / 낱말 상자: will · surprised · sure · tell
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: virtual (가상의(컴퓨터 속의)), obsolete (더는 쓰이지 않는, 구식이 된), horizon (지평선, 수평선), longevity (장수, 오래 삶), transform (완전히 바꾸다, 탈바꿈시키다), emerging (새로 떠오르는), scenario ((일어날 수 있는) 상황, 시나리오), speculate ((근거가 적은 채) 추측하다), staggering (믿기 어려울 만큼 엄청난), overestimate (실제보다 크게 보다, 과대평가하다), underestimate (실제보다 작게 보다, 과소평가하다), plausible (그럴듯한, 있을 법한).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: The pace of change is staggering.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: transformation (탈바꿈, 완전한 변화) — "the transformation of our city"; forecast (예측, 예보; 예측하다) — "a weather forecast"; remote (원격의; 멀리 떨어진) — "remote work"; pace (속도) — "The pace of change is staggering."; commute (통근(하다)) — "My commute takes thirty minutes."; workshop (워크숍(함께 배우고 생각하는 모임)) — "a workshop on future cities"; self-driving (자율 주행의) — "a self-driving bus"; prediction (예측) — "a bold prediction".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What will your daily life look like in 2040?
What wouldn’t surprise you in the next ten years?
What do you think will stay the same?
Some things will stay the same, like ___.
What’s something that might become obsolete?
___ might become obsolete. / It’s hard to say for sure.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What will your daily life look like in 2040?" (hint on screen: By 2040, I think ___ will have ___.)
- "What wouldn’t surprise you in the next ten years?" (hint on screen: I wouldn’t be surprised if ___.)
- "What do you think will stay the same?" (hint on screen: Some things will stay the same, like ___.)
- "What’s something that might become obsolete?" (hint on screen: ___ might become obsolete. / It’s hard to say for sure.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Letters to 2040
steps.text: At the end of the evening, Daniel handed out small cards. “At the workshop, we asked people to write a note to their 2040 selves,” he said. “Let’s do the same.” Work on a new bike lane was already *under way* near Jiwoo’s office, so she wrote, “By 2040, our street will have become car-free. I hope you walk to work.” Ben wrote that teachers would still be needed, “because robots can’t laugh at my jokes.” Maya started writing *straight away*, but Grace took a long time. “It’s hard to imagine the future when the present moves this fast,” she said. Daniel collected the cards in an envelope and promised to keep *the whole thing* safe. “We’ll open it together in 2040,” he said. Chloe laughed. “By then, you’ll have lost it.”
steps.gloss: selves (self의 복수) 자신들 · under way 진행 중인 · bike lane 자전거 도로 · car-free 차가 다니지 않는 · straight away 곧바로 · the whole thing 그 모든 것, 전부 · envelope 봉투
questions: What was under way near Jiwoo’s office?
What did Daniel promise to do with the cards?

Reading on screen: "Letters to 2040". Text: "At the end of the evening, Daniel handed out small cards. “At the workshop, we asked people to write a note to their 2040 selves,” he said. “Let’s do the same.” Work on a new bike lane was already under way near Jiwoo’s office, so she wrote, “By 2040, our street will have become car-free. I hope you walk to work.” Ben wrote that teachers would still be needed, “because robots can’t laugh at my jokes.” Maya started writing straight away, but Grace took a long time. “It’s hard to imagine the future when the present moves this fast,” she said. Daniel collected the cards in an envelope and promised to keep the whole thing safe. “We’ll open it together in 2040,” he said. Chloe laughed. “By then, you’ll have lost it.”" Words: selves (self의 복수) 자신들 · under way 진행 중인 · bike lane 자전거 도로 · car-free 차가 다니지 않는 · straight away 곧바로 · the whole thing 그 모든 것, 전부 · envelope 봉투.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was under way near Jiwoo’s office?" / "What did Daniel promise to do with the cards?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘By 2040, ___ will have ___.’로 미래에 끝나 있을 변화를 예측할 수 있어요.
‘I wouldn’t be surprised if ___.’로 그럴 법한 일을 조심스럽게 예측할 수 있어요.
‘It’s hard to say for sure.’로 예측의 확신을 낮출 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘By 2040, ___ will have ___.’로 미래에 끝나 있을 변화를 예측할 수 있어요.
- ‘I wouldn’t be surprised if ___.’로 그럴 법한 일을 조심스럽게 예측할 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s hard to say for sure.’로 예측의 확신을 낮출 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 고기 덜 먹기
steps.title_en: It doesn’t have to be all or nothing.
steps.goal: 개인 선택과 사회 책임을 나눠 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 3층 벤의 집 부엌. 앞치마를 두른 벤이 큰 냄비의 채소 칠리를 국자로 떠 지우에게 맛보게 하고, 지우는 두부 샐러드 그릇을 든 채 놀란 얼굴로 맛을 봄. 식탁에는 여섯 사람 몫의 그릇과 옥수수빵, 거실 쪽에서 친구들이 웃으며 이야기 중(글자·상표 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It doesn’t have to be all or nothing." (고기 덜 먹기). Goal: 개인 선택과 사회 책임을 나눠 말하기. Today's scene: 10월 첫 토요일 저녁, 3층 벤의 집 부엌. 앞치마를 두른 벤이 큰 냄비의 채소 칠리를 국자로 떠 지우에게 맛보게 하고, 지우는 두부 샐러드 그릇을 든 채 놀란 얼굴로 맛을 봄. 식탁에는 여섯 사람 몫의 그릇과 옥수수빵, 거실 쪽에서 친구들이 웃으며 이야기 중(글자·상표 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "It’s not up to ___ to ___.".

steps.when: 누가 정하거나 책임질 일인지 선을 그어요. *up to + 사람* = 그 사람이 정할 일.

steps.teach:

lines.en: Here, taste this. Vegetable chili with beans. No meat tonight.
lines.ko: 자, 맛 좀 봐요. 콩을 넣은 채소 칠리예요. 오늘 밤은 고기가 없어요.

lines.en: Wow, I honestly {{can’t tell}}. Since when do you cook without meat?
lines.ko: 와, 솔직히 전혀 모르겠어요. 언제부터 고기 없이 요리했어요?

lines.en: Since summer. I skip meat three days a week. I’m a flexitarian, a fancy word for “I still love a good burger.”
lines.ko: 여름부터요. 일주일에 사흘은 고기를 빼요. ‘버거는 아직 좋아함’의 멋진 말, 플렉시테리언이죠.

lines.en: Ha! So what made you start?
lines.ko: 하하! 그럼 왜 시작했어요?

lines.en: Mostly the environment. {{There’s growing evidence that}} meat, especially beef, has a much bigger footprint than plant-based food.
lines.ko: 주로 환경 때문이에요. 고기, 특히 소고기가 식물성 음식보다 환경 발자국이 훨씬 크다는 근거가 점점 늘고 있어요.

lines.en: I’ve heard that. But {{it’s not up to}} individuals {{to}} fix the whole food system. Big farms and companies have a much bigger impact than my lunch.
lines.ko: 들어 봤어요. 그래도 식품 시스템을 다 고치는 건 개인 몫이 아니에요. 큰 농장·회사 영향이 훨씬 크죠.

lines.en: Fair point. And it’s not up to me to tell anyone what to eat. That usually backfires.
lines.ko: 일리 있어요. 그리고 남한테 뭘 먹으라고 하는 건 제 몫이 아니에요. 그러면 대개 역효과가 나요.

lines.en: Also, near my hometown, many families do agricultural work, raising livestock or growing crops. And on holidays, my family always grills meat together.
lines.ko: 제 고향 근처엔 가축이나 농작물을 키우는 농가가 많아요. 명절엔 우리 가족도 늘 고기를 구워요.

lines.ko: 맞아요. 문화가 큰 역할을 하죠. 그래도 전부 아니면 전무일 필요는 없어요. 조금만 줄여도 쌓여요.

lines.ko: 맞아요. 그래도 가격이 큰 문제예요. 우리 동네 가게에서는 식물성 버거가 소고기 버거보다 비싸요.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: It’s not up to ___ to ___. / There’s growing evidence that ___. Table (It’s not up to … → to …):
- me → tell people what to eat.
- one person → fix the whole system.
- restaurants → decide for customers.
- farmers alone → solve the problem.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.

items:
It’s *up to* you. 당신이 정할 일이에요. 
It’s *not up to* me *to* decide. 제가 정할 일이 아니에요. 
*It’s up to* all of us. 모두의 몫이에요.

*Even cutting back* a little helps. -ing 덩어리가 주어 → *helps* 
There’s *growing evidence that* … evidence는 셀 수 없어요.
errors: It’s not up to me decide.
It’s not up to me to decide.
Even cut back a little helps.
Even cutting back a little helps.
There’s growing evidences that it helps.
There’s growing evidence that it helps.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- It’s (not) up to + 사람 + to ~: It’s up to you. 당신이 정할 일이에요. / It’s not up to me to decide. 제가 정할 일이 아니에요. / It’s up to all of us. 모두의 몫이에요.
- Even + -ing · growing evidence: Even cutting back a little helps. -ing 덩어리가 주어 → helps / There’s growing evidence that … evidence는 셀 수 없어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s not up to me decide. → It’s not up to me to decide. (사람 뒤에 to + 동사원형.)
- Even cut back a little helps. → Even cutting back a little helps. (주어 자리에는 -ing.)
- There’s growing evidences that it helps. → There’s growing evidence that it helps. (evidence는 셀 수 없어요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: It’s (not) up to + 사람 + to ~: It’s up to you. 당신이 정할 일이에요. It’s not up to me to decide. 제가 정할 일이 아니에요. It’s up to all of us. 모두의 몫이에요.
Even + -ing · growing evidence: Even cutting back a little helps. -ing 덩어리가 주어 → helps There’s growing evidence that … evidence는 셀 수 없어요.

Even cut back a little helps. → Even cutting back a little helps.
There’s growing evidences that it helps. → There’s growing evidence that it helps.

steps.note: 예) me / tell people what to eat → It’s not up to me to tell people what to eat.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) me / tell people what to eat → It’s not up to me to tell people what to eat. Items (situation → model answer): me → tell people what to eat | one person → fix the whole system | schools alone → plan every meal | restaurants → decide for customers.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "It doesn’t have to be all or nothing." (고기 덜 먹기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "It’s not up to ___ to ___." / "There’s growing evidence that ___." / "Even cutting back a little ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Meat production has a huge footprint.
Telling people what to eat backfires.
It doesn’t have to be all or nothing.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 환경과 새로운 선택지: "Meat production has a huge footprint." (고기 생산은 환경 발자국이 커요., 보통); "Plant-based options are getting better." (식물성 제품이 점점 나아지고 있어요., 보통); "Lab-grown meat might change things." (배양육이 판을 바꿀지도 몰라요., 보통)
- 개인의 선택: "It’s a personal choice." (개인이 선택할 일이에요., 보통); "Culture plays a big role." (문화가 큰 역할을 해요., 보통); "Price is a big factor." (가격이 큰 요인이에요., 보통); "Telling people what to eat backfires." (뭘 먹으라고 하면 역효과가 나요., 친근)
- 현실적으로 시작하기: "Meatless Mondays are a start." (‘고기 없는 월요일’부터 시작하면 돼요., 친근); "It doesn’t have to be all or nothing." (전부 아니면 전무일 필요는 없어요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 근거와 의견 구별하기

There’s growing evidence that … 확인한 연구가 같은 쪽을 가리킬 때 
I think … / In my view, … 내 생각일 때 
연구 — 약 4만 개 농장 자료를 모아 보니, 같은 양의 단백질을 얻을 때 육류(특히 소고기)가 콩·두부 같은 식물성 식품보다 온실가스 배출과 땅 사용이 훨씬 많았어요(Poore & Nemecek, 2018). 식단·건강 조언이 아니에요.
덩어리 표현

I *can’t tell*. (보거나 맛봐도) 모르겠어요, 구별이 안 돼요. 
My wallet is *better off*. 형편이 더 나아요. · You’re *better off* cooking at home. ~하는 게 나아요. 
*owing to* the price 가격 때문에(조금 격식 있는 말)
steps.blank:
A: Should everyone go vegan?   B: No. It’s not up to me ___ tell people what to eat. 
A: But there’s growing ___ that beef has a big footprint.   B: True. Even ___ back a little helps. 
낱말 상자: to · evidence · cutting
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 근거와 의견 구별하기: There’s growing evidence that … 확인한 연구가 같은 쪽을 가리킬 때 / I think … / In my view, … 내 생각일 때 / 연구 — 약 4만 개 농장 자료를 모아 보니, 같은 양의 단백질을 얻을 때 육류(특히 소고기)가 콩·두부 같은 식물성 식품보다 온실가스 배출과 땅 사용이 훨씬 많았어요(Poore & Nemecek, 2018). 식단·건강 조언이 아니에요.
- 덩어리 표현: I can’t tell. (보거나 맛봐도) 모르겠어요, 구별이 안 돼요. / My wallet is better off. 형편이 더 나아요. · You’re better off cooking at home. ~하는 게 나아요. / owing to the price 가격 때문에(조금 격식 있는 말)
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Should everyone go vegan? B: No. It’s not up to me ___ tell people what to eat. / A: But there’s growing ___ that beef has a big footprint. B: True. Even ___ back a little helps. / 낱말 상자: to · evidence · cutting
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

items.ko: 비건(동물성 식품을 전혀 먹지 않는 사람)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: plant-based (식물성의, 식물로 만든), tofu (두부), livestock (가축(소·돼지·닭처럼 기르는 동물)), protein (단백질), vegan (비건(동물성 식품을 전혀 먹지 않는 사람)), vegetarian (채식주의자(고기·생선을 먹지 않는 사람)), flexitarian (플렉시테리언(주로 채식, 가끔 고기)), cultivated ((세포를) 배양한 · cultivated meat 배양육), crop (농작물), emission ((가스 등의) 배출, 배출물), footprint ((환경) 발자국(온실가스·땅 사용 같은 환경 부담)), diet ((평소에 먹는) 식단, 식사).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Big farms have a bigger impact.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: impact ((큰) 영향) — "Big farms have a bigger impact."; moderation (적당함, 지나치지 않음) — "I eat meat in moderation."; slaughter ((고기를 얻으려고 가축을) 도살하다; 도살) — "Livestock are slaughtered for meat."; alternative (대안, 대신할 것) — "Tofu is a cheap alternative."; culture (문화) — "Food is part of culture."; choice (선택) — "It’s a personal choice."; sustainable (지속 가능한) — "a sustainable change"; consumption (소비(량)) — "our meat consumption"; ethical (윤리적인) — "ethical questions about food".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Is it up to each person to eat less meat? Why or why not?
It’s not up to ___ to ___. / I think it’s up to ___.
What’s a meal without meat that you enjoy?
I really like ___. You can’t even tell there’s no meat.
What would make it easier to cut back a little?
Even cutting back a little ___. / Price is a big factor.
What food is hard to give up in your culture?
Culture plays a big role. For example, ___.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Is it up to each person to eat less meat? Why or why not?" (hint on screen: It’s not up to ___ to ___. / I think it’s up to ___.)
- "What’s a meal without meat that you enjoy?" (hint on screen: I really like ___. You can’t even tell there’s no meat.)
- "What would make it easier to cut back a little?" (hint on screen: Even cutting back a little ___. / Price is a big factor.)
- "What food is hard to give up in your culture?" (hint on screen: Culture plays a big role. For example, ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Ben’s Meatless Night
steps.text: By eight, Ben’s pot of chili was almost empty, and nobody had missed the meat. Over dessert, the six friends kept talking. Chloe said she could never be a strict vegetarian, *owing to* her love of fried chicken. Maya said strict rules never work for her, but moderation does. Daniel was more interested in the ethical side, like how animals are raised. Grace pointed out that beans and tofu are a cheap alternative and a good source of protein. Nobody tried to change anyone’s mind. It was a personal choice, they agreed. Still, Jiwoo set herself a small goal of two meatless lunches a week. “Small changes in consumption add up,” Ben said. Then he handed her a box of leftover chili.
steps.gloss: owing to ~ 때문에 · moderation 적당함 · ethical 윤리적인 · alternative 대안 · source 공급원 · consumption 소비 · leftover 먹고 남은
questions: Why couldn’t Chloe be a strict vegetarian?
What small goal did Jiwoo set?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Ben’s Meatless Night". Text: "By eight, Ben’s pot of chili was almost empty, and nobody had missed the meat. Over dessert, the six friends kept talking. Chloe said she could never be a strict vegetarian, owing to her love of fried chicken. Maya said strict rules never work for her, but moderation does. Daniel was more interested in the ethical side, like how animals are raised. Grace pointed out that beans and tofu are a cheap alternative and a good source of protein. Nobody tried to change anyone’s mind. It was a personal choice, they agreed. Still, Jiwoo set herself a small goal of two meatless lunches a week. “Small changes in consumption add up,” Ben said. Then he handed her a box of leftover chili." Words: owing to ~ 때문에 · moderation 적당함 · ethical 윤리적인 · alternative 대안 · source 공급원 · consumption 소비 · leftover 먹고 남은.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why couldn’t Chloe be a strict vegetarian?" / "What small goal did Jiwoo set?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘It’s not up to ___ to ___.’로 누구의 몫인지 선을 그어 말할 수 있어요.
‘There’s growing evidence that ___.’로 확인된 근거를 조심스럽게 전할 수 있어요.
‘Even cutting back a little ___.’로 작은 실천의 의미를 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘It’s not up to ___ to ___.’로 누구의 몫인지 선을 그어 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘There’s growing evidence that ___.’로 확인된 근거를 조심스럽게 전할 수 있어요.
- ‘Even cutting back a little ___.’로 작은 실천의 의미를 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 살기 좋은 도시
steps.title_en: If it were up to me…
steps.scene_desc: 10월 중순 일요일 오후, 서울숲 근처 하천 산책로. 단풍이 든 나무 아래 넓은 보행로를 대니얼과 지우가 나란히 걷고, 대니얼이 손으로 벤치와 나무 줄을 가리키며 이야기함. 자전거를 탄 사람, 유모차를 미는 사람, 멀리 고층 건물 스카이라인(글자·간판 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "If it were up to me…" (살기 좋은 도시). Goal: 돋보이는 점을 말하고 바람을 말하기. Today's scene: 10월 중순 일요일 오후, 서울숲 근처 하천 산책로. 단풍이 든 나무 아래 넓은 보행로를 대니얼과 지우가 나란히 걷고, 대니얼이 손으로 벤치와 나무 줄을 가리키며 이야기함. 자전거를 탄 사람, 유모차를 미는 사람, 멀리 고층 건물 스카이라인(글자·간판 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What makes ___ stand out is ___.".

steps.when: 어떤 곳의 가장 큰 장점을 짚어요. *make + 대상 + stand out*(동사원형).
steps.extra: What makes this path stand out is the trees.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What makes ___ stand out is ___." (~가 돋보이는 건 ~ 때문이에요.). When to use it: 어떤 곳의 가장 큰 장점을 짚어요. make + 대상 + stand out(동사원형). Note: What makes this path stand out is the trees.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’d love to see more ___.".

steps.when: 바라는 변화를 부드럽게 말해요. 뒤에는 *복수 명사*나 셀 수 없는 명사.
steps.extra: I’d love to see more benches on main streets.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’d love to see more ___." (~가 더 많아지면 좋겠어요.). When to use it: 바라는 변화를 부드럽게 말해요. 뒤에는 복수 명사나 셀 수 없는 명사. Note: I’d love to see more benches on main streets.

steps.title: A Walk by the Stream · 10월 중순 일요일 오후, 서울숲 근처 산책로에서

lines.en: This is one of my favorite walks in Seoul. Trees, water, and no cars.
lines.ko: 서울에서 제일 좋아하는 산책길 중 하나예요. 나무와 물이 있고, 차는 없어요.

lines.en: It’s lovely. Is this the kind of place your thesis is about?
lines.ko: 정말 좋네요. 박사 논문이 이런 곳에 관한 거예요?

lines.en: Exactly. Walkable cities. So tell me, what makes a street great for you?
lines.ko: 맞아요. 걷기 좋은 도시요. 그럼 지우 씨는 어떤 길이 좋은 길이에요?

lines.en: {{What makes}} this path {{stand out is}} that nobody’s rushing. But my daily walk is a narrow sidewalk next to a busy road.
lines.ko: 이 길이 돋보이는 건 아무도 서두르지 않아서예요. 그런데 제가 매일 걷는 길은 큰 도로 옆 좁은 인도예요.

lines.en: That’s the problem in many cities. Cars come first, and pedestrians come second.
lines.ko: 그게 많은 도시의 문제예요. 차가 먼저고, 걷는 사람은 그다음이죠.

lines.en: I agree, up to a point. But some people really need cars, like delivery drivers or parents with small kids.
lines.ko: 어느 정도는 동의해요. 그래도 배달 기사나 어린아이 부모처럼 차가 꼭 필요한 사람도 있어요.

lines.en: Fair. So what would you change?
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그럼 뭘 바꾸고 싶어요?

lines.en: {{If it were up to me,}} I’d plant trees on every main street and make the sidewalks wider. {{I’d love to see more}} benches, too, places to stop, not just pass through.
lines.ko: 제가 정한다면 큰길마다 나무를 심고 인도를 넓히겠어요. 그냥 지나가는 곳 말고 쉬어 갈 벤치도 더 많으면 좋겠어요.

lines.en: Nice. For me, public transport makes or breaks it. Without good transit, people have to drive.
lines.ko: 좋네요. 저는 대중교통이 성패를 가른다고 봐요. 대중교통이 좋지 않으면 운전할 수밖에 없으니까요.

lines.en: True. Near my place, they promised a bike lane two years ago. Still {{no sign of}} it.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Walk by the Stream · 10월 중순 일요일 오후, 서울숲 근처 산책로에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "This is one of my favorite walks in Seoul. Trees, water, and no cars." (서울에서 제일 좋아하는 산책길 중 하나예요. 나무와 물이 있고, 차는 없어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "It’s lovely. Is this the kind of place your thesis is about?" (정말 좋네요. 박사 논문이 이런 곳에 관한 거예요?)
3. Daniel: "Exactly. Walkable cities. So tell me, what makes a street great for you?" (맞아요. 걷기 좋은 도시요. 그럼 지우 씨는 어떤 길이 좋은 길이에요?)
4. Jiwoo: "What makes this path stand out is that nobody’s rushing. But my daily walk is a narrow sidewalk next to a busy road." (이 길이 돋보이는 건 아무도 서두르지 않아서예요. 그런데 제가 매일 걷는 길은 큰 도로 옆 좁은 인도예요.)
5. Daniel: "That’s the problem in many cities. Cars come first, and pedestrians come second." (그게 많은 도시의 문제예요. 차가 먼저고, 걷는 사람은 그다음이죠.)
6. Jiwoo: "I agree, up to a point. But some people really need cars, like delivery drivers or parents with small kids." (어느 정도는 동의해요. 그래도 배달 기사나 어린아이 부모처럼 차가 꼭 필요한 사람도 있어요.)
7. Daniel: "Fair. So what would you change?" (맞아요. 그럼 뭘 바꾸고 싶어요?)
8. Jiwoo: "If it were up to me, I’d plant trees on every main street and make the sidewalks wider. I’d love to see more benches, too, places to stop, not just pass through." (제가 정한다면 큰길마다 나무를 심고 인도를 넓히겠어요. 그냥 지나가는 곳 말고 쉬어 갈 벤치도 더 많으면 좋겠어요.)
9. Daniel: "Nice. For me, public transport makes or breaks it. Without good transit, people have to drive." (좋네요. 저는 대중교통이 성패를 가른다고 봐요. 대중교통이 좋지 않으면 운전할 수밖에 없으니까요.)
10. Jiwoo: "True. Near my place, they promised a bike lane two years ago. Still no sign of it." (맞아요. 우리 집 근처에 2년 전에 자전거 도로를 만든다고 했는데, 아직 그럴 기미도 없어요.)
11. Daniel: "Can you think of a counterexample? A city that’s walkable but not livable?" (반례를 떠올릴 수 있어요? 걷기는 좋은데 살기는 좋지 않은 도시요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Maybe a pretty area that’s too expensive. If housing isn’t affordable, the people who make it vibrant move out." (예쁘지만 너무 비싼 동네요. 집값이 감당할 만하지 않으면, 동네를 활기차게 만드는 사람들이 떠나요.)
13. Daniel: "That’s chapter three of my thesis! It’s about the people, not the buildings." (그게 제 논문 3장이에요! 핵심은 건물이 아니라 사람이에요.)

frame: If it were up to me, I’d ___. I’d love to see more ___.
head: 장소
What makes it stand out is …
If it were up to me, I’d …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What makes ___ stand out is ___. / If it were up to me, I’d ___. I’d love to see more ___. Table (장소 → What makes it stand out is …):
- this path → the trees.
- my street → the small shops.
- our park → the open space.
- downtown → the old buildings.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: If it were up to me, I’d ~

*If it were up to me*, *I’d* plant more trees. (실제로는 제가 정하지 않아요.) 
if 쪽은 과거형 *were*, 뒤쪽은 *I’d(would) + 동사원형*.
What makes A stand out is B

*What makes* this street *stand out is* the trees. 이 길이 돋보이는 건 나무 덕분이에요. 
*make + 대상 + 동사원형* → stand(○) stands(×)
errors: If it were up to me, I will add benches.
If it were up to me, I’d add benches.
What makes it stands out is the trees.
What makes it stand out is the trees.
I’d love to see more bench.
I’d love to see more benches.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- If it were up to me, I’d ~: If it were up to me, I’d plant more trees. (실제로는 제가 정하지 않아요.) / if 쪽은 과거형 were, 뒤쪽은 I’d(would) + 동사원형.
- What makes A stand out is B: What makes this street stand out is the trees. 이 길이 돋보이는 건 나무 덕분이에요. / make + 대상 + 동사원형 → stand(○) stands(×)
Common mistakes on screen:
- If it were up to me, I will add benches. → If it were up to me, I’d add benches. (뒤쪽은 would(I’d).)
- What makes it stands out is the trees. → What makes it stand out is the trees. (make + 대상 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- I’d love to see more bench. → I’d love to see more benches. (셀 수 있는 명사는 복수로.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: If it were up to me, I’d ~: If it were up to me, I’d plant more trees. (실제로는 제가 정하지 않아요.) if 쪽은 과거형 were, 뒤쪽은 I’d(would) + 동사원형.
What makes A stand out is B: What makes this street stand out is the trees. 이 길이 돋보이는 건 나무 덕분이에요. make + 대상 + 동사원형 → stand(○) stands(×)
mistakes: If it were up to me, I will add benches. → If it were up to me, I’d add benches.
What makes it stands out is the trees. → What makes it stand out is the trees.
I’d love to see more bench. → I’d love to see more benches.

steps.note: 예) trees / plant one on every street → I’d love to see more trees. If it were up to me, I’d plant one on every street.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) trees / plant one on every street → I’d love to see more trees. If it were up to me, I’d plant one on every street. Items (situation → model answer): trees → plant one on every street | sidewalks → make them wider | parks → add small ones | buses → run them later.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: If it were up to me, ___.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "If it were up to me…" (살기 좋은 도시); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What makes ___ stand out is ___." / "I’d love to see more ___." / "If it were up to me, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Public transport makes or breaks it.
여러 쓰임이 섞인 동네가 더 활기차요.
Every city has its own character.
It’s about the people, not the buildings.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 좋은 도시의 조건: "A great city is walkable." (좋은 도시는 걷기 좋아요., 보통); "Public transport makes or breaks it." (대중교통이 성패를 갈라요., 보통); "Green spaces matter." (녹지가 중요해요., 보통); "Housing has to be affordable." (집값이 감당할 만해야 해요., 보통)
- 동네의 모습: "Mixed neighborhoods are more vibrant." (여러 쓰임이 섞인 동네가 더 활기차요., 보통); "Cars shouldn’t come first." (차가 우선이면 안 돼요., 보통); "Every city has its own character." (도시마다 고유한 개성이 있어요., 보통)
- 정리하기: "It’s about the people, not the buildings." (핵심은 건물이 아니라 사람이에요., 보통); "Good design is invisible." (좋은 디자인은 눈에 띄지 않아요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

items.ko: 용도 지역 나누기(주거·상업 등 땅의 쓰임 정하기)

steps.teach:
Picture words on screen. New: walkable (걷기 좋은), pedestrian (보행자, 걷는 사람), sidewalk (인도, 보도), green space (녹지(공원·숲 같은 초록 공간)), transit (대중교통), congestion ((교통) 혼잡, 정체), skyline ((높은 건물이 이루는) 하늘 윤곽, 스카이라인), architecture (건축, 건축 양식), density (밀도(얼마나 빽빽한가)), infrastructure (기반 시설(도로·다리·수도처럼 생활을 받치는 시설)), vibrant (활기찬), zoning (용도 지역 나누기(주거·상업 등 땅의 쓰임 정하기)).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

items: Every city has its own character.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: affordable ((값이) 감당할 만한, 알맞은) — "affordable housing"; livable (살기 좋은) — "a livable city"; urban (도시의) — "urban planning"; green (초록의; 나무·풀이 많은) — "a green neighborhood"; design (설계, 디자인) — "Good design is invisible."; character ((장소의) 특징, 개성) — "Every city has its own character."; planning (계획 (urban planning 도시 계획)) — "careful planning"; diversity (다양성) — "a diversity of shops".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

items: What makes your favorite street or park stand out?
What would you like to see more of in your neighborhood?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What makes your favorite street or park stand out?" (hint on screen: What makes ___ stand out is ___.)
- "What would you like to see more of in your neighborhood?" (hint on screen: I’d love to see more ___.)
- "If it were up to you, what would you change in your city?" (hint on screen: If it were up to me, I’d ___.)
- "What makes a city livable for you?" (hint on screen: For me, a livable city has ___. / It’s about ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Daniel’s Ten-Minute Test
steps.text: On the way back, Daniel explained a simple test from his thesis. Can you reach a grocery store, a park, and a bus stop within a ten-minute walk? In his view, streets that pass it usually have some density and a diversity of homes, shops, and offices. He thinks strict zoning that keeps them far apart can mean more driving and more congestion. “Urban planning isn’t only about a nice skyline or famous architecture,” he said. “It’s also about everyday infrastructure, like crossings and benches.” Just then, an older man *came up to* them and asked for the nearest subway station. It was a seven-minute walk away. Daniel smiled. “That’s a good sign.” For Jiwoo, a livable city now *stands for* small things that just work.
steps.gloss: density 밀도 · diversity 다양성 · zoning 용도 지역 나누기 · congestion 혼잡 · come up to ~에게 다가오다 · stand for ~을 뜻하다, 상징하다
questions: What three places are in Daniel’s test?
What did the older man ask for?

steps.title: 관광객 수 제한
steps.scene_desc: 10월 말 토요일 오후, 기와지붕 전통 가옥이 늘어선 오래된 동네의 좁은 골목. 관광객들이 한 집 대문 앞에 줄지어 사진을 찍고, 대니얼과 지우는 담장 옆에 비켜서서 이야기함. 대문 앞에서 비질을 하던 나이 든 주민이 손가락을 입에 대고 조용히 해 달라는 몸짓(글자·간판 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It cuts both ways." (관광객 수 제한). Goal: 진짜 쟁점을 짚고 대안을 내기. Today's scene: 10월 말 토요일 오후, 기와지붕 전통 가옥이 늘어선 오래된 동네의 좁은 골목. 관광객들이 한 집 대문 앞에 줄지어 사진을 찍고, 대니얼과 지우는 담장 옆에 비켜서서 이야기함. 대문 앞에서 비질을 하던 나이 든 주민이 손가락을 입에 대고 조용히 해 달라는 몸짓(글자·간판 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "The real issue is ___.".

steps.when: 겉으로 보이는 문제 말고 핵심을 짚어요. 뒤에는 명사나 *(that) + 문장*.
steps.extra: The real issue is the number of visitors.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "The real issue is ___." (진짜 문제는 ~예요.). When to use it: 겉으로 보이는 문제 말고 핵심을 짚어요. 뒤에는 명사나 (that) + 문장. Note: The real issue is the number of visitors.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "It cuts both ways.".

steps.when: 좋은 점과 나쁜 점이 함께 있을 때 짧게 정리해요.
steps.extra: Tourism brings money, but it brings noise, too. It cuts both ways.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "It cuts both ways." (양쪽 면이 다 있어요.). When to use it: 좋은 점과 나쁜 점이 함께 있을 때 짧게 정리해요. Note: Tourism brings money, but it brings noise, too. It cuts both ways.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Rather than ___, we could ___.".

steps.when: 한 가지 방법 대신 다른 대안을 내요. *rather than* 뒤에는 주로 *-ing*.
steps.extra: Rather than limiting visitors, we could spread them out.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Rather than ___, we could ___." (~하는 대신 ~할 수도 있어요.). When to use it: 한 가지 방법 대신 다른 대안을 내요. rather than 뒤에는 주로 -ing. Note: Rather than limiting visitors, we could spread them out.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Too Many Visitors? · 10월 말 토요일 오후, 오래된 한옥 동네 골목에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Too Many Visitors? · 10월 말 토요일 오후, 오래된 한옥 동네 골목에서

lines.en: Wow, it’s packed. When I first came here a few years ago, it was so quiet.
lines.ko: 와, 사람이 꽉 찼네요. 몇 년 전에 처음 왔을 땐 정말 조용했는데요.

lines.en: Look at that line of people taking photos at that gate. Someone actually lives there, right?
lines.ko: 저 대문 앞에 줄 서서 사진 찍는 것 좀 봐요. 저기 실제로 누가 살죠?

lines.en: Yes, these are real homes. That’s why some people want a cap on visitor numbers.
lines.ko: 네, 다 실제로 사는 집이에요. 그래서 방문객 수에 상한을 두자는 사람들도 있어요.

lines.en: I’m not sure a cap is fair. I’m {{fond of}} this place, too. Everyone wants to visit, nobody wants the crowds.
lines.ko: 상한이 공평한지는 모르겠어요. 저도 이 동네를 좋아하거든요. 다들 오고 싶어 하면서 붐비는 건 싫어하죠.

lines.en: Ha, fair. But {{the real issue is}} rent. It {{keeps on}} rising, so locals are being priced out.
lines.ko: 하하, 그렇죠. 그런데 진짜 문제는 임대료예요. 계속 올라서 주민들이 비싼 값에 밀려나고 있어요.

lines.en: On the other hand, tourism keeps the economy going. The cafés and guesthouses here depend on visitors.
lines.ko: 반면에 관광이 지역 경제를 돌아가게 하잖아요. 여기 카페랑 게스트하우스는 방문객 덕에 운영돼요.

lines.en: True. {{It cuts both ways.}}
lines.ko: 맞아요. 양쪽 면이 다 있어요.

lines.en: Excuse me, could you keep your voices down? My grandson is napping.
lines.ko: 저기요, 목소리 좀 낮춰 줄래요? 손자가 낮잠을 자고 있어서요.

lines.en: Oh, I’m so sorry. We’ll be quiet.
lines.ko: 아, 정말 죄송해요. 조용히 할게요.

lines.en: (quietly) See? It’s not the tourists, it’s the numbers.
lines.ko: (작은 목소리로) 봤죠? 관광객이 문제가 아니라 숫자가 문제예요.

lines.en: (quietly) So {{rather than}} limiting visitors, {{we could}} spread them out, with weekday events or tours of other neighborhoods.
lines.ko: (작은 목소리로) 그럼 방문객을 제한하는 대신 분산시킬 수도 있겠네요. 평일 행사나 다른 동네 투어로요.

lines.en: Spreading visitors out is smarter, I agree. Some people think a tourist tax might help, too.
lines.ko: 분산시키는 게 더 현명하다는 데 동의해요. 관광세가 도움이 될 수도 있다는 사람들도 있고요.

lines.en: Maybe, if the money goes back to residents. It’s a delicate balance.
lines.ko: 그 돈이 주민에게 돌아간다면요. 균형 잡기가 까다로운 문제예요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Too Many Visitors? · 10월 말 토요일 오후, 오래된 한옥 동네 골목에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "Wow, it’s packed. When I first came here a few years ago, it was so quiet." (와, 사람이 꽉 찼네요. 몇 년 전에 처음 왔을 땐 정말 조용했는데요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Look at that line of people taking photos at that gate. Someone actually lives there, right?" (저 대문 앞에 줄 서서 사진 찍는 것 좀 봐요. 저기 실제로 누가 살죠?)

7. Daniel: "True. It cuts both ways." (맞아요. 양쪽 면이 다 있어요.)
8. Resident: "Excuse me, could you keep your voices down? My grandson is napping." (저기요, 목소리 좀 낮춰 줄래요? 손자가 낮잠을 자고 있어서요.)
9. Jiwoo: "Oh, I’m so sorry. We’ll be quiet." (아, 정말 죄송해요. 조용히 할게요.)
10. Daniel: "(quietly) See? It’s not the tourists, it’s the numbers." ((작은 목소리로) 봤죠? 관광객이 문제가 아니라 숫자가 문제예요.)
11. Jiwoo: "(quietly) So rather than limiting visitors, we could spread them out, with weekday events or tours of other neighborhoods." ((작은 목소리로) 그럼 방문객을 제한하는 대신 분산시킬 수도 있겠네요. 평일 행사나 다른 동네 투어로요.)
12. Daniel: "Spreading visitors out is smarter, I agree. Some people think a tourist tax might help, too." (분산시키는 게 더 현명하다는 데 동의해요. 관광세가 도움이 될 수도 있다는 사람들도 있고요.)
13. Jiwoo: "Maybe, if the money goes back to residents. It’s a delicate balance." (그 돈이 주민에게 돌아간다면요. 균형 잡기가 까다로운 문제예요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

frame: The real issue is ___. It cuts both ways.
head: 문제
Rather than …
we could …
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: The real issue is ___. It cuts both ways. / Rather than ___, we could ___. Table (문제 → Rather than …):
- crowds on weekends → limiting visitors,
- noise at night → closing the area,
- rising rents → blaming tourists,
- long lines → banning photos,
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*Rather than* limit*ing* visitors, we could spread them out. 방문객을 제한하는 대신 분산시킬 수 있어요. 
Let’s take the bus *rather than* drive. (두 동사의 모양을 맞춰도 돼요)

*The real issue is* rent. (+ 명사) 
*The real issue is that* locals are leaving. (+ that + 문장)
errors: The real issue are the crowds.
The real issue is the crowds.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Rather than + -ing: Rather than limiting visitors, we could spread them out. 방문객을 제한하는 대신 분산시킬 수 있어요. / Let’s take the bus rather than drive. (두 동사의 모양을 맞춰도 돼요)
- The real issue is …: The real issue is rent. (+ 명사) / The real issue is that locals are leaving. (+ that + 문장)
Common mistakes on screen:
- The real issue are the crowds. → The real issue is the crowds. (주어가 issue(하나)라서 is.)
- Locals are being price out. → Locals are being priced out. (be being + 과거분사(priced).)
- It cuts both way. → It cuts both ways. (both 뒤에는 복수 ways.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) limiting visitors / spread them out → Rather than limiting visitors, we could spread them out. Items (situation → model answer): limiting visitors → spread them out | closing the street → set quiet hours | adding parking → run more buses | building hotels → use empty houses.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "It cuts both ways." (관광객 수 제한); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "The real issue is ___." / "It cuts both ways." / "Rather than ___, we could ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):

items: Have you been to a place with too many tourists? What was the real issue?

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Have you been to a place with too many tourists? What was the real issue?" (hint on screen: The real issue was ___.)
- "Is tourism good or bad for a neighborhood?" (hint on screen: It cuts both ways. On one hand, ___. On the other hand, ___.)
- "Should popular places put a cap on visitors?" (hint on screen: Rather than ___, we could ___.)
- "How do you like to visit a popular place?" (hint on screen: I usually go ___ rather than ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: A Quieter Visit
steps.text: On the way home, Daniel admitted that *at the outset* he had wanted a strict cap. “Now I’m not so sure,” he said. “Overtourism is real, but a cap could hurt small shops.” Jiwoo pointed out that the problem is partly seasonal. In spring and autumn, the alleys are packed, but in winter they’re almost empty. Rather than cutting visitor numbers, she said, the goal could be to spread them out over the year. In Daniel’s view, tourism revenue should help preserve the heritage houses and fix old infrastructure, like narrow roads and pipes. He added that in some port cities, people feel cruise ships bring too many visitors at once. Jiwoo was still fond of the neighborhood. She just wanted a more sustainable way to visit, on a quiet weekday morning.
steps.gloss: at the outset 처음에 · overtourism 과잉 관광 · seasonal 계절에 따른 · revenue 수입 · preserve 보존하다 · heritage 유산

He added that in some port cities, people feel cruise ships bring too many visitors at once. Jiwoo was still fond of the neighborhood. She just wanted a more sustainable way to visit, on a quiet weekday morning." Words: at the outset 처음에 · overtourism 과잉 관광 · seasonal 계절에 따른 · revenue 수입 · preserve 보존하다 · heritage 유산.

React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "In the grand scheme of things" (우주 탐사). Goal: 큰 투자를 정당화하거나 반박하기. Today's scene: 11월 첫 토요일 밤, 저녁 모임 1주년을 맞아 그레이스·지우가 사는 아파트 옥상. 담요를 두른 마야와 지우가 난간 옆에 서서 밤하늘을 올려다보고, 마야가 별 사이를 지나가는 작은 불빛을 손가락으로 가리킴. 뒤쪽 돗자리에 그레이스·벤·클로이·대니얼이 케이크와 따뜻한 차를 두고 앉아 있음. 도시 불빛 위로 별 몇 개(글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Some would say it’s a waste of ___.".

steps.en: Some would say it’s a waste of ___.
